->### **Bible. Greek. Codex Alexandrinus.**<-

**Facsimile of the Codex Alexandrinus.** London: British Museum, 1879-83. <term>Folio extra</term> <note>A term for a very large book size, typically exceeding 15 inches in height.</note>. 4 volumes.

The best facsimile of this famous and extraordinarily important early 5th-century manuscript of the Greek Bible. Produced in an <term>autotype facsimile</term> <note>An early photographic printing process used in the late 19th century to create high-quality, permanent reproductions of documents.</note>, i.e., a photographic process, to full size. The volumes are:

*   **I**, Genesis–2 Chronicles; 
*   **II**, Hosea–4 Maccabees; 
*   **III**, Psalms–Ecclesiasticus <note>Also known as the Wisdom of Sirach.</note>;
*   **IV**, New Testament and Clementine epistles <note>Early Christian writings formerly attributed to Pope Clement I, which were included in some ancient versions of the New Testament.</note>. 

Issued unbound, as folded sheets in <term>portfolios</term> <note>Cases for holding loose papers.</note>, here in recent acid-free, <term>quarter calf clamshell cases</term> <note>A protective box where the spine is covered in calf leather and the rest in cloth or paper, designed to open like a clam.</note>. A few <term>blind stamps</term> <note>Impression marks made without ink or foil, usually indicating library ownership.</note>, a library bookplate in each case, else very good condition.

--- Page 5 ---
<meta>Continuity note: This page follows the archival shelfmark page (23360). It transitions from cataloging data to the formal historical introduction of the Codex Alexandrinus facsimile edition published by the British Museum.</meta>

The publication of an autotype facsimile <note>A high-quality photographic reproduction that looks like the original.</note> of the <term>Codex Alexandrinus</term> <note>One of the three oldest and most complete manuscripts of the Greek Bible, dating to the 5th century.</note> was three years ago authorized by the Trustees of the British Museum from a desire to place the text within the reach of scholars in a form free from the errors of the printing press and untouched by the hand.

The fourth volume, containing the New Testament and <term>Clementine Epistles</term> <note>Letters attributed to Pope Clement I, early Christian writings not included in the modern Bible.</note>, was the first to be issued, in 1879, for reasons then stated in the preface. But the general description of the MS. <note>Manuscript.</note>, which is now given, has been appropriately reserved to accompany the present first volume. The second and third volumes will follow and complete the work.

The <term>Codex Alexandrinus</term> contains the Bible, in Greek, written in the middle of the fifth century. At the end originally followed the Epistles of St. Clement of Rome to the Corinthians and the <term>Psalms of Solomon</term> <note>A group of eighteen Jewish psalms written in the 1st or 2nd century BCE, not actually by King Solomon.</note>; but only portions of the former remain, and the latter are entirely lost.

The MS. forms part of the Old Royal Library which was incorporated with the early collections of the British Museum in the year 1757. It is bound in four volumes bearing the press-marks 1 D. v to 1 D. viii. On the covers are stamped the arms of king Charles the First.

The title which has been given to this MS. is derived from the fact of its having been dedicated to the Patriarchal Chamber at Alexandria, as recorded in a note written by Athanasius the Patriarch, in Arabic, at the foot of the first page of Genesis, vol. i. f. 5 (1): 

> “Made an inalienable gift to the Patriarchal cell in the city of Alexandria. Whosoever shall remove it thence shall be accursed and cut off. Written by Athanasius the humble.” 

The writer was probably Athanasius III., the <term>Melchite Patriarch</term> <note>The leader of the Greek Orthodox Church in Alexandria.</note>, who succeeded in the latter part of the 13th century, and who was still living in the year 1308. On a fly-leaf at the beginning of vol. i. is a note in a hand of the latter part of the 17th century: 

> “Gift given to the Patriarchal chamber in the year 814 of the Martyrs,” <note>original: "Donum datum cubiculo Patriarchali anno 814 Martyrum". The 'Year of the Martyrs' refers to the Coptic Era, starting in 284 AD.</note> 

to which is added, in pencil, “+ A.D. 284 = 1098.” But for this date of gift there is no authority whatever in any part of the MS.

Another note in Arabic, of the 13th or 14th century, is written on the back of the Table of Books, to which a Latin translation is added in the hand of Dr. Richard Bentley, who held the office of Royal Librarian from 1693 to 1724: 

> “They record that this book was written by the hand of Thecla the Martyr.” <note>original: "Memorant hunc librum scriptum fuisse manu Theclæ Martyris"</note> 

The tradition that the MS. was written by the martyr <term>Thecla</term> <note>A legendary saint of the early church and follower of the Apostle Paul.</note> is repeated in a statement, prefixed to the first volume,

<summary>This preface describes the 19th-century publication of a photographic facsimile of the Codex Alexandrinus, detailing its history, contents, and its journey from Alexandria to the British Museum's Royal Library.</summary>
<keywords>Codex Alexandrinus, British Museum, New Testament, Clementine Epistles, Athanasius III, Richard Bentley, Saint Thecla, Biblical manuscripts, facsimile edition</keywords>

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>Continuity note: This page continues the introduction to the Codex Alexandrinus facsimile, moving from the manuscript's general description to its specific history of ownership and physical condition.</meta>

by its former owner, Cyril Lucar, Patriarch of Constantinople, where he assumes that the name of Thecla was originally written at the end of the work.

As an explanation of this tradition, Tregelles <note>Samuel Prideaux Tregelles (1813–1875), an influential English biblical scholar.</note> has suggested that the Arabic inscription was mistakenly added by someone who had seen the name of **Thecla** written in the now damaged upper margin of the first leaf of the New Testament. This leaf begins with Matthew 25:6, and the name would have been an indication of the Lesson <note>A specific passage of scripture assigned to be read on a particular day.</note> (Matthew 25:1-13) appointed by the Greek Church for the festival of **St. Thecla**. (See F. H. Scrivener, *Plain Introduction to the Criticism of the New Testament*, 2nd edition, 1874, page 93). 

However, this theory assumes that in the 14th century, the Gospel of Matthew was already in its current incomplete state, and that the New Testament was a separate volume from the Old Testament, as it is today. Yet the Arabic numbering of the leaves—which is roughly the same age as the inscription—continues through both Testaments. By calculating the numbers that were not cut away when the edges were trimmed, it appears that twenty-five leaves containing most of St. Matthew were lost at a later date. The last leaf of the Old Testament was numbered 641, and the current first leaf of the New Testament is 667.

There is little doubt that Cyril Lucar removed the manuscript from Alexandria. He had served as patriarch there before his promotion to Constantinople in 1621. This is despite the claim by Wetstein in the *New Testament in Greek* <note>original: "Nov. Test. Græc.", Amsterdam, 1751-2, vol. i., prolegomena p. 10</note>, who cites Cyril’s deacon, Matthew Muttis, as saying he obtained it from **Mount Athos** <note>A famous center of Orthodox monasticism in Greece.</note>.

Cyril first presented the manuscript to King James I of England through Sir Thomas Roe, the English ambassador at Constantinople, but he did not manage to get it to the ambassador until after the king’s death. Sir Thomas Roe announced he had the manuscript in his letter to George Abbot, Archbishop of Canterbury, dated February 17/27, 1626/7 (see *Negotiations of Sir Thomas Roe*, London, 1740, page 618), in which he states that the Patriarch is now presenting it to King **Charles I**.

The manuscript is written on <term>vellum</term> <note>A high-quality writing surface made from specially prepared animal skin.</note>, generally of fine texture, and consists of 773 leaves and 6 modern <term>fly-leaves</term> <note>Blank pages at the very beginning or end of a book.</note>, measuring 12 5/8 by 10 inches. 
- **Volume 1** has 279 leaves, including three fly-leaves.
- **Volume 2** has 238 leaves, including one fly-leaf.
- **Volume 3** has 118 leaves, including one fly-leaf.
- **Volume 4** has 144 leaves, including one fly-leaf.

The leaves are numbered with Arabic numerals from the 14th century in the lower corners of the <term>verso</term> <note>The back side of a leaf; the left-hand page when a book is open.</note> sides. They were later re-numbered by Patrick Young, librarian to Charles I, with separate numbering for each Testament. The New Testament begins with the number 26 to account for the loss of the first 25 leaves.* The pages have generally suffered some damage, particularly at the top.

---

\* In volume 2, due to an error in Young’s numbering, page 470 immediately follows page 460.

In the Table of Books the Clementine Epistles <note>Two early Christian letters attributed to Pope Clement I, which were highly regarded but eventually not included in the standard New Testament canon.</note> are included among the canonical works; and, after an interval, is separately added the title of the Psalms of Solomon, which are now lost.

The Psalter and following books of the Old Testament are written <term>stichometrically</term> <note>original Greek: *stichērōs* (στιχηρῶς); this means the text is laid out in lines that correspond to the rhythm or sense of the poetry, rather than in continuous prose blocks.</note>.

The names of the several Books are written as superscriptions <note>titles at the beginning</note> and colophons <note>notes at the end of a book providing administrative details or a formal conclusion</note>. In a few instances the former have been cut away by the binder. In the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> and in Deuteronomy, Joshua, 3 and 4 Kings, and Isaiah, some of the numbers of sections are written in the margin by the first hand. The Psalms are also numbered. The Gospels are marked with the Ammonian sections and Eusebian canons <note>An early system of cross-referencing similar passages across the four Gospels</note>; and are also divided into <term>chapters</term> <note>original Greek: *kephalaia* (κεφάλαια)</note> by the paragraph marks noticed below, with the addition of the numbers in red in Saints Luke and John. The <term>titles</term> <note>original Greek: *titloi* (τίτλοι)</note> were written in red in the upper margins, but have been, in most instances, cut away by the binder. A few references to Lessons <note>portions of scripture designated to be read during church services</note> have been added in the margin by a hand of the 16th century.

The modern numeration of chapters, in Greek numerals in Genesis and in Arabic numerals elsewhere, is in the hand of Patrick Young <note>A 17th-century scholar and librarian to King James I and King Charles I, who was the first to study the codex in England</note>.

The following leaves are lost:—

Vol. i. One leaf after folio 171 (167); from 1 Kings xii. 19, **FOR THEMSELVES A KING ——** <note>original Greek: ΕΑΥΤΟΙC ΒΑCΙ ——</note>, to xiv. 9, **AND BY NO MEANS** <note>original Greek: ΚΑΙ ΟΥ ΜΗ</note>.

Vol. iii. Nine leaves after folio 25 (546); containing Psalms xlix. 19—lxxix. 10.

Vol. iv. Twenty-five leaves at the beginning; containing the table of <term>chapters</term> <note>original Greek: *kephalaia*</note> to St. Matthew, and Matthew i.—xxv. 6, to **GO OUT TO MEET HIM** <note>original Greek: ΕΞΕΡΧΕCΘΕ ΕΙC ΑΠΑΝΤΗCΙΝ ΑΥΤΟΥ</note>.

Two leaves after folio 46 (70); from John vi. 50, **THE ONE COMING DOWN OUT OF HEAVEN** <note>original Greek: Ο ΕΚ ΤΟΥ ΟΥΡΑΝΟΥ ΚΑΤΑΒΑΙΝΩΝ</note>, to viii. 52, **[you] say, IF ANYONE KEEPS MY WORD** <note>original Greek: [λεγ]ειϲ ΕΑΝ ΤΙC ΤΟΝ ΛΟΓΟΝ ΜΟΥ ΤΗΡΗCΗ</note>.

Three leaves after folio 100 (126); from 2 Corinthians iv. 13, **ACCORDING TO WHAT IS WRITTE—** <note>original Greek: ΚΑΤΑ ΤΟ ΓΕΓΡΑΜΜΕ—</note>, to xii. 6.

All these <term>gaps</term> <note>original Latin: *lacunæ*</note> are noted in the manuscript by Patrick Young.

In addition, one leaf, which contained a portion of the first Clementine Epistle, is lost after folio 142 (167) of vol. iv.; and the latter part, or about two-fifths, of the second Clementine Epistle, which was probably contained in two leaves, is wanting, together with the Psalms of Solomon, at the end of the manuscript.

The lower part of vol. i. folio 12 (8) is mutilated, whereby the text in Genesis xiv. 14—17, xv. 1—5, 16—19, xvi. 6—9, is lost. The following leaves are also torn: vol. i. folios 4, 5 (1), 67 (63), vol. iii. folio 118 (639). The ornamental colophon of the Epistle

<meta>This page continues the technical description of the physical state of the Codex Alexandrinus, specifically detailing damage to the leaves and the history of its publication and scholarly study by various editors since the 17th century.</meta>

<page-num>( 7 )</page-num>

to Philemon has been cut out; and, as already noticed, many of the leaves, particularly those at the end of the manuscript, have been injured on the inner margins.

In volume two, at the foot of folio 142b (417b), is a note, which appears to be written in Greek cursive characters, perhaps of the 9th century; and in volume three, at the foot of folio 83b (604b), is another note, also in Greek cursive characters, of rather later date, which has been repeated in the margin of the next page, but is there partially cut away.

In addition to the various <term>collations</term> <note>A collation is a detailed line-by-line comparison of different manuscript copies to identify variations in the text.</note> from this manuscript which have been printed in the editions of the Scriptures by Walton, Mills, Wetstein, and others, the following editions of different portions of the text itself have been issued:—

In 1633, Patrick Young edited the first Epistle of Clement, with a Latin translation, under the title *The First Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians* <note>original Latin: *Clementis ad Corinthios epistola prior*</note>, Oxford, small quarto; and appended to it the text of the fragments of the second Epistle. In 1637 he printed the Book of Job at the end of his *Chain of Greek Fathers on the Blessed Job* <note>original Latin: *Catena Græcorum Patrum in Beatum Job*</note>, London, folio. His copies of other books of the Old Testament, with collations, are extant in Harley manuscript 7522.

Archbishop Ussher printed the text of chapters six and eighteen of the Book of Judges in his *Treatise on the Greek Septuagint Version of the Interpreters* <note>original Latin: *De Græcâ Septuaginta Interpretum versione Syntagma*</note>, London, 1655, small quarto.

In 1678, Thomas Gale printed the Psalter "according to the Alexandrian Copy" <note>original Latin: *juxta Exemplar Alexandrinum*</note>, Oxford, small octavo; with a Latin version.

Johann Ernst Grabe adopted this text for his edition of the Septuagint <note>The earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Old Testament.</note>, in four volumes, Oxford, 1707—1720, folio.

In 1786, Charles Godfrey Woide, Librarian in the British Museum, published by subscription the New Testament (not including the Clementine Epistles) in facsimile type <note>A specialized typeface designed to look like the handwriting in the original manuscript.</note>, London, folio.*

In 1812, Henry Hervey Baber, Librarian in the British Museum, published the Psalter, London, folio; and in 1816—1821, at the cost of the nation, the Old Testament, in three volumes, folio; both works being printed in facsimile type.

In 1856, the leaves containing the Clementine Epistles were photographed by order of the Trustees of the British Museum. Among the various editions of the Clementine Epistles, subsequent to that of Patrick Young, the latest are those of Dr. Constantine Tischendorf, Leipzig, 1873, quarto, and Dr. J. B. Lightfoot (Bishop of Durham), London and Cambridge, 1869, octavo. The latter of these is supplemented by an Appendix, London, 1877, which contains the newly-recovered portions of the Epistles, as found in a manuscript at Constantinople and edited by Philotheos Bryennios, Metropolitan of Serrae, in 1875.

---

\* A revised edition of Woide's text was published by B. H. Cowper, London, 1860, octavo.

<meta>This page continues the technical description of the Codex Alexandrinus, moving from the history of its collation and publication to a physical analysis of its structure, specifically the "quires" (gatherings of pages) and the markings used by early scribes and later binders.</meta>

### ( 8 )

The <term>quires</term> <note>A quire is a gathering of parchment sheets folded together. Most in this manuscript consist of eight leaves (sixteen pages).</note> are composed of eight leaves, with the following exceptions:—
Volume 1: quire 19 <note>original Greek: ιq</note> = 4 leaves, folios 125–129 (121–124); quire 21 <note>original: ικα</note> = 4, folios 161–164 (157–160); quire 22 <note>original: ικβ</note> = 7 (one leaf lost), folios 165–171 (161–167); quire 29 <note>original: ικq</note> = 6, folios 196–201 (193–198); quire 32 <note>original: λβ</note> = 2, folios 242, 243 (239, 240); quire 37 <note>original: λζ</note> (the last quire) = 4, folios 276–279 (273–276);—Volume 2: quire 51 <note>original: να</note> = 7, folios 106–112 (381–387); quire 55 <note>original: νε</note> = 6, folios 137–142 (412–417); quire 58 <note>original: νη</note> = 4, folios 159–162 (434–437); quire 61 <note>original: ξα</note> = 7, folios 179–185 (452–460); quire 69 <note>original: ξq</note> = 7, folios 218–224 (502–508); quire 78 <note>original: ζη</note> (the last quire) = 6, folios 233–238 (517–522);—Volume 3: quire 72 <note>original: οβ</note>, missing; quire 73 <note>original: ογ</note> = 7 (the first leaf lost), folios 26–32 (547–553); quire 81 <note>original: ττα</note> (the last quire) = 6, folios 113–118 (634–639);—Volume 4: quires 85–87 <note>original: ττε–ττζ</note>, missing; quire 88 <note>original: ττη</note> = 7 (the first leaf lost), folios 2–8 (26–32); quire 90 <note>original: q</note> = 11, folios 17–27 (41–51); quire 91 <note>original: qr</note> = 6 (two leaves lost), folios 44–49 (68–70, 73–75, the missing leaves being allowed for in the numbering); quire 99 <note>original: qq</note> = 6, folios 66–71 (92–97); quire 100 <note>original: p</note> = 5 (three leaves lost), folios 96–100 (122–126); quire 109 <note>original: pq</note> (the last quire) = 3, folios 142–144 (167–169). In most cases, the end of a quire containing fewer than eight leaves matches the end of a Biblical Book.

When the manuscript was re-bound in the present <note>that is, the 19th</note> century, the original formation of the quires was ignored; the leaves were separated, given new paper supports at the spine, and grouped into sets of six.*

The original quires are marked with <term>signatures</term> <note>A signature is a letter or number written on the first or last page of a quire to guide the binder.</note> at the top of the first page. The first few signatures, 1 through 5 <note>original Greek: α–ε</note> (of which '1' has been touched up), are possibly written by a hand contemporary with the main text; the rest are certainly of a later date, and in the final volumes, they are quite modern. Some of these marks have been lost because the edges of the leaves were trimmed <note>often called "shearing" or "cropping" during the binding process</note>. The signatures are decorated with lines and flourishes above and below, and usually have a cross on either side—sometimes with dots in the corners of the cross—placed near the two upper corners of the page. In some instances, there are two additional crosses immediately flanking the signatures themselves. These crosses and the decorative parts of the signatures were added by hands nearly, if not entirely, contemporary with the original scribe. The signatures are generally placed within the blank space originally left for them, but in a few cases, such as volume 2, folio 194 (478), they are placed under the lower ornament.

In volume 2, folio 18 (293), a small drawing of a vase takes the place of the signature for quire 40 <note>original Greek: μ</note>.

At the time the <term>Arabic numeration</term> <note>The familiar 1, 2, 3 numbering system, likely added long after the original Greek production.</note> was added, quire 49 <note>original: μq</note> in volume 2, folio 66 (341), was placed before quire 45 <note>original: με</note>, volume 2, folio 58 (333).

The ruling <note>The process of scratching or drawing lines to guide the scribe's writing.</note> is irregular. A guide line is drawn for every line of text, or more commonly, for every other line. In some cases, every third line is skipped. The sheets were ruled across their full width before being folded into quires; consequently, the lines on the 1st and 8th leaves, the 2nd and 7th leaves, and so on, match up within each quire.

The writing, which is executed in neatly formed <term>uncials</term> <note>A script consisting entirely of capital letters, common in ancient manuscripts.</note>, varies in different parts of the...

\* This modern arrangement was not noticed before the remarks on the quires in volume 4 were written. See the *Preface to the Facsimile of the New Testament*, page 5.

### ( 9 )

The manuscript, though sufficient uniformity is maintained to make it difficult to decide the exact place where a new hand begins. The differences, however, which are observed in the forms of paragraph signs, diacritical points, the apostrophe, and marks of punctuation, are probably owing to changes of hand <note>In manuscript studies, a "hand" refers to the distinct style of an individual scribe.</note>. The style of writing in volume 3 is for the most part different from that of the other volumes; and the system almost uniformly observed in this volume, of keeping the large initial letters within the marginal line of the text, is contrary to the usual practice. In volume 4, also, the difference is very evident between the hand in which folios 20-95 (44-121), from Saint Luke (exclusive of the table of **chapters** <note>original Greek: κεφάλαια (*kephalaia*)</note>) to 1 Corinthians 10:8, are written and the rest of the volume. In this hand the letters are more widely spaced and are rather larger than elsewhere; and **Delta** <note>original: Δ</note> with an extended base and **Pi** <note>The OCR reads "TT", which represents the Greek letter Π (Pi).</note> with an extended cross-stroke are here generally used, while elsewhere they are commonly of the more simple form in which the horizontal line is kept within the limit of the letter.*

The opening lines of each Book are written in red; the number of lines so written varying from one to seven (except in Ezekiel, which begins with ten), but most usually being three. In the first page of Genesis the first four lines of both columns are in red. In 1 Peter and 1 and 2 John the red are alternated with black lines. The titles of the Psalms and introductory passages in the prophetical Books are also in red.

The writing of the **Table of Books** placed at the beginning of the manuscript differs from that of the text, the letters being larger, and **Theta** and **Omicron** <note>original: Θ and Ο</note> being laterally compressed. It is probably of a somewhat later date.

The <term>superscriptions</term> <note>Titles or headings written at the beginning of a text.</note> and <term>colophons</term> <note>Notes at the end of a book providing details about its production.</note> of the Books are generally in smaller letters than the text, but some of the colophons are in larger characters. In some instances they are in red. Occasionally they appear to have been added by the writers of the text, but for the most part they seem to be the work of others, differing in forms of letters and colour of ink. Whether they were inserted contemporaneously with the text it is difficult to say, but some at least are later. It is interesting to observe in a few of them the occurrence of Egyptian forms of the Greek letters, proving that the manuscript, if not absolutely written in Egypt, must have been immediately—

---

* <term>Woide</term> <note>Charles Godfrey Woide (1749–1790), a scholar who published a famous edition of the New Testament from this manuscript.</note>, who has also noticed this change of hand, in the preface to his edition of the New Testament (1786), page 4, cites, in addition to other marks of distinction, small differences in the references to the **Eusebian canons** <note>A system of dividing the four Gospels to show which stories they have in common.</note> and in the forms of marginal quotation-signs. As regards the former, an examination of the manuscript proves that he is only partially correct; while, as regards the latter, it shows that he is absolutely wrong. The horizontal stroke between the **Ammonian number** <note>A system of numbering sections of the Gospels.</note> and the Eusebian canon, which he regards as a distinguishing mark of the second hand, is also found in the earlier part of the volume, for example folios 9 b (33 b), 11 b (35 b); and on the other hand it is not infrequently wanting in Saints Luke and John. And the ordinary mark of quotation is the small arrow-head without the accompanying dot (the form which he confines to the second hand), except in a few places, for example folios 13 (37), 14 (38), 15 (39), 50 (76), 57 (83), where too the dot is only an addition by the <term>rubricator</term> <note>A specialized scribe who added text or decorations in red ink.</note>.

### ( 10 )

afterwards removed there. See the title of Exodus, volume 1, folio 34 (38) <note>A "folio" refers to a single leaf of parchment; "f." is the abbreviation.</note>, letter **A** <note>original: alpha</note>; title of Deuteronomy, volume 1, folio 103 (107), and title of 2 Chronicles, volume 1, folio 256b (259b) <note>The "b" refers to the "verso" or back side of the leaf.</note>, letter **M** <note>original: mu</note>; <term>colophon</term> <note>A statement at the end of a book giving details about its production.</note> of Proverbs, volume 3, folio 78 (599), letters **Δ** <note>original: delta</note> and **M** <note>original: mu</note>.

Sections and paragraphs, when they commence at the beginning of a line, have large initials standing in the margin; except in volume 3, where the initials are nearly always kept within the limits of the text. When they begin in the middle of a line, the capital leads the next line, even though it be in the middle of a word.

The ancient system of dividing paragraphs by inserting between the first words of the lines a wedge or horizontal stroke became unnecessary when large initial letters came into use. But the scribes, at the same time as they used the large letters, continued to copy the paragraph marks mechanically, although the positions in which they placed them prove that they did not understand their meaning.

In this manuscript, the sign in common use is <insert>$\Gamma$</insert> <note>The Greek letter gamma, used here as a paragraph marker.</note>, less frequently a horizontal line, placed in the left-hand margin. When at the foot of a column, <insert>$\Gamma$</insert> is also often below the level of the last line, in a position which most nearly represents its ancient use. But the scribes seem generally to have thought that these signs belonged to the line *above* which they were inserted, and not to the line *below*, or, in other words, that they marked the beginning of a paragraph and not the close of one. They are accordingly very frequently found standing above the large initial letters of the paragraphs. They even take this position at the beginning of a Book, the first large letter being accompanied by the sign. From this latter fact it might be inferred that in the <term>archetype</term> <note>The original manuscript from which this copy was made.</note> such Books and those which immediately preceded them were written continuously without any other mark of severance than the paragraph sign. Such may have been the case in certain instances, though it is probable that the sign was more generally attached by later scribes as a meaningless ornament. The attribution of the sign to the beginning of the paragraph is carried a step farther by attaching one mark or the other to the first letter of a paragraph beginning in the middle of a line, as well as by writing it in the margin, as will be seen in the Gospels; and when the <term>rubricator</term> <note>A scribe who added red ink for titles and decorative marks.</note> came to work on this portion of the manuscript, he went still farther by adding in the margin the horizontal stroke to the <insert>$\Gamma$</insert> which already stood there.*

Other varieties of the paragraph sign are found in different parts of the manuscript:— <insert>$\sim$</insert>, which is apparently only an elaborate form of <insert>$\Gamma$</insert>, occurs often in the Psalms, and is also found occasionally in other places, as in volume 1, folios 75b (71b), 268b (265b).

\* An instance of the incorrect use of the same sign is seen in volume 1, folio 145 b (141 b), column 2, where <insert>$\Gamma$</insert> is inserted between the last words of lines 18 and 19.

### ( 11 )

Another kindred form ⳨ <note>A "staurogram," a monogram combining the Greek letters rho and tau to represent the cross of Christ.</note> is used, as in vol. ii. ff. 92 (367), 214b (498b), vol. iii. f. 23b (544b), vol. iv. f. 104 (130).

An oblique cross ☓ <note>Similar to a Saint Andrew's cross.</note>, probably arising out of a misinterpretation of 𐅵 <note>A specialized paragraph marker.</note>, appears in vol. iii. ff. 49-118 (570-639), and occasionally in the portion of vol. iv., ff. 20-95 (44-121), written by the second hand; but the more usual sign in this latter portion is a straight cross +.

The contractions <note>These are "Nomina Sacra," or "Sacred Names," which were shortened by ancient scribes as a mark of reverence.</note> in ordinary use are **God**, **Lord**, **Jesus**, **Christ**, **Father**, **Mother**, **Son**, **Human**, **Heaven** <note>original: ΘC, KC, IC, XC, ΠΗΡ, ΜΗΡ, YC, ΑΝOC, ΟYΝOC</note>, and their cases; also **David**, **Israel**, **Jerusalem**, **Spirit**, **Spiritual**, **Savior**, and **Cross** <note>original: ΔΑΔ, ΙΗΛ, ΙΛΗΜ, ΠΝΑ, ΠΝΙΚΟC, CHΡ, CΡOC (σταυρος)</note>, and their cases. The words **and**, **my**, **your**, and the terminating **-nai**, **-tai** <note>original: ΚΑΙ, ΜΟY, COY, ΝΑΙ, ΤΑΙ</note>, have also abbreviated forms. A horizontal stroke at the end of the line marks omission of **N** <note>original: Ν</note>. Numerals in the text are rarely represented by single letters.

There are no breathings or accents <note>Marks used in Greek to indicate pronunciation or pitch.</note>, properly so called, by the first hand; but some have been added in a few places in recent times.

The apostrophe, besides being used for elision <note>The dropping of a vowel at the end of a word when the next word begins with a vowel.</note>, separates words, as in **PAS'OSAN**, **OUN'OUK** <note>original: ΠΑC'OCAN, ΟYΝ'ΟYΚ</note>; and it is also found inserted between two consonants in the middle of a word, as **ENEG'KEN** <note>original: ΗΝΕΓ'ΚΕΝ</note>. It is likewise used after **K** and **Ch**, as in the words **OUK** and **OUCH** <note>original: ΟYΚ and ΟYΧ</note>, after **X** <note>original: ξ</note>, and after words ending with **R** <note>original: ρ</note>; and generally after proper names which have not a Greek termination, as **ABRAHAM'** <note>original: ΑΒΡΑΑΜ'</note>. The apostrophe is in some parts of the MS. represented by a heavy point. This form is found in vol. i., from f. 165 (161) to the end of the volume, vol. ii. ff. 143-185 (418-460), vol. iii. ff. 1-48 (523-569).*

The diacritical mark <note>Marks used to distinguish how a letter should be sounded.</note> over **I** and **U** <note>original: Ι and Y</note> varies in form. In the greater part of the MS. it is either one or two light points or a minute horizontal stroke. In other places, however, it is a heavy square point or <term>virgule</term> <note>A small slanting line.</note> turning to the right. This latter shape accompanies the heavy form of apostrophe noticed above.

A mark, resembling an accent or a short horizontal stroke or, in some instances, an apostrophe, is occasionally used to distinguish words consisting of a single letter, and to separate words where there might be difficulties in reading, as, *e.g.*, to separate the article. These marks are very frequently applied to **E** <note>The Greek letter Eta (Η), which can mean "or," "than," or "the" depending on context.</note> in its various meanings as a separate word, but also when it stands as an initial letter or even in the body of a word.

The mark of punctuation is a single point, occasionally middle, but generally high <note>In ancient Greek, the height of a point indicated the length of the pause.</note>. It is followed by a space at the end of a paragraph when the next paragraph begins in the same line. In company with the heavy apostrophe and diacritical point noticed above, a heavy square mark of punctuation appears.

\* The scribe or scribes who used this form of apostrophe also inserted, with more than ordinary frequency, the middle point as a mark of punctuation. The concurrence of the apostrophe and point has led some to suppose that a colon (:) was intended to represent the apostrophe.

<meta>This page concludes the paleographic and decorative analysis of the manuscript, detailing the specific symbols for quotations, methods of correction, and the artistic designs found in the concluding inscriptions of the books.</meta>

### ( 12 )

Quotations are marked with an arrow-head in the margin <note>These marks, known as *diplai*, functioned like modern quotation marks to indicate text cited from other parts of the Bible.</note>.

A short oblique stroke appears with frequency in the margin of the text of **Ezekiel**, volume 2, folios 95-127 (370-402), and symbols such as **\*** <note>An asterisk-like symbol.</note>, for example in volume 3, folio 49b (570b), column 2, and **/.**, for example in volume 3, folio 31b (552b), line 1, are used; but the value of these and other minute signs remains undetermined.

The corrections, which are numerous, have generally been written over erasures, some of the passages extending to several lines.

Single letters are also struck out with the pen, or are marked for omission with a fine oblique stroke resembling an acute accent, for example in volume 1, folio 82 (78), **of the** <note>original: των´</note>. In the case of a word the same mark is placed above the first and last letters, for example in volume 2, folio 59b (334b), **all things** <note>original: π´αντα´</note>; folio 98 (373), **the** <note>original: τ´α</note>. A corresponding mark stands in the margin.

The <term>colophons</term> <note>The concluding statement or ornamental design at the end of a book, often containing the title or the scribe's details.</note> are ornamented with patterns in black and red, sometimes forming a frame, but more usually being composed of a band running immediately under the text, with another depending from its left extremity, so as to form two sides of a square, within which the name of the Book is written, ornamented with <term>arabesques</term> <note>Flowing, interlacing patterns of lines and foliage.</note>. Among the designs are the cable, zig-zag, chequers, arrow-head, and a modification of the <term>Greek key-pattern</term> <note>A decorative border constructed from a continuous line, shaped into a repeated motif; also known as a meander.</note>. Other objects are sometimes added, namely: a tall vase and plant in flower, volume 2, folio 14 (289); baskets of fruit, volume 2, folios 27 (302), 89b (364b), volume 3, folio 10 (531), volume 4, folio 84b (110b); vases, volume 2, folio 148b (423b), volume 4, folios 5b (29b), 76 (102); and shrubs, volume 4, folio 41b (65b).

This book of Sacred Script<gloss>ure</gloss>, <note>original Latin: "Scriptae Sacrae."</note> of the O<gloss>ld</gloss> and N<gloss>ew</gloss> Testam<gloss>ent</gloss>, <gloss>as</gloss> we have received from tradition, was written by the hand of Thecla, a noble Egyptian woman, about one thousand three hundred years ago—shortly after the Council of Nicaea <note>The Council of Nicaea, held in 325 CE, was a landmark gathering of Christian bishops; this note dates the manuscript to the mid-4th century.</note>. The name of Thecla was once inscribed at the end of the book; however, after Christianity was extinguished in Egypt by the Muslims <note>original Latin: "Mahometanis." This refers to the Islamic conquest of Egypt in the 7th century and the subsequent decline of the Greek-speaking Christian population.</note>, and the books of the Christians were reduced to a similar condition <note>referring to being damaged, lost, or censored.</note>, the name of Thecla was likewise extinguished and torn away. Nevertheless, memory and living tradition continue to observe this fact.

### The Book of Genesis

->**The Creation of the World**<-

IN THE BEGINNING GOD <note>The scribe uses "Nomina Sacra," which are traditional abbreviated forms for sacred names (e.g., ΘΣ for Θεός/God).</note> MADE THE HEAVEN AND THE EARTH. BUT THE EARTH WAS INVISIBLE AND UNFORMED <note>The Greek "αόρατος" (invisible) and "ακατασκεύαστος" (unprepared/unformed) is the Septuagint’s rendering of the Hebrew "tohu wa-bohu."</note> AND DARKNESS WAS OVER THE ABYSS AND THE SPIRIT OF GOD WAS BORNE OVER THE WATER. AND GOD SAID, “LET THERE BE LIGHT,” AND THERE WAS LIGHT. AND GOD SAW THE LIGHT, THAT IT WAS GOOD. AND GOD DIVIDED BETWEEN THE LIGHT AND BETWEEN THE DARKNESS. AND GOD CALLED THE LIGHT DAY AND THE DARKNESS HE CALLED NIGHT. AND THERE WAS EVENING AND THERE WAS MORNING, ONE DAY.

And God said, “Let there be a firmament <term>firmament: from the Greek 'stereoma,' implying a solid, hammered-out expanse or dome that separates the heavens from the earth</term> in the midst of the water, and let it be dividing between water and water.” And it was so. And God made the firmament, and God divided between the water that was below the firmament and between the water that was above the firmament. And God called the firmament Heaven. And there was evening and there was morning, a second day.

And God said, “Let the water below the heaven be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear.” And it was so. And the water below the heaven was gathered into their gatherings, and the dry land appeared. And God called the dry land Earth, and the collections of the waters he called Seas. And God saw that it was good.

And God said, “Let the earth sprout herb of grass, sowing seed according to its kind and according to its likeness, and the fruitful tree making fruit whose seed is in it, according to its kind upon the earth.” And it was so. And the earth brought forth herb of grass, sowing seed according to its kind and according to its likeness, and the fruitful tree making fruit whose seed is in it, according to its kind upon the earth. And God saw that it was good.

<column-break/>

AND THERE WAS EVENING AND THERE WAS MORNING, A THIRD DAY.

And God said, “Let there be luminaries in the firmament of <unclear>heaven</unclear> <note>The OCR shows a highly compressed or damaged abbreviation for 'heaven' (ουρανου) here.</note> for light upon the earth, and to rule over the day and the night, and to divide between the day and between the night; and let them be for signs and for seasons and for days and for years. And let them be for light in the firmament of heaven so as to shine upon the earth.” And it was so.

And God made the two great luminaries: the great luminary for the beginnings of the day and the lesser luminary for the beginnings of the night, and the stars. And God placed them in the firmament of heaven so as to shine upon the earth and to rule the day and the night, and to divide between the light and between the darkness. And God saw that it was good. And there was evening and there was morning, a fourth day.

And God said, “Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls, and winged creatures flying above the earth against the firmament of heaven.” And it was so. And God made the great sea monsters <note>original: "κητη" (kete), meaning huge aquatic creatures, whales, or sea dragons.</note> and every soul of living creeping things which the waters brought forth according to their kinds, and every winged bird according to its kind. And God saw that they were good. And God blessed them, saying, “Increase and multiply and fill the waters in the seas, and let the winged creatures multiply upon the earth.” And there was evening and there was morning, a fifth day.

And God said, “Let the earth bring forth the living soul according to its kind: four-footed beasts and creeping things and wild animals of the earth according to their kind.” And it was so. <unclear>And God made</unelinear> <unclear>the wild animals of the earth according to their kind.</unclear>

After these things, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the double cave of the field, which is opposite Mamre. This is Hebron in the land of Canaan. And the field and the cave that were in it were legally confirmed to Abraham for a possession of a burial place by the sons of Heth.

[Abraham] sent them away from Isaac his son while he was still living. And these are the days of the years of the life of Abraham which he lived: one hundred and seventy-five years. # THE CONFRONTATION AT GILEAD

### Jacob Defends His Departure

...to depart to the house of your father <note>original: "ΠΡΣ", a shorthand for *patros* (father)</note>, but why did you steal my gods? <note>These "gods" were small household idols or *teraphim*, which often represented family inheritance rights.</note> And Jacob answered and said to Laban: "Because I was afraid; for I thought that you might take your daughters from me and all that is mine. And Jacob said to him: "With whomever you find your gods, he shall not live in the presence of our kinsmen. Identify what of yours is with me and take it." But Jacob did not know that Rachel his wife had stolen them.

### The Search for the Household Idols

Laban went in and searched in Leah's house and did not find them. And going out of Leah's house, he searched in Jacob’s house and in the house of the two handmaids, and he did not find them. Then he also entered Rachel’s house. Now, Rachel had taken the idols and put them into the camel’s saddle and sat upon them. And she said to her father: "Do not take it heavily, my lord, that I cannot rise before you, for the manner of women <note>A polite reference to her menstrual cycle.</note> is upon me." And Laban searched through the whole house and did not find the idols.

### Jacob’s Rebuke

Then Jacob became angry and argued with Laban. Jacob answered and said to Laban: "What is my wrongdoing, and what is my sin, that you have hotly pursued me? And because you have searched all the goods of my house, what have you found from all the goods of your house? Set it here before your kinsmen and my kinsmen, and let them judge between the two of us! These twenty years I have been with you; your sheep and your goats have not miscarried, and I have not eaten the rams of your sheep. That which was torn by wild beasts <term>torn by beasts: livestock killed by predators which a shepherd was usually not responsible for replacing</term> I did not bring to you; 

<column-break/>

I made restitution from myself for the thefts of the day and the thefts of the night. By day I was consumed by the burning heat, and by frost by night, and my sleep departed from my eyes. These twenty years I have been in your house; I served you fourteen years for your two daughters and six years for your sheep, and you changed my wages by ten lambs <note>The Greek text specifies "lambs," though other traditions translate this as "ten times."</note>. If the God <note>original: "ΘΣ", shorthand for *Theos*</note> of my father Abraham and the Fear of Isaac <note>A unique title for God, emphasizing the deep reverence or "awe" Isaac held for the Divine.</note> were not with me, you would have sent me away empty-handed. God saw my humbleness and the labor of my hands and rebuked you yesterday."

### The Covenant of the Stone Heap

And Laban answered and said to Jacob: "The daughters are my daughters, and the sons are my sons, and the livestock is my livestock, and all that you see is mine. But what can I do today for these my daughters or for their children whom they have borne? Now therefore, come, let us make a covenant <term>covenant: a formal, binding agreement or treaty</term>, I and you, and let it be for a witness between me and you." And Jacob said to him: "Behold, no one is with us; see, God is witness between me and you." Then Jacob took a stone and set it up as a pillar.

And Jacob said to his kinsmen: "Gather stones." And they gathered stones and made a heap, and they ate and drank there upon the heap. And Laban said to him: "This heap witnesses between me and you today." And Laban called it "The Witness Heap" <note>original: *Bounos Martys*. In Hebrew, Laban uses the Aramaic *Jegar-sahadutha*.</note>, but Jacob called it "The Heap Witnesses" <note>In Hebrew, *Galeed*.</note>. And Laban said to Jacob: "Behold this heap and this pillar which I have set between me and you; this heap witnesses and this pillar witnesses."

# JACOB SETTLES IN GOSHEN AND THE SEVERITY OF THE FAMINE

For the famine prevailed in the land of Canaan. "Now therefore, let us, your servants, dwell in the land of Goshen <note>original: "ΓΕΣΕΜ" (Gesem), the region in the eastern Nile Delta granted to the Israelites</note>." 

And Pharaoh said to Joseph: "Let them dwell in the land of Goshen. And if you know that there are capable men among them, appoint them as rulers over my own livestock." 

Then Jacob and his sons came into Egypt to Joseph. And Pharaoh, the King of Egypt, heard of it. And Pharaoh spoke to Joseph, saying: "Your father and your brothers have come to you. Behold, the land of Egypt is before you; in the best part of the land, settle your father and your brothers."

And Joseph brought in Jacob his father and stood him before Pharaoh; and Jacob blessed Pharaoh. Then Pharaoh said to Jacob: "How many are the years of the days of your life?" 

And Jacob said to Pharaoh: "The days of the years of my life which I sojourn <note>original: "ΠΑΡΟΙΚΩ", referring to a temporary dwelling or pilgrimage</note> are one hundred and thirty years. Small and evil have been the days of the years of my life; they have not reached the days of the years of the life of my fathers during the days of their sojourn." 

And having blessed Pharaoh, Jacob went out from his presence. Joseph then settled his father and his brothers and gave them a possession in the land of Egypt, in the best part of the land, in the land of Rameses <note>original: "ΡΑΜΕΣΣΗ", a district within or near Goshen</note>, just as Pharaoh had commanded. And Joseph provided rations of grain <note>original: "ΕΣΙΤΟΜΕΤΡΕΙ", literally 'measured out corn'</note> for his father, his brothers, and all his father’s household, providing grain for each person <note>original: "ΚΑΤΑ ΣΩΜΑ", literally 'according to the body' or 'per head'</note>.

But there was no grain in all the land, for the famine prevailed exceedingly. Both the land of Egypt and the land of Canaan fainted because of the famine. And Joseph gathered all

<column-break/>

the money that was found in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan in exchange for the grain which they were buying; and Joseph provided them with grain rations. And Joseph brought all the money into the house of Pharaoh. 

When the money failed from the land of Egypt and from the land of Canaan, all the Egyptians came to Joseph, saying: "Give us bread! Why should we die before your eyes? For our money is gone." 

And Joseph said to them: "Bring your livestock, and I will give you bread in exchange for your livestock, if your money is gone." So they brought their livestock to Joseph, and Joseph gave them bread in exchange for their horses, and for their sheep, and for their cattle, and for their donkeys. And he sustained them with bread in exchange for all their livestock during that year.

When that year had ended, they came to him in the second year and said to him: "Let us not be wiped out from the sight of our lord. For since our money has failed, and our possessions and livestock have passed to you, our lord, nothing is left before our lord except our own bodies and our land. Therefore, so that we do not die before you and the land become a waste, acquire us and our land in exchange for bread. We and our land will then be servants to Pharaoh. Give us seed so that we may sow and live and not die, and so the land will not become a desert."

And Joseph acquired all the land of the Egyptians for Pharaoh; for the Egyptians sold their land to Pharaoh, because the famine prevailed over them. Thus the land became Pharaoh’s. And as for the people, he reduced them to servitude <note>original: "ΚΑΤΕΔΟΥΛΩΣΑΤΟ", meaning he brought them into a state of bond-service or total dependency on the crown</note>.

And see how, in ancient times, he who was striving <note>original: "οπονευόμενος" (hoponeuomenos), likely a variant of "πονούμενος," meaning to labor or struggle for a goal</note> for the beginning of the kingdom—the symbolic one <note>original: "εικονικήν" (eikonikēn), referring to the representative or image-based nature of earthly rule</note>—neither desired those who held authority to be the ones setting up his image, nor did he permit those who possessed the power and were willing to set it up.

But if her husband, **forbidding her**, should forbid her on the day he hears, all her vows and the obligations she bound upon her soul shall not remain, because her husband forbade her, and the Lord will clear her.

And the vow of a **widow** or a **divorced woman** <note>original: "ΕΚΒΕΒΛΗΜΕΝΗϲ." Literally "one who has been cast out."</note>, whatever she vows against her soul, shall remain for her.

But if her husband should **utterly void them** <note>original: "ΠΕΡΙΕΛΩΝ ΠΕΡΙΕΛΗ." A Greek grammatical construction indicating total cancellation.</note> on the day he hears, everything that proceeds from her lips concerning her vows and the obligations concerning her soul shall not remain for her.

And they departed from **Kadesh** and encamped at **Mount Hor**, near the land of **Edom**. And **Aaron** was one hundred and twenty-three years old when he died on **Mount Hor**.

# The Borders of the Land and Cities for the Levites

The border of the sea shall be yours, even the **Great Sea** <note>The Mediterranean Sea</note> shall be the border. And this shall be your northern border: from the **Great Sea** you shall measure for yourselves to **Mount Hor**. # Cities for the Levites and Cities of Refuge

And you shall give the cities from the possession of the children of **Israel**; from those who have many, you shall take many, and from those who have few, you shall take fewer. Each shall give of their cities to the **Levites** <note>The tribe of Levi did not receive a continuous territory but was granted specific cities within other tribal lands.</note> according to the inheritance that they possess.

And the **Lord** <note>original: "ΚΣ," a common scribal abbreviation for *Kyrios*.</note> spoke to **Moses**, saying: "Speak to the children of **Israel** and say to them: 'When you cross the **Jordan** into the land of **Canaan**, you shall designate for yourselves cities to be cities of refuge <note>original: "φυγαδευτηρια" (phygadeuteria), literally "places of flight" or "sanctuaries."</note> for you, so that the slayer who strikes a soul <note>original: "ψυχην" (psychen), often translated as "person" or "life."</note> unintentionally may flee there. And the cities shall be a refuge for you from the avenger of blood <note>original: "αγχιστευοντος" (anchisteuontos), referring to the next of kin who had the legal right/duty to reclaim "blood-debt."</note>, so that the slayer may not die until he stands before the assembly for judgment. And the cities which you shall give—these six cities—shall be cities of refuge for you. You shall give three cities on the other side of the **Jordan**, and you shall give three cities in the land of **Canaan**; they shall be cities of refuge. For the children of **Israel**, for the proselyte <note>A convert or foreigner who has joined the community.</note>, and for the resident alien among you, these cities shall be a refuge, for anyone who strikes a soul unintentionally to flee there.

But if he strikes him with an instrument of iron and he dies, he is a murderer; the murderer shall surely be put to death <note>original: "θανατω θανατουσθω," a Greek rendering of a Hebrew idiom meaning "by death let him be put to death," signifying a mandatory sentence.</note>. And if he strikes him with a stone in his hand by which he might die, and he dies, he is a murderer; the murderer shall surely be put to death. And if he strikes him with a <margin>either with it</margin> wooden instrument in his hand from which he might die, and he dies, he is a murderer; the murderer shall surely be put to death. The avenger of blood himself shall kill the murderer; when he meets him, he shall kill him. 

But if he pushes him out of hatred, or throws any object at him 

<column-break/>

from an ambush and he dies, or if out of enmity he strikes him with his hand and he dies, the one who struck him shall surely be put to death; he is a murderer. The avenger of blood shall kill the murderer when he meets him.

But if he pushes him suddenly, not out of enmity, or throws any object at him not from an ambush, or any stone by which he might die, without knowing it, and it falls upon him and he dies, but he was not his enemy nor seeking to do him harm: then the assembly shall judge between the one who struck him and the avenger of blood according to these judgments. And the assembly shall rescue the slayer from the hand of the avenger of blood, and the assembly shall restore him to the city of his refuge where he fled. And he shall dwell there until the death of the **High Priest** <note>original: "ιερευς ο μεγας" (hiereus ho megas).</note> who was anointed with the holy oil.

But if the slayer ever goes outside the borders of the city of refuge where he fled, and the avenger of blood finds him outside the borders of his city of refuge, and the avenger of blood kills the slayer, he is not guilty of blood. For the slayer must dwell in the city of refuge until the death of the **High Priest**; but after the death of the **High Priest**, the slayer shall return to the land of his own possession. And these things shall be a statute of judgment for you throughout your generations in all your dwellings.

Whoever strikes a soul shall be killed as a murderer on the testimony of witnesses <note>original: "δια μαρτυρων" (dia martyron).</note>; but the testimony of one witness shall not suffice against a soul to put them to death. Moreover, you shall take no ransom for the life <note>original: "ψυχης" (psyches).</note> of a murderer who is guilty of death, but he shall surely be put to death.

You shall not take **ransom** <note>original: "λυτρα" (lytra) - a payment made to remit a punishment.</note> for the one who has fled to a city of **refuge** <note>original: "φυγαδευτηριων" (phygadeuteria) - places of sanctuary for those who committed unintentional manslaughter.</note> to allow him to return to dwell upon the land until the **High Priest** dies.

And you shall not murder the land on which you dwell, for this blood murders the land; and the land shall not be atoned for from the blood shed upon it, except by the blood of the one who shed it. <margin>36.]</margin> ## The Inheritance of Daughters

And the leaders of the ancestral houses of the sons of **Gilead**, son of **Machir**, son of **Manasseh**, from the tribe of the sons of **Joseph**, approached and spoke before **Moses** and before **Eleazar** the priest, and before the leaders of the ancestral houses of the sons of **Israel**.

And they said: "The **Lord** commanded our lord to give the land of inheritance by lot to the sons of **Israel**; and our lord was commanded by the **Lord** to give the inheritance of **Zelophehad** <note>original: "ΣΑΛΠΑΑΔ" (Salpaad).</note> our brother to his daughters. But if they become wives to men of one of the other tribes of the sons of **Israel**, their lot will be taken away from the possession of our fathers and will be added to the inheritance of the tribe to which they become wives; thus it will be taken away from the lot of our inheritance. 

And when the release <note>A reference to the Jubilee year, when property was meant to return to its original owners.</note> of the sons of **Israel** occurs, their inheritance will be added to the inheritance of the tribe to which they become wives, and their inheritance will be taken away from the inheritance of our ancestral tribe."

<column-break/>

And **Moses** commanded the sons of **Israel** through the decree of the **Lord**, saying: "Thus the tribe of the sons of **Joseph** says. This is the word which the **Lord** has commanded for the daughters of **Zelophehad**, saying: 'Let them become wives to whomever it pleases them, provided they marry within the clan <note>original: "δημου" (demou) - a local community or subdivision of a tribe.</note> of their father's tribe.'

And an inheritance shall not be transferred for the sons of **Israel** from tribe to tribe, because each shall cling to the inheritance of his ancestral tribe. And every daughter who possesses an inheritance from the tribes of the sons of **Israel** shall become a wife to one of the men from the clan of her father, so that the sons of **Israel** may each inherit their ancestral property.

The lot shall not be transferred from one tribe to another, but each of the sons of **Israel** shall remain attached to his own inheritance."

In the manner the **Lord** commanded **Moses**, so did the daughters of **Zelophehad**: **Mahlah**, **Tirzah**, **Hoglah**, **Milcah**, and **Noah**. All the daughters of **Zelophehad** became wives to their cousins <note>The Greek term implies kinship, specifically sons of their father's brothers.</note> from the clan of **Manasseh**, son of **Joseph**; and their inheritance remained with the tribe of their father's clan.

These are the commandments, the ordinances, and the judgments which the **Lord** commanded by the hand of **Moses** in the plains of **Moab** by the **Jordan** across from **Jericho**.

And you shall give the silver for whatever your soul desires: for cattle, or for sheep, or for wine, or for strong drink <note>original: "σικερα" (sikera) — a term for fermented liquors other than grape wine.</note>, or for anything your soul desires; and you shall eat there before the **Lord** your **God**, and you and your household shall rejoice. And you shall not abandon the Levite who is in your cities, because he has no portion or inheritance with you.

<margin>~</margin> Every three years you shall bring out all the tithe of your produce in that year and store it in your cities. And the Levite shall come, because he has no portion or inheritance with you...

<column-break/>

...and the proselyte <note>original: "προσηλυτος" (proselytos) — a convert or newcomer to the community.</note>, and the orphan, and the widow who are in your cities, and they shall eat and be filled, so that the **Lord** your **God** may bless you in all the works which you may do.

<margin>15: ~</margin> Every seven years you shall perform a release <note>original: "αφεσιν" (aphesin) — a remission of debts or a "letting go."</note>. And this is the ordinance of the release: you shall remit every private debt which your neighbor owes you, and you shall not demand it from your brother, because it has been called a "Release for the **Lord** your **God**." You may demand it from the stranger, as much as he owes you; but to your brother you shall grant a release of your debt.

There shall be no needy person among you, because the **Lord** your **God** will surely bless you in the land which the **Lord** your **God** gives you as an inheritance to possess.

<margin>~</margin> Provided that you diligently listen to the voice of the **Lord** your **God** to keep all these commandments which I command you today. For the **Lord** your **God** has blessed you in the manner He spoke to you; and you shall lend to many nations, but you shall not borrow; and you shall rule over many nations, but they shall not rule over you.

<margin>~</margin> If there should be a needy person among your brothers in one of your cities in the land which the **Lord** your **God** gives you as an inheritance, you shall not turn away your heart nor shall you close your hand <note>original: "συνσφιγξεις την χειρα" (synsphigxeis ten cheira) — literally "tighten the hand" or clench it shut.</note> from your brother who is in need. You shall surely open your hands to him; you shall lend him a loan for as much as he requires according to his need.

<margin>~</margin> Watch yourself, lest there be a hidden word in your heart, a lawless thought, saying, "The seventh year, the year of release, is drawing near," and your eye should be evil toward your brother who is in need and you give him nothing; and he will cry out against you to the **Lord**, and it will be a great sin in you. You shall surely give to him, and you shall lend him a loan for as much as he requires, and you shall not be grieved in your heart when you give to him; because for this thing the **Lord** your **God** will bless you in all your works.

### Deuteronomy: Laws of Purity and Marriage

You shall not wear a garment of mixed weave, wool and linen together. You shall make for yourself **twisted tassels** <note>original: στρεπτά (strepta) – these tassels, later called tzitzit, served as a visual reminder of the commandments</note> on the four corners of your cloak with which you cover yourself.

If a man takes a wife and lives with her, but then hates her and brings **malicious charges** <note>original: προφασικούς λόγους (prophasikous logous) – literally "pretextual words," referring to false or trumped-up accusations</note> against her and gives her an evil name, saying, "I took this woman, and when I approached her I did not find the tokens of her virginity"; then the father of the girl and her mother shall take and bring out the tokens of the girl's virginity to the **council of elders** <note>original: γερουσίαν (gerousian)</note> at the gate. And the father of the girl shall say to the council of elders: "I gave my daughter to this man as a wife; and now, having hated her, he brings malicious charges against her, saying: 'I did not find tokens of virginity in your daughter.' Yet here are the tokens of my daughter's virginity." And they shall spread out the garment <note>The "garment" or cloth was presented as physical evidence to the elders to prove the girl's innocence</note> before the elders of the city.

Then the council of elders of that city shall take that man and discipline him; they shall fine him **one hundred shekels** <note>original: σίκλους (siklous)</note> and give them to the father of the young woman, because he brought an evil name upon a virgin of Israel. She shall remain his wife; he may not divorce her all his days.

But if this charge is true and tokens of virginity were not found for the young woman, then they shall lead the young woman to the doors of her father's house, and the men of her city shall stone her with stones and she shall die; for she has committed a **shameful act** <note>original: ἀφροσύνην (aphrosunēn) – literally "folly" or "senselessness," used here for a grave moral violation</note> among the sons of Israel by playing the harlot in her father’s house. To the young woman you shall do nothing; there is no sin in the young woman deserving death. For this matter is like a man rising up against his neighbor and murdering him; for he found her in the field, and the betrothed girl cried out, but there was no one to help her.

If a man finds a young girl, a virgin who is not betrothed, and forces her and lies with her and they are discovered, the man who lay with her shall give **fifty didrachmas** <note>original: δίδραχμα (didrachma) – a unit of silver currency</note> of silver to the girl’s father, and she shall be his wife because he humbled her; he may not divorce her all his days.

### Deuteronomy: Laws of Purity and Social Conduct

And because they hired against you **Balaam son of Beor** <note>original: Βαλαάμ (Balaam) — a non-Israelite prophet mentioned in the Book of Numbers</note> from **Mesopotamia** <note>original: Μεσοποταμίας (Mesopotamias) — literally "the land between rivers"</note> to curse you. However, the Lord your God was not willing to listen to Balaam; and the Lord your God turned the curses into blessings, because the Lord your God loved you. You shall not seek their peace or their prosperity all your days, forever. You shall not abhor an **Edomite**, for he is your brother; you shall not abhor an **Egyptian**, for you were a resident alien in his land. If sons are born to them, the third generation may enter the assembly of the Lord.

When you go out to encamp against your enemies for war, you shall keep yourself from every evil thing. If there is a man among you who is not **ritually clean** <note>original: καθαρός (katharos)</note> because of a nocturnal emission, he shall go outside the camp; he shall not come into the camp. And it shall be toward evening that he shall wash his body with water, and when the sun has set, he may enter the camp. You shall also have a place outside the camp, and you shall go out there. And you shall have a **peg** <note>original: πάσσαλος (passalos) — a small spade or stake for digging</note> on your belt; and it shall be that when you sit down outside, you shall dig with it, and turning back, you shall cover your **unseemliness** <note>original: ασχημοσύνην (aschémosunén) — a euphemism for excrement or nakedness</note> with it.

Because the Lord your God walks in your camp to deliver you and to hand over your enemy to you, your camp shall be holy; and no **unseemly thing** <note>original: ασχημοσύνη πράγματος (aschémosuné pragmatos)</note> shall be seen among you, lest He turn away from you.

You shall not hand over a slave to his master who has fled to you from his master. He shall dwell with you; he shall dwell among you in whatever place he chooses, wherever it pleases him; you shall not oppress him. There shall be no **cult prostitute** <note>original: πόρνη (porné) — here referring to female practitioners of cultic rites</note> from the daughters of Israel, nor shall there be a **male cult prostitute** from the sons of Israel.

There shall be no female initiate from the daughters of Israel, and no **male initiate** <note>original: τελεσκόμενος (teleskomenos) — one initiated into pagan mystery rites</note>

You shall not bring the hire of a prostitute or the **price of a dog** <note>original: άλλαγμα κυνός (allagma kynos) — "dog" was a derogatory term for a male cult prostitute</note> into the house of the Lord your God for any vow; for both are an abomination to the Lord your God. You shall not charge your brother **interest** <note>original: εκτοκιείς (ektokieis) — the practice of charging usury on loans</note> on food or interest on money or interest on any thing that you might lend. You may charge interest to a foreigner, but to your brother you shall not charge interest, so that the Lord your God may bless you in all your works upon the land that you are entering to inherit.

But if you make a vow to the Lord your God, you shall not delay in paying it; for the Lord your God will surely require it of you, and it would be a sin in you. But if you do not wish to make a vow, it is not a sin in you.

That which proceeds from your lips you shall observe, and you shall do according as you have vowed to the Lord your God, a gift which you have spoken.

And you shall not defile the land which the Lord your God is giving you as an inheritance.

**Y**ou shall not take a millstone or an upper millstone as a pledge <note>original: ενεχυράσεις (enechyraseis) — to take personal property as collateral for a debt</note>, for he who does so takes a life as a pledge. If a man is found stealing a soul <note>original: ψυχήν (psychēn) — here meaning a person or a life</note> from among his brothers, the sons of **Israel** <note>original: ιηλ (Israel) — abbreviated in the text as a sacred name</note>, and having overpowered him, he sells him and that thief dies, then you shall remove the evil from among yourselves.

<margin>REMEMBER WHAT THE LORD YOUR GOD DID</margin>

**R**emember what the **Lord your God** <note>original: κσ ο θσ (Kyrios ho Theos) — abbreviated sacred names</note> did to **Miriam** on the way as you were coming out of **Egypt**. If there is a debt <note>original: οφείλημα (opheilēma)</note> owed by your neighbor, any debt at all, you shall not enter into his house to take his pledge. You shall stand outside, and the man to whom your loan is made shall bring the pledge out to you. And if the man is poor, you shall not sleep in his pledge; you shall surely return the pledge to him before the sun sets, and he shall sleep in his garment and bless you, and it shall be **righteousness** <note>original: ελεημοσύνη (eleēmosynē) — literally "mercy" or "charity," but here functioning as religious merit</note> for you before the Lord your God.

**Y**ou shall not withhold the wages of a poor and needy man from among your brothers or from the **proselytes** <note>original: προσηλύτων (prosēlytōn) — foreigners or resident aliens who have joined the community</note> who are in your cities. On the same day you shall give him his wages; the sun shall not set upon it, because he is poor and has set his hope upon it; otherwise he will cry out against you to the **Lord** and it will be a sin in you.

**F**athers shall not die for their children, and sons shall not die for their fathers; each shall die for his own sin. **Y**ou shall not pervert the justice due to a proselyte or an orphan or a widow, and you shall not take a widow’s garment as a pledge. And you shall remember that you were a servant in the land of **Egypt**, and the Lord your God ransomed you

<column-break/>

from there. Therefore, I command you to do this thing. **I**f you reap your harvest in your field and forget a sheaf in your field, you shall not turn back to get it; it shall be for the **proselyte**, the orphan, and the widow, so that the **Lord your God** may bless you in all the works of your hands. And if you gather your olives, you shall not go over the branches a second time; it shall be for the proselyte, the orphan, and the widow. And you shall remember that you were a servant in the land of **Egypt**; therefore, I command you to do this thing.

**I**f you gather the grapes of your vineyard, you shall not glean it afterward; it shall be for the proselyte, the orphan, and the widow. And you shall remember that you were a servant in the land of **Egypt**; therefore, I command you to do this thing.

<margin>24.</margin> <note>This marginal number marks the beginning of a new section or chapter</note> **I**f there is a dispute between men and they come to judgment, and they judge and justify the righteous and condemn the ungodly, it shall be that if the ungodly man is worthy of stripes <note>original: πληγών (plēgōn) — lashes or blows</note>, you shall lay him down before the judges and they shall scourge him in their presence according to his ungodliness. They shall scourge him with **forty** <note>original: τεσσαράκοντα (tessarakonta)</note> stripes by number; they shall not add more. For if they should add to scourge him with more stripes than these, your brother will be disgraced before you.

**Y**ou shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.

**I**f brothers dwell together and one of them dies and has no seed <note>original: σπέρμα (sperma) — offspring or child</note>, the wife of the deceased shall not belong to a man outside the family. Her husband's brother shall go in to her and take her to himself as a wife and live with her. And it shall be that the child she bears shall be established in the name of the deceased, so that his name may not be blotted out from **Israel**.

### DEUTERONOMY

<term>DEUTERONOMY: Meaning 'Second Law,' this book contains the final speeches of Moses to the Israelites before they enter the Promised Land.</term>
<term>SEPTUAGINT: The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, which this manuscript follows.</term>
<term>UNCIAL: A script written entirely in capital letters, used in Greek manuscripts from the 4th to 8th centuries AD.</term>

<summary>This concluding page of Deuteronomy narrates the death of Moses after viewing the Promised Land, the transition of leadership to Joshua, and an epitaph celebrating Moses' unique relationship with God.</summary>

# JOSHUA’S FAREWELL ADDRESS

...and you yourselves have seen all that the **Lord your God** <note>original: "KC O ΘC," Nomina Sacra (sacred names) abbreviated by scribes to show reverence.</note> has done to all these nations before your face; for the **Lord your God** himself has fought for you. See, I have allotted to you these remaining nations as an inheritance for your tribes—from the **Jordan** <note>The primary river of the region.</note> and all the nations I have destroyed, even unto the **Great Sea** <note>The Mediterranean Sea.</note> toward the setting of the sun, which shall be your boundary.

And the **Lord your God**, He shall destroy them from before your face until they perish; and He will send wild beasts against them until He has destroyed them and their kings from before your face. And you shall inherit their land, just as the **Lord our God** spoke to you.

Therefore, be very strong to keep and to do all that is written in the **Book of the Law of Moses**, <note>The Torah or the first five books of the Bible.</note> so that you do not turn aside from it to the right or to the left; so that you do not enter among these remaining nations. The names of their gods shall not be named among you, neither shall you swear by them, nor serve them, nor bow down to them. But you shall cling to the **Lord our God**, just as you have done until this day.

And look, I am now going the way of all who are on the earth <note>A poetic way of saying he is about to die.</note>; and you shall know in your heart and in your soul that not one word has failed of all the words which the **Lord our God** spoke to you. All have come to pass for you; not one of them has failed. Now **Eglon** was an exceedingly **stout man** <note>original: "ἀστεῖος" (*asteios*). On that day, it happened to Sarah, the daughter of Raguel in Ecbatana <note>a major city in the ancient Persian Empire</note> of Media, that she also heard reproaches from one of her father's maidservants. This was because she had been given in marriage to seven husbands, and Asmodeus <note>original: *ΑϹΜΟΔΑΥϹ* (Asmodaus), an evil demon known in Jewish folklore as the "king of demons"</note>, the evil demon, killed them before they could be with her according to the custom of women. 

And the maidservant said to her: "You are the one who strangles your husbands! Look, you have already been given to seven men, and you have not benefited from a single one of them! Why do you lash out at us? If they are dead, go with them! May we never see a son or daughter of yours forever!"

<column-break/>

On that day, she was deeply grieved in her soul and wept, and she went up to the upper room of her father’s house, intending to hang herself. But again she thought: "Lest they reproach my father and say, 'You had one beloved daughter, and she hanged herself because of her misfortunes,' and I would bring down the old age of my father with sorrow to Hades <note>original: *ΑΔΟΥ* (Adou), the realm of the dead</note>. It is better for me not to hang myself, but to pray to the Lord that I might die and no longer hear reproaches in my life."

At that time, stretching out her hands toward the window, she prayed and said: "Blessed are You, O Lord my God, and blessed is Your holy and honorable name forever! May all Your works bless You forever! And now, Lord, I have set my face and my eyes toward You. Command that I be released from the earth and no longer hear reproach. 

You know, Lord, that I am pure from every sin with a man, and I have not defiled my name or the name of my father in the land of my captivity. I am the only child of my father, and he has no other child to inherit from him, nor a brother nearby, nor a son, for whom I should keep myself as a wife. Seven of my husbands have already perished; why should I live? And if it does not seem good to You to kill me, Lord, look upon me and have mercy on me, that I may no longer hear such reproach."
