And he commanded that she be brought in where his silver vessels were kept, and he ordered that they should spread a table for her from his own delicacies and that she should drink of his own wine. But Judith said: “I will not eat of them, lest it become a <term>stumbling block</term> <gloss>original: σκάνδαλον (skandalon) — an occasion for sin or ritual impurity</gloss>; but I will be provided for from the things that I have brought with me.” 

And Holofernes said to her: “If the provisions you have with you run out, where shall we get similar things to give to you? For there is no one of your race here with us.” And Judith said to him: “As your soul lives, my lord, your servant will not consume what I have with me before the Lord <note>original: KC (Kyrios)</note> performs by my hand what He has planned.” 

And the servants of Holofernes led her into the tent, and she slept until midnight. And she rose towards the morning <term>watch</term> <note>The "morning watch" was the last period of the night, just before dawn.</note> and sent a message to Holofernes, saying: “Let my lord now command that your servant be allowed to go out for prayer.” And Holofernes commanded the bodyguards not to hinder her. And she remained in the camp for three days, and went out each night to the valley of Bethulia and <term>washed herself</term> <gloss>original: εβαπτίζετο (ebaptizeto) — ritually immersed herself</gloss> in the camp at the spring of water. And when she came up from the water, she prayed to the Lord God of Israel <note>original: ΚΥ ΘΥ ΙCΛ (Kyriou Theou Israel)</note> to direct her way for the restoration of the sons of His people. And entering the camp purified, she remained in her tent until her food was brought to her toward evening.

And it happened on the fourth day, Holofernes prepared a feast for his own servants only, and he did not invite any of the officials who were on duty.

# The Banquet of Holofernes and the Triumph of Judith

And Bagoas said to the eunuch who was in charge of all his affairs: "Go now and persuade the Hebrew woman who is with you to come to us and eat and drink with us. For look, it would be a disgrace to our reputation if we let such a woman go without having been with her; for if we do not draw her to us, she will laugh at us." 

And Bagoas went out from the presence of Holofernes and went in to her. He said, "Let not this beautiful young woman hesitate to come to my lord, to be honored in his presence, and to drink with us for merriment, as one of the daughters of the Assyrians <note>original: ΥΙΩΝ ΑΣΣΟΥΡ (huion Assour)</note> who serve in the house of Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: ΝΑΒΟΥΧΟΔΟΝΟΣΟΡ (Nabouchodonosor)</note>."

And Judith said to him, "And who am I to refuse my lord? For everything that is pleasing in his eyes I will do quickly, and this shall be a joy to me until the day of my death."

And rising, she adorned herself with her garments and all her feminine finery. And her maid <gloss>original: ΑΒΡΑ (abra) — a personal handmaid or favorite servant</gloss> went ahead and spread out on the ground for her, in front of Holofernes, the fleeces she had received from Bagoas for her daily use <gloss>original: δίαιταν (diaitan)</gloss>, so that she might recline upon them while eating.

And when Judith entered, she reclined. And the heart of Holofernes was amazed by her, and his soul was moved, and he greatly desired to be with her; he had been watching for an opportunity to deceive <note>or "seduce"</note> her from the day he first saw her.

And Holofernes said to her, "Drink now, and be merry with us."

And Judith said, "I will drink indeed, my lord, because my life has been magnified within me today more than all the days since my birth."

And she took what her maid had prepared and ate and drank in his presence. And Holofernes was delighted with her and drank a great deal of wine, 

<column-break/>

so much more than he had ever drunk since the day he was born. Now when evening came, his servants hurried to depart. 

<margin>13:</margin> And Bagoas shut the tent from the outside and dismissed those standing in the presence of his lord. And they went to their beds, for they were all weary because the drinking had gone on for so long.

But Judith was left alone in the tent, and Holofernes was slumped over upon his bed, for he was drenched in wine. 

And Judith told her maid to stand outside her bedchamber and to watch for her exit, just as she did every day; for she said she would be going out for her prayer. And she had spoken to Bagoas in these same words.

And everyone departed from his presence, and no one was left in the bedchamber, from the least to the greatest.

And Judith, standing by the head of his bed, said: "Lord God of all power, look upon the works of my hands in this hour for the exaltation of Jerusalem. For now is the time to take up your inheritance and to carry out my plan for the destruction of the enemies who have risen up against us."

And going to the bed-post <gloss>original: ΚΑΝΟΝΙ (kanoni)</gloss> at Holofernes' head, she took down his <term>scimitar</term> <gloss>original: ΑΚΙΝΑΚΗΝ (akinakēn) — a short, straight or slightly curved Persian sword</gloss> from its place.

And drawing near the bed, she seized the hair of his head and said, "Strengthen me, Lord God of Israel, on this day!"

And she struck his neck twice with all her might and took his head away from him.

And she rolled his body off the bedding and pulled down the <term>canopy</term> <gloss>original: ΚΩΝΩΠΙΟΝ (kōnōpion) — literally "mosquito net," a luxury item in the ancient world</gloss> from the pillars. A moment later, she went out and gave the head of Holofernes to her maid.

# The Return to Bethulia and the Display of the Trophy

...our God, who [has heard] our prayer <note>original: ΤΟΝ ΘΝ ΗΜΩΝ ΤΟΝ ΕΠΙ ΤΗΝ ΠΡΟΕΥΧΗΝ (ton theon hēmon ton epi tēn proseukhēn)</note>. The leaders of the people and of the priests also committed many lawless acts and exceeded all the impurities of all the nations. These men killed their young men with the sword all around their holy temple. They spared neither young man nor virgin, neither old man nor the younger among the holy ones, but He delivered everything into their hands. They took all the large and small holy vessels of the Lord, the vessels of the ark of the Lord, and the royal storehouses, and carried them away to Babylon. They burned the house of the Lord, broke down the walls of Jerusalem, and destroyed its towers with fire.

This was to fulfill the word of the Lord spoken through the mouth of Jeremiah: "Until the land has enjoyed its sabbaths; for all the time of its desolation it shall keep sabbath <note>A 'sabbath' for the land was a period of rest from farming, here used to describe the 70-year exile</note> until the completion of seventy years."

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the Jewish return from exile. Having previously described the decree of Cyrus, it now details the specific inventory of the Temple vessels being returned and the subsequent political opposition faced during the reign of Artaxerxes. ### The Return of the Holy Vessels

The **holy vessels of the Lord** <note>original: ΤΑ ΙΕΡΑ ΣΚΕΥΗ ΤΟΥ ΚΥ</note> which **Nebuchadnezzar** <note>The Babylonian king who destroyed the first Temple</note> had carried away from **Jerusalem** <note>original: ΙΛΗΜ, a common abbreviation for Ierousalem</note> and deposited in his own idol-temple, were brought forth by **Cyrus**, the King of the Persians. He delivered them to **Mithridates**, his own treasurer, and through him they were handed over to **Sanabassar** <note>Likely the same person as Sheshbazzar mentioned in the Book of Ezra</note>, the governor of Judea.

The inventory of these items was as follows:
*   **One thousand** gold libation bowls
*   **One thousand** silver libation bowls
*   **Twenty-nine** silver cooling vessels
*   **Thirty** gold vials
*   **Two thousand seven hundred and ten** silver vials
*   **One thousand** other vessels

In total, the gold and silver vessels that were brought back numbered **five thousand four hundred and ninety-nine**. These were carried up by Sanabassar, along with those returning from the captivity, from Babylon to Jerusalem.

### The Letter to Artaxerxes

But in the time of **Artaxerxes**, the King of the Persians, a letter was written against those living in Judea and Jerusalem by **Bishlam**, **Mithridates**, **Tabeel**, **Rathumus**, **Beeltethmus**, and **Shimshai** <note>original: ΣΑΜΣΑΙΟΣ</note> the scribe, along with the rest of their associates living in **Samaria** and other places. The following is the letter written to King Artaxerxes, their lord:

"To King Artaxerxes, our lord: from your servants **Rathumus** the recorder <note>literally "the one in charge of things that fall to him"</note> and **Shimshai** <note>original: ΣΕΜΕΛΛΙΟΣ</note> the scribe, and the rest of their council, and the judges in **Coele-Syria** <note>term: Coele-Syria; literally "Hollow Syria," a regional administrative district including much of the Levant</note> and **Phoenicia**.

"Let it now be known to our lord the king, that the Jews who came up from you to us have arrived in Jerusalem—that rebellious and wicked city. They are rebuilding it, repairing its marketplaces and walls, and laying the foundations for a temple. If this city is rebuilt and its walls are completed, they will not endure paying taxes, but will even stand against kings. And because the work on the temple is proceeding,

<column-break/>

we consider it right not to overlook this matter, but to address our lord the king. If it seems good to you, let a search be made in the books of your ancestors <note>original: πατερων, "fathers"</note>. You will find in these records what has been written about these things, and you will learn that this city was a rebel, troubling both kings and cities. The Jews are rebels who have been instigating sieges within it since ancient times; for this reason, the city was made desolate. Now, therefore, we declare to you, lord king, that if this city is rebuilt and its walls raised up, you will no longer have a route of access into Coele-Syria and Phoenicia."

### The King’s Decree

Then the king wrote back to Rathumus the recorder, Beeltethmus, Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of their associates living in Samaria, **Cyprus**, and Phoenicia, as follows:

"I have read the letter which you sent to me. Therefore, I ordered a search to be made, and it was found that this city has from ancient times opposed kings, and its people have carried out rebellions and wars within it. Powerful kings were once in Jerusalem, ruling and taxing Coele-Syria and Phoenicia. Now, therefore, I have ordered that these men be forbidden from building the city, and that care be taken so that nothing further is done contrary to this, lest these evil dealings proceed further to annoy kings."

When the letter from King Artaxerxes was read, Rathumus and Shimshai the scribe and their associates set out in haste to Jerusalem with horsemen and a great crowd...

<margin>Chapter 3</margin> And King Darius gave a great feast for all his subjects, and for all his household, and for all the nobles of **Media** and **Persia**, and for all the **satraps** <term>satrap: a provincial governor in the ancient Persian Empire</term>, and the generals, and the governors under him, from **India** to **Ethiopia**—one hundred and twenty-seven provinces. And they ate and drank, and being satisfied, they departed. Then Darius the king went into his bedchamber and slept, and then he woke up.

Then the three young men of the bodyguard who protected the king's person said to one another: "Let each of us speak one sentence that shall prevail. And to him whose sentence appears wiser than the others, King Darius shall give great gifts and great honors of victory: he shall be clothed in **purple** <note>A dye so expensive in antiquity it was reserved for royalty</note>, and drink from gold vessels, and sleep on a gold bed, and have a chariot with gold bridles, and a turban of fine linen, and a necklace around his neck. And he shall sit second after Darius because of his wisdom, and shall be called the **Kinsman** <note>original: ΣΥΓΓΕΝΗΣ, an honorary title for the king's closest advisors</note> of Darius." Then each of them, having written his own sentence, sealed it with their rings and put it under the pillow of King Darius.

The first wrote: **Wine is the strongest.**

The second wrote: **The king is the strongest.**

The other wrote: **Women are the strongest, but above all things, Truth conquers.** <note>original: ΥΠΕΡ ΔΕ ΠΑΝΤΑ ΝΙΚΑ Η ΑΛΗΘΕΙΑ, a famous phrase often quoted in Latin as "Magna est veritas et praevalebit"</note>

And when the king was awakened, they took the writing and gave it to him, and he read it. And sending out, he called all the nobles of Persia and Media, and the satraps, generals, governors, and chief officers. And he sat in the council chamber, and the writing was read before them. Then the first, who had spoken of the strength of wine, began and said: "Men, how is it that wine is the strongest? It deceives the mind of all men who drink it. It makes the mind of the king and the orphan to be one and the same; likewise of the slave and the free man, of the poor and the rich. And it turns every thought into cheerfulness and joy, and it remembers no sorrow or debt. And it makes every heart feel rich, and remembers neither king nor satrap; and it makes all speak in **talents** <term>talent: a very large unit of weight or money, suggesting extravagant talk</term>. And when they drink, they do not remember friendship or brothers, and after a little while they draw their swords. And when they are recovered from the wine, they do not remember what they have done. O men, is not wine the strongest, since it forces men to do such things?" And having said this, he fell silent.

Besides all this, he himself lies down, eats, drinks, and sleeps. But these guards keep watch around him in a circle; no one can leave to attend to his own business, nor do they ever disobey him. O men, how can the King not be the strongest, since he is obeyed in such a fashion? And then he fell silent.

### COPY OF THE LETTER WHICH HE WROTE TO DARIUS AND SENT

**Sisinnes**, the governor of Syria and Phoenicia, and **Sathrabuzanes**, and their companions, the rulers in Syria and Phoenicia, to King Darius, greetings. Let all things be known to our lord the king, that when we came into the country of Judea and entered the city of Jerusalem <note>original: "ΙΑΗΜ" — an abbreviation for Hierousalem (Jerusalem)</note>, we found the elders of the Jews who had been in captivity in the city of Jerusalem building a great and costly house to the Lord <note>original: "Κυ" — Nomina Sacra for "Κυριου" (Lord)</note>, made of polished, expensive stones, with timber laid into the walls. And those works are being done with great speed and are prospering in their hands, and are being completed with all glory and care.

Then we questioned those elders, saying, "By whose decree are you building this house and finishing this roof and these other things?" Therefore, we questioned them so that we might write to you the names of the men who are the leaders, and we requested from them a list of the names of those who are in charge.

And they answered us, saying, "We are servants of the Lord <note>original: "Κυ"</note> who created the heaven and the earth. And the house was built many years ago by a king of Israel <note>original: "ΙCΛ" — abbreviation for Israel</note>, great and strong, and it was completed. But when our fathers provoked the God <note>original: "Θν" — Nomina Sacra for "Θεον" (God)</note> of heaven, He gave them into the hands of **Nebuchadnezzar** <note>original: "ΝΑΒΟΥΧΟΔΟΝΟCΟΡ"</note>, the king of Babylon, of the Chaldeans; and they pulled down the house and burned it, and they led the people away captive to Babylon."

<column-break/>

"But in the first year of the reign of **Cyrus** over the land of Babylonia, King Cyrus wrote that this house should be rebuilt. And the holy gold and silver vessels, which Nebuchadnezzar had carried out of the house in Jerusalem and placed in his own temple, King Cyrus brought out again from the temple in Babylon, and they were delivered to **Zerubbabel** and to **Sanabassarus** the governor. And it was commanded him that he should carry these vessels back and put them in the temple in Jerusalem, and that this temple of the Lord <note>original: "Κυ"</note> should be rebuilt on its site. Then that Sanabassarus, having come here, laid the foundations of the house of the Lord <note>original: "Κυ"</note> in Jerusalem; and from that time until now it has been under construction and has not reached completion." Now therefore, if it is judged right by the king, let search be made in the royal archives <note>original: "βιβλιοφυλακίοις" — literally 'book-safes' or libraries</note> of our lord the king in Babylon. And if it be found that the building of the house in Jerusalem was done with the consent of King Cyrus, let him inform us concerning these things as is fitting.

Then King Darius commanded a search to be made in the archives located in Babylon; and there was found in Ecbatana, the fortress in the land of Media, a scroll <note>original: "τόμος" — a volume or roll of papyrus/parchment</note> in which this memorandum was recorded:

---

In the first year of the reign of Cyrus, King Cyrus commanded that the house of the Lord <note>original: "Κυ"</note> in Jerusalem should be rebuilt, where they offer sacrifices with continual fire; its height to be sixty cubits and its breadth sixty cubits, with three layers of polished stones and one layer of new local wood, and the expense to be given out of the house <note>the royal treasury</note>...

For they have been joined in marriage with the daughters of these people, both they and their sons, and the <term>holy seed</term> <note>original: "ϲπέρμα το ἅγιον" — This refers to the lineage of the Israelites, which was intended to remain distinct according to the Mosaic Law</note> has been mixed with the foreign nations of the land. And as soon as I heard these things, I tore my garments and the **holy robe** <note>original: "ἱερὰν ἐϲθῆτα"</note>, and I pulled out the hair of my head and my beard, and I sat down heavy-hearted and full of sorrow. And rising from my fast with my garments and the **holy robe** torn, I knelt down and stretched out my hands toward the Lord, saying: "O Lord, I am ashamed and disgraced before you. mercy has come to us from you, O Lord, that there should be left to us a **root** <note>original: "ρίζαν" — a metaphor for a remnant or a surviving group of people from which a nation can grow again</note> and a name in the place of your sanctuary, and to reveal a light for us in the house of the Lord our God, and to give us food in the time of our servitude. 

Even while we were in servitude, we were not abandoned by our Lord, but He brought us into favor before the kings of the Persians, to give us sustenance and to glorify the temple of our Lord, and to raise up the desolate Zion and give us a stronghold in Judea and Jerusalem.

And now, O Lord, what shall we say, having these things? And all that has happened to us has come about because of our evil deeds and our great sins. For you, Lord, lightened the weight of our sins and gave us such a root; yet we turned back again to transgress your law by mixing with the uncleanness of the nations of the land. 

Were you not angry enough with us to destroy us until no root, seed, or name of ours was left? Behold, we are now before you in our lawlessness; for it is no longer possible to stand in your presence because of these things."

And they were called by their names. They sought their registry of genealogy but they were not found, and so they were excluded from the priesthood as defiled. And the Tirshatha <note>original: "Athersatha"—a title for the Persian governor, likely referring here to Zerubbabel</note> told them not to eat of the most holy things until a priest should arise for the "Illuminations" and the "Perfections." <note>original: "tois phōtizousin kai tois teleiois"—these terms refer to the Urim and Thummim, the sacred lots used by the High Priest to discern the divine will.</note>

The entire assembly of those who had returned from the captivity of Israel numbered in the myriads. Besides their male and female servants—of whom there were seven thousand three hundred and thirty-seven—there were also two hundred and fifty male and female singers. Their mules numbered seven hundred and thirty-six; their camels, four hundred and thirty-five; and their donkeys, six thousand seven hundred and twenty.

And some of the heads of the families, upon coming to the House of the Lord in Jerusalem, gave free-will offerings for the House of God to set it up on its site. According to their ability, they gave to the treasury of the work sixty-one thousand drachmas <note>original: "mna"—the Greek text uses "mna" (minas) but often represents the Persian daric or drachma in these lists</note> of gold, and five thousand minas of silver, and one hundred priestly tunics. So the priests, the Levites, some of the people, the singers, the gatekeepers, and the temple servants <note>term: "Natheneim"—descendants of those given to the service of the Levites, often non-Israelite in origin</note> dwelt in their cities, and all Israel lived in their towns.

<margin>3~</margin> And when the seventh month arrived and the children of Israel were in their cities, the people gathered together as one man to Jerusalem.

Then Jeshua <note>original: "Iēsous"</note> the son of Jozadak arose, with his brothers the priests, and Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel with his brothers, and they built the altar of the God of Israel to offer burnt offerings upon it, as it is written in the Law of Moses, the man of God. And they prepared the altar upon its base, for they were in fear because of the peoples of the lands; and they offered burnt offerings upon it to the

<column-break/>

Lord, burnt offerings for the morning and the evening. And they celebrated the Feast of Tabernacles <note>original: "skēnopēgias"—also known as Sukkot, a harvest festival where people lived in temporary booths</note> as it is written, with the required number of daily burnt offerings according to the ordinance for each day. And after that, they offered the continual burnt offerings, and those for the New Moons, and for all the hallowed feasts of the Lord, and for everyone who offered a voluntary gift to the Lord.

From the first day of the seventh month, they began to offer burnt offerings to the Lord, though the foundation of the House of the Lord was not yet laid. They gave money to the stone-cutters and the carpenters, and food, drink, and oil to the Sidonians and Tyrians to bring cedar wood from Lebanon by sea to Joppa, according to the grant given to them by Cyrus, King of the Persians.

And in the second year of their coming to the House of God at Jerusalem, in the second month, Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel and Jeshua the son of Jozadak began the work, along with the rest of their brothers the priests, the Levites, and all who had come from the captivity to Jerusalem. They appointed the Levites from twenty years old and upward to oversee the work in the House of the Lord. And Jeshua stood with his sons and his brothers, Kadmiel and his sons, the sons of Judah, together to oversee those doing the work in the House of God; also the sons of Henadad, with their sons and their brothers the Levites. And the builders laid the foundation of the House of the Lord. Then the priests stood in their vestments with trumpets,

and the Levites, the sons of Asaph, with cymbals, to praise the Lord according to the directions of David, King of Israel. And they sang responsively with praise and thanksgiving to the Lord, saying, "For He is good, for His mercy endures forever toward Israel."

And all the people shouted with a great shout to praise the Lord because the foundation of the House of the Lord was laid.

...[the laying of the] foundation of the house of the Lord. <note>The text begins mid-sentence, describing the ceremony for the second Temple.</note> And many of the priests and the Levites and the heads of the ancestral houses—the elders who had seen the first house <note>This refers to Solomon's Temple, destroyed by the Babylonians about 50 years earlier.</note> on its foundation—when they saw this house with their own eyes, they wept with a loud voice. <margin>4:~</margin> And the enemies of Judah and Benjamin heard that the sons of the exile were building a house to the Lord God of Israel. <note>original: "ΚΩ ΘΩ ΙΣΛ" — a contraction of "Kyrio Theo Israel" (Lord God of Israel).</note> And they approached Zerubbabel and the heads of the ancestral houses and said to them: “Let us build with you, for we seek your God just as you do, and we have been sacrificing to Him since the days of Esarhaddon, king of Assyria, who brought us here.”

But Zerubbabel and Jeshua and the rest of the heads of the ancestral houses of Israel said to them: “It is not for us and you together to build a house to our God; for we ourselves will build together to the Lord our God, just as Cyrus the king of the Persians commanded us.” And the people of the land <note>This term refers to the local inhabitants who were not part of the returning exile group.</note> weakened the hands of the people of Judah and hindered them from building. They even hired counselors against them to frustrate their plan all the days of Cyrus, king of the Persians, and until the reign of Darius the king.

And in the reign of Ahasuerus <note>Also known as Xerxes I.</note> of the Persians, at the beginning of his reign, they wrote a letter against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem. <note>original: "ΙΛΗΜ" — abbreviation for Jerusalem.</note>

Rehum the chancellor, and Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of our fellow servants—the Dinaites, the Apharsathchites, the Tarpelites, the Apharsites, the Archyites, the Babylonians, the Susanchites, the Dehavites <note>These represent various ethnic groups settled in the region by the Assyrians.</note>—and the rest of the nations whom the great and honorable Osnappar <note>Likely a reference to the Assyrian King Ashurbanipal.</note> deported and settled in the cities of Samaria and the rest of the region beyond the River. <note>The "River" refers to the Euphrates; this was the name of the Persian province "Across-the-River."</note>

This is the copy of the letter which they sent to him:

To Artaxerxes the king, from your servants, the men beyond the River: Let it be known to the king that the Jews who came up from you to us have come to Jerusalem, the rebellious and wicked city. They are rebuilding it, its walls are being repaired, and they have raised up its foundations.

<margin>1</margin> Now let it be known to the king that if that city is built and its walls are completed, they will not pay tribute to you, nor will they give [taxes], and this does harm to kings. And since it is not permitted for us to see the king’s dishonor, for this reason we have sent word and made it known to the king, so that search may be made in the book of the records of your fathers. You will find and know that this city is a rebellious city, doing harm to kings and regions, and that acts of rebellion by slaves have occurred within it from ancient times. For these reasons this city was laid waste. We therefore make it known to the king that if that city is built and its walls are repaired, you will have no peace.

And the king sent a reply to Rehum the chancellor, and Shimshai the scribe, and the rest...

...their associates who dwell in Samaria and the rest of the regions across the River <note>This refers to the Euphrates River, denoting the western part of the Persian Empire.</note>, greeting.

<margin>K</margin>And they say: "The tax official whom you sent to us has read [your letter] before me. I have given orders and a search has been made, and it has been discovered that that city has from ancient times risen up against kings, and that rebellions and desertions are carried out within it. And strong kings have arisen in Jerusalem, ruling and collecting taxes from the region across the River. And now, taxes shall be levied. This command has been given. And now, be firm in stopping those men, so that that city shall not be built anymore, lest we should eventually have to watch for whatever troubles might arise, being concerned that evils might clearly be brought upon the kings."

<margin>T</margin>Then, the letter from King Artaxerxes having been read before Rehum and Shimshai the scribe <note>original: "ΣΑΜΕΟΥ" (Sameou) — a Greek variant of the name Shimshai.</note> and their associates, they hurried in haste to Jerusalem and returned to those in Judea; and they stopped the building of Jerusalem. <meta>This page continues the narrative from the Book of 1 Esdras (also known as 3 Ezra in some traditions). On the previous page, the local officials of the Persian Empire had questioned the legality of the Jews rebuilding the Temple in Jerusalem. This page contains the quoted contents of the historical search for King Cyrus’s original decree and the subsequent decree issued by King Darius confirming the Jews' right to build.</meta>

### THE RECOVERY OF THE DECREE OF CYRUS

And the vessels of the house of God <note>original: "ΘΥ" (Theou) — a common abbreviation for God used by scribes.</note>, the gold and the silver, which Nebuchadnezzar took from the house in Jerusalem and brought into the King's temple—King Cyrus brought them out from the King's temple and gave them to Sheshbazzar <note>original: "ΣΑΣΑΒΑΣΣΑΡΩ" — a Persian official or perhaps another name for Zerubbabel, the leader of the returning exiles.</note>, the treasurer in charge of the treasury. And he commanded him: "Take these vessels and go, and place them in the house in Jerusalem, and let the site of the temple be built in its own place." Then that Sheshbazzar came and laid the foundations of the house of God in Jerusalem; and from that time until now it is being built and has not been finished. And now, if it seems good to the King, let a search be made in the royal treasury of the King of Babylon, so that it may be known if a decree was issued by King Cyrus to build the house of God in Jerusalem; and whatever the King judges right concerning this, let him write and send word to us.

<margin>6: - |</margin>When King Darius read the letter, he ordered a search, and the records of the past were found in Ecbatana <note>The summer capital of the Persian Empire, located in modern-day Iran.</note>, the fortress in the land of the Medes. And in that same place a scroll was found, and in it was written a record concerning us: "In the first year of the reign of Cyrus, he commanded that the house of God in Jerusalem be built, where they offer sacrifices continually by fire. Its height shall be sixty cubits and its width sixty cubits, with three courses of polished stones and one course of new timber; and let the expense be sent from the house of the King. And the silver and gold vessels of the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar took from the house in Jerusalem and carried to Babylon, let them be restored to the temple in Jerusalem, to the place of the foundations of God."

<column-break/>

### THE DECREE OF KING DARIUS

"Now therefore, Sisinnes, governor of the region across the River <note>This refers to the province 'Trans-Euphrates,' the western part of the empire.</note>, and Sathrabuzanes and their fellow-servants, the Apharsachaeans who are across the River—stay far away from there! And let the work of the house of God be done. Let the governor of the Jews and the elders of the Jews build that house of God in its place. And it has been decreed and established by me: 'Lest you ever act against the elders of the Jews to build this house for God—that one—and from the royal taxes across the River, let the expense be diligently given to those men so the work is not hindered. And whatever is lacking—young bulls and rams and lambs for whole burnt offerings to the God of heaven, wheat, salt, wine, oil—according to the word of the priests of the Jews who are in Jerusalem, let it be given to them day by day, whatever they ask for without fail, so they may offer sacrifices to the God of heaven and pray for the life of the King and his sons.'"

"And it has been proclaimed that if anyone violates or changes anything of what I have written, a beam shall be taken from his own property and he shall be hanged on it, and his property shall become the King’s. And may the Lord <note>original: "ΚΣ" (Kyrios) — a scribal abbreviation for the Lord.</note> whose name is called upon there destroy every king and nation that stretches out its hand to hinder or harm that house of God in Jerusalem. I, King Darius, have decreed that it be done thus according to these things."

### THE RESUMPTION OF THE WORK

Then Sisinnes, governor of the region across the River, and Sathrabuzanes and their fellow-servants followed the orders of King Darius. They oversaw the works with great care, assisting the elders of the Jews; and the works progressed through the prophets Haggai and Zechariah the son of Iddo <note>original: "ΙΔΔΩ" — the prophets who encouraged the people to finish the Temple after the long delay.</note>.

# The Prayer of the Levites
## Historical Recounting of the Covenant

You give life to all things, and the hosts of heaven worship you.
<margin>—</margin> You are the Lord <note>original: ΘϹ (Theos), a shortened "sacred name" (Nomina Sacra) for God</note>, you who chose Abram and brought him out of the land of the Chaldeans <note>Ancient region in Mesopotamia, modern-day Iraq</note> and gave him the name Abraham. You found his heart faithful before you, and you made a covenant with him to give to him 
<margin>—</margin> the land of the Canaanites,
and the Hittites,
and the Amorites,
and the Perizzites,
and the Jebusites,
and the Girgashites,
and to his descendants.
<margin>—</margin> And you have kept your words, because you are righteous. You saw the suffering of our fathers in Egypt, and you heard their cry at the Red Sea. You performed signs and wonders against Pharaoh, and against all his servants, and against all the people of his land, because you knew that they acted insolently against them. You made a name for yourself, as it is this day. You divided the sea before them, and they passed through the middle of the sea on dry land; but those who pursued them you threw into the depths like a stone into mighty water.
<margin>—</margin> And in a pillar of cloud you led them by day, and in a pillar of fire by night, to light for them the way in which they should travel. You also came down upon Mount Sinai and spoke to them from heaven; you gave them right judgments and laws of truth, good statutes and commandments. You made known to them your holy Sabbath, and you commanded them commandments and statutes and a law by the hand of Moses your servant. You gave them bread from heaven <note>referring to Manna</note> for their hunger, and you brought water for them out of a rock for their thirst.

<column-break/>

You told them to go in to inherit the land which you had sworn <note>literally "stretched out your hand"</note> to give to them. But they 
<margin>—</margin> and our fathers acted proudly; they stiffened their necks and did not listen to your commandments. They refused to obey and did not remember your wonders which you performed among them. They stiffened their necks and appointed a leader to return to their slavery
<margin>—</margin> in Egypt. But you are a God <note>original: ΘϹ (Theos)</note> of forgiveness, merciful and compassionate, long-suffering and rich in mercy, and you did not forsake them. Even when they 
<margin>—</margin> made for themselves a molten calf and said, "These are the gods who brought us up out of Egypt," and committed great provocations, 
<margin>—</margin> you, in your many mercies, did not forsake them in the wilderness. The pillar of cloud did not depart from them by day to lead them on the way, nor the pillar of fire by night to light for them the way in which they should travel. 
<margin>—</margin> You gave your good Spirit to instruct them, and you did not withhold your manna from their mouth, and you gave them water for their thirst. 
<margin>—</margin> For forty years you sustained them in the wilderness; they lacked nothing. Their clothes did not wear out and their feet did not swell <note>literally "break out" or "become raw"</note>. 
<margin>—</margin> You gave them kingdoms and peoples and divided them among them. So they inherited the land of Sihon king of Heshbon and the land of Og king of Bashan.
<margin>—</margin> And you multiplied their children like the stars of heaven, and you brought them into the land which you told their fathers to enter and inherit. And they entered...

**A**nd before this, Eliashib the priest, who lived in the chamber of the house of our God, was close to Tobiah <note>An official and opponent of Nehemiah who had been given a room in the Temple courts</note>. And during all this, I was not in Jerusalem <note>original shorthand: "ΙΛΗΜ" (ILĒM)</note>; for in the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes <note>A Persian King, though here titled "King of Babylon" as the Persians ruled over that territory</note>, king of Babylon, I went to the king; and after a period of days, I asked leave of the king and I came to Jerusalem. And I understood the evil that Eliashib had done for Tobiah by making for him a chamber in the court of the house of God. And it seemed very evil to me; and I threw all the household vessels of Tobiah out of the chamber. And I spoke, and they cleansed the chambers; and I returned there the vessels of the house of God, the grain offering, and the frankincense.

**A**nd I recognized that the portions of the Levites had not been given; and they had fled, each man to his own field—the Levites and the singers who performed the work. And I fought <note>In the sense of rebuking or contending with the officials</note> and said: "Why has the house of God been forsaken?" And I gathered them and set them in their stations. And all Judah brought the tithe of the wheat, and the wine, and the oil into the treasuries under the hand of Shelemiah the priest, and Zadok the scribe, and Pedaiah from the Levites.

In those days I saw in Judah people treading winepresses on the Sabbath <note>The holy day of rest</note>, and bringing in heaps of grain, and loading them onto donkeys, and wine, and grapes, and figs, and every kind of burden, and bringing them into Jerusalem on the day of the Sabbath.

**A**nd I testified against them on the day of their selling. And they sat there bringing in fish and every kind of merchandise, selling it on the Sabbath to the children of Judah and in Jerusalem. And I fought with the free men <note>The nobles or leaders</note> of Judah and said to them: "What is this evil thing that you are doing, profaning the day of the Sabbath? Did not your fathers do this very thing, and our God brought upon them and upon us all these evils, and upon this city? And you are adding more wrath upon Israel by profaning the Sabbath."

**A**nd it happened when the gates were set in Jerusalem before the Sabbath, I spoke, and they closed the gates; and I spoke so that they should not be opened until after the Sabbath. And I stationed some of my young men at the gates, so that no burdens might enter on the day of the Sabbath. And they all lodged and performed their selling outside Jerusalem once or twice. And I testified among them and said to them: "Why do you lodge in front of the wall? If you do it a second time, I will stretch out my hand against you."

And it happened, after Alexander the son of Philip, the Macedonian, who came out of the land of Kittim <note>original: "Χεττιειμ" (Chettieim); here referring to Greece or Macedonia</note>, had defeated Darius, king of the Persians and Medes, that he reigned in his place, having previously ruled over Greece. He waged many wars, captured strongholds, and slaughtered the kings of the earth. He advanced to the ends of the earth and took spoils from a multitude of nations. The earth was silent before him, and his heart was exalted and lifted up. He gathered a very powerful army and ruled over countries, nations, and tyrants, and they became tributary to him.

And after these things, he fell upon his bed and realized that he was dying. So he called his most honored officers <note>original: "παιδας" (paidas); literally 'boys' or 'servants', but referring to his high-ranking companions and generals</note>, who had been brought up with him from his youth, and divided his kingdom among them while he was still alive. Alexander reigned twelve years and then died.

Then his officers took over the government, each in his own place. After he died, they all put on crowns, as did their sons after them for many years; and they multiplied evils upon the earth.

And this city was large and very strong, situated directly on the road. It was not possible to turn aside from it to the right or to the left, but they had to pass through the middle of it. <margin>—</margin>And Judas sent a message to them with peaceful words, saying: "We will pass through your land only to go into our own land, and no one will harm you; we will only pass through on foot." But they were not willing to open for him.

And Judas ordered it to be proclaimed in the camp that each man should encamp in the place where he was. And the men of the army encamped, and they fought against the city all that day and all that night, and the city was delivered into his hands. And he destroyed every male with the edge of the sword, and he razed <note>literally "uprooted"</note> the city and took its spoils. And he passed through the city over those who had been slain. And they crossed the Jordan into the great plain <note>the Jezreel Valley</note> opposite **Beth-shan** <note>original: "ΒΑΙΘCΑ^"; a major Greco-Roman city also known as Scythopolis</note>.

<margin>—</margin>And Judas was gathering the stragglers and encouraging the people all along the way until he came to the land of Judah. And they went up to **Mount Zion** with gladness and joy, and they offered burnt offerings because not one of them had fallen until they returned in peace.

<column-break/>

And in those days when Judas and Jonathan were in Gilead, and Simon his brother was in Galilee opposite **Ptolemais**, **Joseph** the son of Zacharias and **Azarias** <note>the transcription reads "Zacharias" here, though the text later identifies him as Azarias, a fellow commander</note>, commanders of the forces, heard of the heroic deeds and the battles they had done. And they said: "Let us also make a name for ourselves and go to fight against the nations around us." And they gave orders to those of the force with them and marched toward **Jamnia** <note>a coastal city in Philistia</note>.

And **Gorgias** <note>a Seleucid general</note> came out from the city with his men to meet them in battle. And Joseph and Azarias were put to flight and were pursued to the borders of Judea. And on that day about two thousand men of the people of Israel fell. And there was a great rout among the people, because they did not listen to Judas and his brothers, thinking they would do heroic deeds.

But they were not of the lineage <note>original: "CΠΕΡΜΑΤOC" (spermatos), meaning 'seed' or 'offspring'</note> of those men to whom the deliverance of Israel was given by their hand. And the man Judas and his brothers were greatly honored in the sight of all Israel and all the nations where their name was heard. And people gathered to them with shouts of praise.

And Judas and his brothers went out and fought against the sons of **Esau** <note>the Edomites</note> in the land toward the south. And he struck **Hebron** and its villages <note>literally "daughters"; meaning the surrounding settlements</note>, and he tore down its fortress and burned its towers all around. And he set out to go into the land of the foreigners <note>the Philistines</note> and passed through **Samaria**. On that day, certain priests fell in battle, desiring to do heroic deeds themselves by going out to war ill-advisedly.

And Judas turned aside to **Azotus** <note>modern Ashdod</note> in the land of the foreigners, and he tore down their altars and burned the carved images of their gods with fire, and he took the spoils of the cities. <meta>catchword: ΠOΛΕΩ (cities)</meta>

# THE DECLINE AND DEATH OF KING ANTIOCHUS

AND KING ANTIOCHUS was passing through the upper countries <note>The "upper countries" refers to the eastern provinces of the Seleucid Empire, specifically the regions of Persia and Media.</note>; and he heard that there was a city in **Elymais** in Persia, renowned for its wealth in silver and gold. And the temple within it was very rich; and there were golden coverings there, and breastplates and weapons which **Alexander**, the son of Philip, the Macedonian king who first reigned over the Greeks, had left there. And he came and sought to take the city and to plunder it. And he was not able, because the plan became known to those of the city, and they stood up against him in battle. And he fled and departed from there with great grief to return to **Babylon**.

And someone came into Persia announcing to him that the armies that had gone into the land of Judah had been put to flight; and that **Lysias** <note>original: "ΛΥΣΙΑΣ"; the high-ranking general and regent appointed by Antiochus to manage the western empire</note> had gone out with a strong force at first, but was turned back from before them; and that they <note>the Maccabees</note> had grown strong in weapons and power and with much spoil which they took from the armies they had cut down. And they had pulled down the **Abomination** <note>original: "ΒΔΕΛΥΓΜΑ"; referring to the pagan altar or "Abomination of Desolation" erected by the King’s orders</note> which he had built upon the altar in Jerusalem; and they had surrounded the sanctuary with high walls as it was before, and also **Beth-zur**, his city.

And it happened that when the king heard these words, he was amazed and greatly shaken. And he fell upon his bed and fell into a sickness from grief, because it had not happened for him as he had desired. And he remained there many days, for great grief was renewed upon him; and he realized that he was dying. And he called all his 

<column-break/>

friends and said to them: "Sleep departs from my eyes, and I have fallen in heart from anxiety. And I said to my heart: 'To what tribulation have I come, and into what a great flood am I now in!' For I was useful and beloved in my power. But now I remember the evils which I did in **Jerusalem** <note>original: "ΙΛΗΜ", an abbreviation for Hierosolyma/Jerusalem</note>; and I took all the silver and gold vessels that were in her, and I sent out to destroy those inhabiting Judah without cause. I know that because of these things, these evils have found me; and behold, I perish with great grief in a foreign land."

And he called **Philip**, one of his friends, and appointed him over all his kingdom. And he gave him the diadem and his robe and the ring, to lead **Antiochus** his son and to bring him up to reign. And King Antiochus died there in the one hundred and forty-ninth year <note>Approximately 164 BCE in the Seleucid calendar.</note>.

And Lysias learned that the king was dead; and he set up Antiochus his son to reign, whom he had brought up as a youth, and he called his name **Eupator** <note>meaning "of a good father"</note>. And those from the **Citadel** <note>The "Akra," a fortress in Jerusalem occupied by Seleucid troops and Hellenized Jews</note> were hemmed in **Israel** <note>original: "ΙΗΛ", an abbreviation for Israel</note> round about the sanctuary, and were seeking evils at all times and a support for the nations. And **Judas** planned to destroy them, and he gathered all the people to besiege them in the one hundred and fiftieth year. And he made siege-towers and engines against them. And some of them escaped from the blockade, and there were joined to them some of the godless of Israel.

# THE ROYAL RESPONSE AND THE MARCH OF THE ELEPHANTS

AND THEY WENT TO THE KING <note>The "they" refers to the Hellenized Jews and supporters of the Seleucid crown who opposed the Maccabean revolt.</note> AND SAID: "How long will you refrain from bringing justice and avenging our brothers? We were content to serve your father and to follow his words and to obey his commands. Because of this, the sons of our people have become strangers to us; furthermore, as many of us as were found were put to death, and our inheritances were seized. And they have not only reached out their hands against us, but also against all their borders.

AND BEHOLD, today they have laid siege to the **Akra** <note>original: "ΑΚΡΑΝ"; the fortified citadel in Jerusalem held by a Seleucid garrison</note> in Jerusalem to capture it; they have also fortified the sanctuary and **Beth-zur**. And unless you act quickly to stop them, they will do even greater things than these, and you will not be able to restrain them."

AND THE KING WAS ANGRY when he heard this, and he assembled all his Friends <note>original: "ΦΙΛΟΥΣ"; a technical title for the high-ranking advisors and nobility of the Seleucid court</note>, the officers of his army, and the commanders of the cavalry. And from other kingdoms and from the islands of the seas, mercenary forces came to him. And the number of his forces was one hundred thousand infantry and twenty thousand cavalry, and thirty-two elephants trained for war. And they came through **Idumea** and encamped against **Beth-zur**; they fought for many days and built siege engines. But the defenders came out and burned the engines with fire and fought bravely. Then **Judas** <note>Judas Maccabeus</note> withdrew from the Akra and encamped at **Beth-zechariah**, opposite the King’s camp.

<column-break/>

AND THE KING ROSE early in the morning and moved the camp in a sudden rush along the road to Beth-zechariah; and the forces were prepared for battle and the trumpets were sounded. To the elephants, they showed the blood of grapes and mulberries <note>original: "ΑΙΜΑ ΣΤΑΦΥΛΗΣ ΚΑΙ ΜΟΡΩΝ"; likely a technique used to incite the animals to a state of battle-rage by showing them red liquid resembling blood</note> to prepare them for the fight. And they divided the beasts among the phalanxes; and they stationed with each elephant a thousand men wearing coats of chain-mail and bronze helmets upon their heads. And five hundred elite cavalry were assigned to each beast. These were stationed beforehand wherever the beast was; and wherever it went, they went together, never leaving it.

AND WOODEN TOWERS were upon them, strong and covered, one on each beast, fastened to it by machines; and upon each were thirty-two <note>This number is exceptionally high for a single elephant tower and may reflect a scribal error or ancient exaggeration; some scholars suggest the original intended "two or three" soldiers.</note> brave men who fought from it, as well as the **Indian** <note>original: "ΙΝΔΟΣ"; the mahout or elephant driver, commonly called an 'Indian' as these trainers were traditionally brought from the East</note> driver. And the rest of the cavalry he stationed on either side, at the two flanks of the army, both to harass the enemy and to be protected by the phalanxes.

<margin>></margin> AND WHEN THE SUN SHONE UPON THE
<margin>></margin> GOLD AND BRONZE SHIELDS,
<margin>></margin> THE MOUNTAINS GLEAMED FROM THEM AND SHONE
<margin>></margin> LIKE TORCHES OF FIRE.

<margin>></margin> AND A PART OF THE KING’S ARMY was spread out over the high mountains, and some over the low places, and they marched safely and in good order. And everyone who heard the noise of their multitude, and the marching of the crowd, and the clashing of their weapons, was shaken; for the army was very great and powerful.

AND JUDAS AND HIS ARMY approached for the battle-line.

AND THERE FELL from the king’s camp six hundred men. And Eleazar Avaran saw one of the beasts <note>original: "ΘΗΡΙΩΝ"; referring here to the war elephants</note> armored with royal breastplates, and it stood out above all the other beasts. And it appeared that the king was upon it.

# THE DEFEAT OF NICANOR AND THE RISE OF THE ROMANS

...[an angel] of the Lord <note>original: "ΛΟCCΟΥ" (partial word continuing from previous page: "ΑΓΓΕΛΟCCΟΥ")</note>, and he struck down among them one hundred eighty-five thousand. In this way, he crushed their army before us today. And let the rest know that he has spoken evilly against your holy things; and judge him according to his wickedness.

And the armies joined in battle on the thirteenth day of the month of **Adar** <note>Adar is roughly February/March in the Jewish calendar</note>. And the army of **Nicanor** was crushed, and he himself fell first in the battle. Now, when his army saw that **Nicanor** had fallen, they threw down their weapons and fled. And [the Jews] pursued them for a full day's journey, from **Adasa** until reaching **Gazara**; and they sounded the signal trumpets behind them. And [people] came out from all the villages of **Judea** round about and outflanked them; and these [the pursuers] turned back toward those [the fugitives], and they all fell by the sword, and not even one of them was left.

And they took the spoils and the plunder; and they cut off the head of **Nicanor** and his right hand, which he had stretched out so arrogantly. And they brought and displayed them near **Jerusalem**. And the people rejoiced greatly, and they observed that day as a day of great gladness. And they established the custom of observing this day every year on the thirteenth of **Adar**. And the land of **Judah** was quiet for a few days.

<margin>8:~</margin> And **Judas** heard the name of the **Romans**, that they are powerful in strength and that they are well-disposed toward all who join them; and that they establish friendship with whoever approaches them. And [he heard] that they are powerful in strength. 

<column-break/>

And King **Alexander** <note>Alexander Balas, a pretender to the Seleucid throne who claimed to be the son of Antiochus IV</note> gathered great forces and encamped against **Demetrius**. And the two kings joined battle, and the army of **Alexander** fled; but **Demetrius** pursued him and prevailed over him. And the battle raged fiercely until the sun went down, and **Demetrius** fell on that day.

And **Alexander** sent ambassadors to **Ptolemy** <note>Ptolemy VI Philometor</note>, the king of **Egypt**, with these words, saying: "Since I have returned to my kingdom and have sat upon the throne of my fathers, and have taken hold of the government and crushed **Demetrius** and gained control of our country—for I joined battle with him, and he and his army were crushed by us, and we have sat upon the throne of his kingdom—now therefore let us establish friendship with one another. Give me your daughter now to be my wife, and I will be your son-in-law, and I will give to you and to her gifts worthy of you."

And King **Ptolemy** answered, saying: "Happy is the day in which you returned to the land of your fathers and sat upon the throne of their kingdom. And now I will do for you what you have written. But meet me at **Ptolemais** <note>A major coastal city, modern-day Acre</note> so that we may see one another, and I will become your father-in-law as you have said."

So **Ptolemy** set out from **Egypt**, he and his daughter **Cleopatra** <note>Cleopatra Thea, who would later become a powerful queen in her own right</note>, and they came to **Ptolemais** in the one hundred and sixty-second year <note>150 BCE, according to the Seleucid calendar</note>.

<column-break/>

And King **Alexander** met him, and **Ptolemy** gave him his daughter **Cleopatra**; and he celebrated her wedding in **Ptolemais** with great glory, as is the manner of kings.

And King **Alexander** wrote to **Jonathan** <note>Jonathan Apphus, the leader of the Jews and brother of Judas Maccabeus</note> to come and meet him. And he went with glory to **Ptolemais** and met the two kings, and he gave them silver and gold, and many gifts to their **Friends** <note>original: "φίλοι" (philoi), a specific rank of high-ranking courtiers in Hellenistic kingdoms</note>, and he found favor in their sight.

Then certain pestilent men <note>original: "ἄνδρες λοιμοί" (andres loimoi), a derogatory term for political troublemakers or rebels</note> from **Israel**, lawless men, gathered against him to testify against him, but the king paid them no attention. Instead, the king gave orders, and they stripped **Jonathan** of his own clothes and clothed him in **purple** <note>A symbol of the highest royal favor and authority</note>. And they did so.

And the king made him sit beside him, and said to his officers: "Go out with him into the middle of the city and proclaim that no one is to bring a charge against him concerning any matter, and let no one trouble him for any reason." And it happened that when those who were bringing charges saw his glory—just as the herald proclaimed—and saw him clothed in **purple**, they all fled. 

And the king honored him and enrolled him among his **Chief Friends**, and appointed him as **General** <term>Strategos; a military commander</term> and **Governor** <term>Meridarch; a civil administrator of a district</term>. Then **Jonathan** returned to **Jerusalem** in peace and gladness. And in the one hundred and sixty-fifth year <note>147 BCE</note>...

**DEMETRIUS** <note>Demetrius II Nicator</note>, SON OF **DEMETRIUS**, CAME FROM **CRETE** INTO THE LAND OF HIS FATHERS <note>The Seleucid Empire, roughly 147 BCE</note>.
And King **Alexander** <note>Alexander Balas</note> heard of it, and he was greatly grieved; and he returned to **Antioch**.
And **Demetrius** appointed **Apollonius**, who was over **Coele-Syria** <note>A region covering much of modern Lebanon and southern Syria</note>; and he gathered a great force and encamped in **Jamnia**.
And he sent word to **Jonathan** the high priest, saying: "You alone rise up against us, and I have become a laughingstock and a reproach because of you. And why do you exercise authority over us in the mountains? Now, therefore, if you trust in your forces, come down to us into the plain, and let us match ourselves against one another there; for with me is the power of the cities. Ask and learn who I am, and who the others are that help us. And they say, 'There is no place for your foot to stand' <note>original: "ουκ εcτιν ημιν cταcιc ποδοc"</note> before our face, because your fathers were twice put to flight in their own land. And now you will not be able to withstand the cavalry and such a force in the plain, where there is neither stone nor pebble, nor a place to flee."

As **Jonathan** heard the words of **Apollonius**, he was moved in his mind; and he chose ten thousand men and went out from **Jerusalem** <note>original: "ϊλημ", a common abbreviation</note>; and **Simon** his brother met him to help him. And he encamped against **Joppa** <note>A strategic port city, modern Jaffa</note>; and those of the city shut him out, because a garrison of **Apollonius** was in **Joppa**. And they fought against it, and those of the city from **Joppa** were afraid; and **Jonathan** became master of **Joppa**.

<column-break/>

And **Apollonius** heard of it, and he set in battle three thousand cavalry and a great force, and he went toward **Azotus** <note>The ancient Philistine city of Ashdod</note> as if he were passing through; and at the same time he advanced into the plain, because he had a great number of cavalry and trusted in them. And he pursued after him to **Azotus**, and the two armies joined in battle.
And **Apollonius** had left a thousand cavalry hidden behind them; and **Jonathan** knew that there was an ambush behind him. And they surrounded his army and showered arrows <note>original: "εξετειναζαν ταc χιζαc", likely a corruption of "arrows" or "darts"</note> at the people from morning until evening. But the people stood firm, as **Jonathan** had commanded, and their [the enemy's] horses grew tired.
And **Simon** drew out his force and joined battle against the phalanx <note>The heavy infantry formation</note>—for the cavalry was exhausted—and they were crushed by him and fled. And the cavalry was scattered in the plain, and they fled to **Azotus** and entered **Beth-dagon**, their idol's temple <note>The temple of the Philistine god Dagon</note>, to save themselves.
And **Jonathan** set fire to **Azotus** and the cities around it, and he took their spoils; and the temple of **Dagon** and those who had fled into it, he burned with fire.
And those who fell by the sword, together with those who were burned, were about eight thousand men.
And **Jonathan** departed from there and encamped against **Ashkelon**, and those of the city came out to meet him with great glory. And **Jonathan** returned with his followers to **Jerusalem**, having many spoils.
And it happened, when King **Alexander** heard these words, he proceeded to honor him even more.

Previously, letters were sent to Onias the High Priest from Arius, who was then king among you, <note>original: "παρα αριου του βαϲιλευοντοϲ" (from Arius the king). We, therefore, at every occasion without fail, both on the festivals and on the other appointed days, remember you in the sacrifices we offer and in our prayers, as it is right and proper to remember brothers. And we rejoice in your glory.

But as for us, many afflictions and many wars have surrounded us, and the kings around us have made war against us. We did not wish, therefore, to trouble you or our other allies and friends during these wars. For we have the help from Heaven that aids us, and we were rescued from our enemies, and our enemies were humbled.

<margin>15</margin> Antiochus, son of King Demetrius, sent letters from the islands of the sea to Simon, the High Priest and <term>Ethnarch</term> <note>A title meaning "ruler of a people," indicating a status slightly below a king</note> of the Jews, and to the whole nation. "**K**ing Antiochus to Simon, the High Priest and Ethnarch, and to the Jewish nation, greetings. I have recruited a great multitude of forces and have prepared ships of war. I intend to land in the country so that I may hunt down those who have devastated our land and those who have ruined many cities in the kingdom.

I have also granted you permission to mint your own **private coinage** for your country. Every royal debt and future royal obligations, from now and for all time, are forgiven you. And when we have established our kingdom, we will glorify you and your nation and the Temple with great glory, so that your glory may become manifest in all the earth."

In the **one hundred and seventy-fourth year** <note>Approximately 138 BCE in the Seleucid calendar</note>, Antiochus marched into the land of his fathers, and all the forces gathered to him, so that only a few remained with Tryphon <note>A rebel general who had usurped the Seleucid throne</note>. King Antiochus pursued him, and he came to Dor, fleeing to the coast; for he knew that troubles had gathered against him and his forces had abandoned him. 

Antiochus camped against Dor with one hundred and twenty thousand men of war and eight thousand cavalry. He surrounded the city, and the ships joined the attack from the sea. He pressured the city from the land and from the sea, and allowed no one to go out or come in.

**N**umenius and his companions arrived from Rome, carrying letters to the kings and the countries, in which the following was written:

"**L**ucius, Consul of the Romans, to King Ptolemy <note>Ptolemy VIII of Egypt</note>, greetings. The ambassadors of the Jews, our friends and allies, came to us to renew the ancient friendship and alliance, being sent by Simon the High Priest and the people of the Jews. They brought a golden shield weighing five thousand <term>minas</term> <note>A very large sum; a mina was a unit of weight/currency</note>. It pleased us, therefore, to write to the kings and the countries, so that they should not seek to do them harm, nor fight against them and their cities and their land, and that they should not form alliances with those who make war against them.

**I**t seemed good to us to accept the shield from them. If, therefore, any pestilent men have fled from their country to you, hand them over to Simon the High Priest..."

# The Prologue and the Peace of Jerusalem

For since [the Lord] has rescued us from great evils and purified the place—the events concerning Judas the Maccabee and his brothers, the purification of the Great Temple, and the dedication of the altar; and also the wars against Antiochus Epiphanes and his son Eupator; and the manifestations <note>original: "ΕΚΦΑΝΕΙΑC" - divine appearances or miracles</note> from heaven that came to those who fought bravely and with honor for Judaism; so that, although they were few, they plundered the whole country and drove out the barbarian hordes, and recovered the Temple renowned throughout the whole world, and freed the city, and restored the laws that were about to be abolished, the Lord having become gracious to them with all kindness—all these things, which were detailed by Jason of Cyrene in five books, we will attempt to condense into a single volume.

For considering the flood of data and the difficulty for those who wish to immerse themselves in historical narratives because of the vastness of the material, we have taken care to provide enjoyment for those who simply wish to read, ease for those who prefer to commit facts to memory, and benefit for everyone who encounters this work.

For us who have taken on the hard labor of this summary <term>summary: "ΕΠΙΤΟΜΗC" - a common Hellenistic literary practice of abridging long works for general readers</term>, the task is not easy; it is a matter of sweat and sleeplessness. It is like someone preparing a banquet and seeking to satisfy the tastes of others; it is not an easy thing. Nevertheless, for the sake of the gratitude of many, we will gladly undergo this hard labor.

<column-break/>

We leave the responsibility for precision in every detail to the original author, while we follow the guidelines of a summary. For just as the architect of a new house must care for the whole structure, while the one who undertakes the decoration and painting <note>The author compares Jason of Cyrene to an architect and himself to an interior decorator</note> must look for what is suitable for the adornment, so I think it is with us. 

To delve deep and wander through discourse and to investigate every detail belongs to the original historian; but to pursue brevity of expression and to avoid an exhaustive treatment of the subject should be granted to the one making the paraphrase.

Therefore, let us begin the narrative here, adding only this much to what has been said before: for it is foolish to be wordy before the history starts, yet to cut the history itself short.

### The Conspiracy of Simon

<margin>3</margin> While the Holy City was inhabited in all peace and the laws were observed as perfectly as possible, because of the godliness of Onias the High Priest <note>Onias III, known for his piety and adherence to the Law</note> and his hatred of wickedness, it happened that even the kings themselves honored the Place <note>original: "ΤΟΝ ΤΟΠΟΝ" - a common Jewish way of referring to the Temple Mount</note> and glorified the Temple with the finest gifts. So much so, that even Seleucus <note>Seleucus IV Philopator, ruler of the Seleucid Empire</note>, the king of Asia, provided from his own revenues all the expenses required for the service of the sacrifices.

But a certain Simon, from the tribe of Benjamin, who had been appointed administrator of the Temple, fell into a dispute with the High Priest concerning the management of the city market. And being unable to prevail over Onias, he went to Apollonius son of Thrasaius, who at that time was governor of Coele-Syria...

# The Mission of Heliodorus and the Threat to the Temple

...and governor of Phoenicia, and reported concerning the untold riches with which the **treasury** <term>treasury: "ΓΑΖΟΦΥΛΑΚΙΟΝ" - a secure chamber in the Temple complex used both for sacred funds and as a bank for private deposits</term> in Jerusalem was filled, so that the number of funds was countless and did not even pertain to the budget for sacrifices, but that it was possible for these to fall under the king’s authority. 

After Apollonius met with the king and informed him about the riches that had been reported, the king selected **Heliodorus**, his chief minister, and sent him with orders to carry out the extraction of the aforementioned money. Immediately, Heliodorus began the journey, ostensibly as if he were to visit the cities throughout *Coele-Syria* and *Phoenicia*, but in reality to carry out the king’s purpose. 

When he arrived in Jerusalem and was kindly received by the High Priest of the city, he revealed the report that had been made and explained for what reason he was present, and he inquired if these things were truly so. The High Priest pointed out that there were deposits belonging to **widows and orphans**, and some belonging to **Hyrcanus son of Tobias**, a man of very high standing—not at all as that slanderer *Simon* had falsely claimed. He explained that the total amount was four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold. He said it was utterly impossible to wrong those who had placed their trust in the holiness of the place and the dignity and inviolability of the Temple, which is honored throughout the whole world. But Heliodorus, because of the royal

<column-break/>

orders, said that in any case these funds must be confiscated for the royal treasury. Having set a day, he entered to conduct an inspection of these matters. There was no small **agony** throughout the whole city. 

The priests prostrated themselves before the altar in their priestly robes and called out to heaven, to Him who had established the law concerning deposits, to keep these things safe for those who had deposited them. To see the appearance of the High Priest was to be wounded in one's mind; for his face and the change in his color revealed the agony of his soul. For a certain fear had enveloped him and a shuddering of the body, through which the internal pain of his heart became obvious to those watching. 

People rushed out of their houses in crowds for a **public supplication** <note>original: "ΙΚΕΤΕΙΑΝ" - a formal, humble prayer or petition made by a community in times of extreme crisis</note> because the holy place was about to be treated with contempt. The women, girded with sackcloth under their breasts, filled the streets. The virgins who were usually kept indoors ran together, some to the gates, some to the walls, and others peered out through the windows. All of them, stretching out their hands to heaven, made their petition. 

It was pitiful to see the multi-colored crowd prostrating themselves, and the fearful expectation of the High Priest in his great agony. They, therefore, called upon the **All-Powerful Lord** <note>original: "ΠΑΝΚΡΑΤΗ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ" - a title emphasizing God's absolute sovereignty over all earthly kings</note> to keep the things entrusted to them safe and with all security for those who had trusted them. Heliodorus, however, proceeded to carry out what had been decided, and was already present with his guards at the treasury.

# The Divine Intervention Against Heliodorus

The Sovereign of spirits and of every authority made a great **epiphany** <term>epiphany: from the Greek "ΕΠΙΦΑΝΙΑ," meaning a visible and glorious manifestation of divine power</term>, so that all those who had dared to join him were struck with dread by the power of God <note>original: "ΘΥ," a contraction for "ΘΕΟΥ" (God)</note> and turned toward fainting and terror.

For there appeared to them a horse carrying a terrifying rider, richly caparisoned, which rushed fiercely and struck at **Heliodorus** with its front hooves. The rider appeared to have golden armor. Two other young men also appeared to him, remarkable in their strength, most beautiful in their glory, and distinguished in their clothing. They stood on either side of him and scourged him incessantly, raining many blows upon him. 

Suddenly he fell to the ground, and as great darkness poured over him, they snatched him up and put him in a litter—the same man who had just entered the aforementioned **treasury** with a great retinue and his entire bodyguard. They now carried him out helpless, he who had clearly recognized the divine sovereignty and lay speechless because of the divine operation, deprived of all hope and safety. 

But the people blessed the Lord <note>original: "ΚΝ," a contraction for "ΚΥΡΙΟΝ" (Lord)</note> who had brought glory to his own place. And the Temple, which a little while before was full of fear and confusion, was filled with joy and gladness now that the Almighty God <note>original: "ΘΥ" (God)</note> had appeared. Quickly, some of Heliodorus’s associates begged **Onias** to call upon the Most High to grant life to the one who was lying utterly at his last breath. 

The High Priest, becoming suspicious that the king might 

<column-break/>

<margin>4</margin> hold some suspicion that some foul play against Heliodorus had been carried out by the Jews, offered a sacrifice for the man’s safety. 

While the High Priest was making the atonement, the same young men appeared again to Heliodorus, standing there in the same clothing. They stood and said: "Give much thanks to Onias the High Priest; for because of him, the Lord <note>original: "ΚΣ," a contraction for "ΚΥΡΙΟΣ" (Lord)</note> has granted you life. And you, having been scourged from heaven, proclaim to all the great power of God <note>original: "ΘΥ" (God)</note>." 

Having said these things, they became invisible. Then Heliodorus, having offered a sacrifice to the Lord <note>original: "ΚΩ" (Lord)</note> and having made great vows to the One who had preserved his life, and having thanked Onias, marched his forces back to the king. He testified to everyone the works of the greatest God <note>original: "ΘΥ" (God)</note> which he had seen with his own eyes. 

When the king asked Heliodorus what sort of person might be suitable to be sent once more to Jerusalem, he said: "If you have any enemy or a conspirator against your affairs, send him there; and you will receive him back scourged, if indeed he survives at all. For there is truly a certain power of God <note>original: "ΘΥ" (God)</note> about that place. For He who has His dwelling in heaven is the Overseer and Helper of that place, and He strikes and destroys those who come to do harm." 

So the matters concerning Heliodorus and the protection of the treasury turned out in this way. But the aforementioned **Simon**, who had become the informer regarding the money and his fatherland, began to speak ill of Onias, claiming that he was the one who had incited Heliodorus and was the author of these evils. He dared to call the guardian and benefactor of the city—
