# The Corruption of the Priesthood and the Rise of Hellenism

Simon, who had previously betrayed the location of the Temple funds and had acted against his own country, began to slander **Onias** <term>Onias III: the righteous High Priest known for his piety and protection of the laws</term>. He dared to claim that it was Onias himself who had incited Heliodorus and was the architect of these troubles. He presumed to call the city’s benefactor, the guardian of his fellow-countrymen, and the zealot for the laws, a "traitor to the state." 

But the hostility reached such a height that murders were committed by one of Simon’s trusted agents. Recognizing the danger of this rivalry, and seeing that **Apollonius** (son of Menestheus), the governor of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia, was fueling Simon's malice, Onias decided to go to the King.

He did not go to act as an accuser of his fellow citizens, but to look after the common and private interests of the entire people. For he saw that without royal intervention it was impossible to achieve peace in public affairs, or for Simon to cease from his madness.

However, when **Seleucus** <note>Seleucus IV Philopator, who died in 175 BCE</note> passed from this life and the kingdom was taken up by **Antiochus**, who was called **Epiphanes** <term>Epiphanes: "the Manifest [God]," a title used by Antiochus IV</term>, Jason, the brother of Onias, usurped the High Priesthood through corruption. He promised the King, in a petition, three hundred and sixty talents of silver, plus eighty talents from another source of revenue.

In addition to this, he promised to pay another one hundred and fifty talents if he were granted authority to establish a **gymnasium** <term>gymnasium: a Greek center for athletic and intellectual training, often associated with Hellenic religious practices</term> and a training center for youths, and to enroll the people of Jerusalem as "Antiochians" <note>This meant granting the people of Jerusalem the status of citizens of a Greek-style city, named after the King</note>.

When the King gave his consent and Jason took power, he immediately began to shift his fellow countrymen toward the Greek way of life. He set aside the royal concessions previously granted to the Jews through John, the father of **Eupolemus** <note>Eupolemus was the man who later negotiated a treaty with the Romans</note>, who had conducted the embassy for friendship and alliance with the Romans. 

<column-break/>

Abolishing the lawful institutions of the state, he introduced new and illegal customs. He took delight in establishing a gymnasium right under the citadel itself, and he forced the noblest of the young men to wear the **petasos** <term>petasos: a broad-brimmed Greek hat associated with the god Hermes, seen here as a symbol of foreign influence</term>.

So great was the peak of **Hellenism** <term>Hellenism: the adoption of Greek language, culture, and customs</term>, and the advance of foreign ways—all because of the extreme wickedness of the ungodly Jason, who was no true High Priest—that the priests were no longer interested in the service of the altar. Instead, they despised the Temple and neglected the sacrifices. They hurried to take part in the unlawful distributions in the wrestling arena after the signal of the **discus** <note>original: "ΔΙCΚΟΥ," the quoit or discus thrown in athletic competitions</note>.

They made light of ancestral honors and considered Greek distinctions to be the finest. Because of this, they were overtaken by a difficult situation: the very people whose way of life they admired and whom they wished to imitate in everything became their enemies and punishers. For it is no small thing to act impiously against the divine laws; but <gloss>the time</gloss> <note>original: "ΚΑΙΡΟC"</note> the upcoming season of events will make this clear.

Now, when a five-year athletic contest was being held at **Tyre** and the King was present, the vile Jason sent spectators from Jerusalem, who were "Antiochians," to carry three hundred drachmas of silver for the sacrifice to **Heracles** <note>The Greek hero/god, often identified with the Tyrian god Melqart</note>. However, those who carried the money requested that it not be used for a sacrifice, as that would be inappropriate, but instead be used for the construction of **triremes** <term>triremes: ancient warships with three banks of oars</term>.

So the money was sent by Jason for the sacrifice to Heracles, but because of those who carried it, it was applied to the building of ships. Now, when Apollonius (son of Menestheus) was sent to Egypt for the enthronement of King **Philometor**, Antiochus learned that the Egyptian king had become alienated from his interests. Therefore, he began to take thought for his own security, which is why...

# The Treachery of Menelaus and the Death of Onias

Arriving at **Joppa** <note>The coastal city of Jaffa</note>, the king then proceeded to **Jerusalem**. He was received with great magnificence by **Jason** and the entire city. He was ushered in with a procession of torches and great shouting. Afterward, he marched his army into **Phoenicia**.

After a period of three years, Jason sent **Menelaus**, the brother of the aforementioned **Simon**, to deliver the money to the king and to provide reports on necessary matters of state. However, Menelaus, having been introduced to the king and having flattered him by his impressive presence, secured the High Priesthood for himself. He outbid Jason by three hundred talents of silver.

<margin>—</margin> Once he received the royal mandates, he returned. Yet he brought with him nothing worthy of the High Priesthood; instead, he possessed the temper of a cruel tyrant and the rage of a savage beast. Thus Jason, who had supplanted his own brother, was himself supplanted by another and was forced to flee as a fugitive to the territory of the **Ammonites** <note>A region in modern-day Jordan</note>.

<margin>></margin> So Menelaus held the office of the High Priesthood, but he failed to pay any of the money he had promised to the king. This was despite the demands made by **Sostratus**, the governor of the **Citadel** <term>Acra: the fortress overlooking the Temple in Jerusalem</term>, for it was Sostratus’s responsibility to collect the revenues. For this reason, they were both summoned by the king. Menelaus left his own brother, **Lysimachus**, as his deputy in the High Priesthood, while Sostratus left **Crates**, the commander of the **Cypriots**, in charge.

While these things were happening, the people of **Tarsus** and **Mallus** <note>Cities in Cilicia, southern Turkey</note> rose up in revolt because their cities had been given as a gift to **Antiochous**, the king’s concubine. Therefore, the king hurried off to settle

<column-break/>

the affairs there, leaving **Andronicus**, one of his high-ranking officials, to act as his deputy.

Thinking he had found a favorable opportunity, Menelaus stole some of the gold vessels from the Temple and presented them to Andronicus as a gift. He had also already managed to sell other vessels in **Tyre** and the surrounding cities. When **Onias** <note>Onias III, the deposed and righteous High Priest</note> became clearly aware of this, he withdrew to a place of sanctuary at **Daphne** <note>A sacred grove and sanctuary near the city of Antioch</note> and spoke out against him.

Therefore, Menelaus took Andronicus aside and urged him to get rid of Onias. Andronicus went to Onias and, using deceit, gave him his right hand in a pledge of friendship and swore an oath. Although Onias was suspicious, Andronicus persuaded him to leave his sanctuary. Immediately, he put him to death, showing no regard for justice.

For this reason, not only the Jews but also many people from other nations were indignant and grieved over the unjust murder of this man. When the king returned from the regions of **Cilicia**, the Jews of the city—along with the Greeks who shared their hatred of such wickedness—complained to him that Onias had been killed without any reasonable cause.

**Antiochus** was deeply grieved in his heart and moved to pity. He even shed tears because of the sobriety and great discipline of the deceased man. Fired with anger, he immediately stripped the purple robe from Andronicus, tore his undergarments, and led him through the entire city to the very spot where he had committed the sacrilege against Onias. There, he executed the murderer, the Lord having rendered to him the punishment he deserved.

Meanwhile, many sacrileges had been committed...

# The Fall of Jason and the Sack of Jerusalem

...enemies, and not thinking that trophies are won by throwing down the monarchy, he did not prevail. The end of his plot brought him shame; a fugitive once again, he went into the region of the Ammonites <note>A territory east of the Jordan River</note>. In the end, he met a wretched fate, being imprisoned by **Aretas**, the Arab tyrant. Fleeing from city to city, pursued by all, hated as a deserter of the laws, and loathed as an executioner of his fatherland and citizens, he was cast out into Egypt. 

And he who had driven many from their fatherland perished in a foreign land, having sailed to the **Lacedaemonians** <note>The Spartans; at the time, some Judeans believed they shared a common ancestry with the Spartans through Abraham</note> hoping to find shelter because of their kinship. He who had cast out many to lie unburied was cast out unburied himself; he had no mourning of any kind, nor did he share in his ancestral grave <note>original: "patroou nomou" — refers to the traditional right of burial in a family tomb</note>.

**W**hen word reached the **King** <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes</note> about these events, he concluded that Judea was in revolt. There was a killing of young and old, a total destruction of men, women, and children, and a slaughter of virgins and infants. In the space of three days, eighty thousand people were destroyed; forty thousand were killed in hand-to-hand combat, and no fewer than those slaughtered were sold into slavery. 

Not satisfied with this, he dared to enter into the most holy temple in all the earth, having as his guide **Menelaus**, the traitor of both the laws and the fatherland. With his polluted hands...

If it had not happened that the people were already involved in many sins, then—just like **Heliodorus** <note>A royal official sent years earlier by King Seleucus; according to tradition, he was stopped from looting the temple by a divine vision of a horseman and two youths who scourged him</note> who was sent to inspect the treasury—this man too, upon approaching, would have been immediately scourged and turned back from his boldness. 

But the Lord did not choose the nation for the sake of the Place, but the Place for the sake of the nation. Therefore, even the Place itself, having shared in the nation's misfortunes, later shared in the benefits of the Lord. What was forsaken during the wrath of the **Almighty** was again, when the Great Master was reconciled, restored with all glory.

The authorities hung the infants from the mothers’ breasts and, after parading them publicly through the city, they threw them off the wall.

When they were reported to **Philip** <note>The Phrygian governor of Jerusalem</note>, they were all burned to death together, because they showed such reverence for the most holy day that they would not even defend themselves.

**I** urge those who read this book not to be discouraged by these calamities, but to consider that these punishments were not for the destruction of our people, but for our discipline <note>original: "paideian" — refers to the educational and corrective training of a child</note>. Indeed, for those who act impiously not to be left alone for long, but to meet retribution immediately, is a sign of great benevolence. For the Lord does not wait for us as He does for other nations, patiently holding back until they reach the full measure of their sins before He punishes them. He has judged it so for us, so that we do not reach the very end of our sins...

# 2 Maccabees: The Rise of the Resistance

Walking alongside him <note>Referring to Judas Maccabeus</note> and secretly entering the villages, they called together their kinsmen. By bringing in those who had remained faithful to Judaism, they gathered about six thousand men. 

And they called upon the Lord <gloss>KYRION</gloss> to look upon the people who were being oppressed by all, and to have pity on the Temple profaned by ungodly men, and to have mercy on the city that was being destroyed and was about to be leveled to the ground, and to hear the blood crying out to Him. They also asked Him to remember the lawless destruction of innocent infants and the blasphemies committed against His name, and to show His hatred of evil.

But when Maccabeus had organized his company, he became irresistible to the Gentiles, as the wrath of the Lord <gloss>KYRIOU</gloss> had now turned to mercy. Attacking cities and villages unexpectedly, he set them on fire; and by taking possession of strategic positions, he put no small number of the enemy to flight. He took advantage of the nights as a primary aid for such attacks, and the report of his courage echoed everywhere.

But Philip, seeing that the man was making progress little by little and advancing more frequently in his successes, wrote to Ptolemy, the governor of Coele-Syria <note>A region comprising much of modern-day Lebanon and Syria</note> and Phoenicia, asking that help be given to the king's affairs. 

He <note>Ptolemy</note> quickly selected Nicanor, the son of Patroclus, one of the First Friends <note>A high-ranking title in the Seleucid court hierarchy</note>, and sent him with no fewer than twenty thousand men of all nations under his command to wipe out the whole race of Judea. He also appointed Gorgias, a general who had experience in military matters.

<column-break/>

Nicanor decided that he would fulfill the tribute of two thousand talents due from the king to the Romans by the sale of Jewish captives. Immediately, he sent word to the coastal cities, inviting them to the purchase of Jewish slaves, promising to deliver ninety slaves for one talent <note>A talent was a massive unit of currency; selling 90 people for one talent was a deeply discounted price, reflecting Nicanor's overconfidence</note>. He did not expect the judgment from the Almighty that was about to follow him.

But word came to Judas concerning Nicanor's invasion, and when he informed those with him of the army's arrival, those who were cowardly and lacked faith in the justice of God <gloss>THEOU</gloss> ran away and removed themselves from the place. But others sold all their remaining possessions and together they entreated the Lord <note>original: "KN" — Kyrion</note> to rescue those who had been sold by the ungodly Nicanor before the battle had even occurred. 

They prayed that if He would not do it for their own sake, He might do it for the sake of the covenants made with their fathers, and because of the invocation of His holy and majestic Name upon them. 

Then Maccabeus, having gathered his followers, numbering six thousand, exhorted them not to be terrified by the enemy nor to fear the great multitude of the nations that had come against them lawlessly, but to fight nobly. He told them to keep before their eyes the lawless outrage committed by the enemy against the Holy Place, and the torture of the afflicted city, and also the destruction of their ancestral way of life. 

"For while they trust in weapons and daring acts," he said...

# The Battle Against Nicanor

"But we trust in the Almighty God <gloss>THEO</gloss>, who is able with a single nod to strike down both those coming against us and the whole world." 

He also recounted to them the instances of help given to their ancestors: how, in the time of Sennacherib <note>An Assyrian king who besieged Jerusalem in 701 BCE</note>, one hundred and eighty-five thousand men perished; and the battle that took place in Babylonia against the Galatians <note>Celtic tribes that had migrated into Asia Minor and served as mercenaries</note>, where they all went into the fray—only eight thousand in all together with four thousand Macedonians. When the Macedonians were at a loss, the eight thousand destroyed the one hundred and twenty thousand because of the help that came to them from Heaven, and they received great benefit.

When he had made them courageous by these words and ready to die for the laws and their country, he divided the army into four parts. He stationed his brothers as leaders of the divisions—Simon, Joseph, and Jonathan—placing under each one thousand five hundred men. Furthermore, he ordered Eleazar to read aloud from the Holy Book. Giving the watchword "God’s Help" <gloss>THEOU BOETHEIAS</gloss>, he himself led the first relief and joined battle with Nicanor.

Because the Almighty <gloss>PANTOKRATOROS</gloss> became their ally, they slaughtered over nine thousand of the enemy. They wounded and disabled in their limbs the greater part of Nicanor’s army and forced them all to flee. They seized the money of those who had come there to buy them <note>Slave traders had followed the Seleucid army, expecting to buy captured Jews</note>. After pursuing them for some distance, they turned back, being constrained by the hour. 

<column-break/>

For it was the day before the Sabbath; for this reason, they did not prolong the pursuit of them. After they had collected the enemy's weapons and stripped them of their spoils, they observed the Sabbath, exceedingly blessing and giving thanks to the Lord <gloss>KYRIO</gloss>, who had kept them safe until this day and had appointed for them this beginning of mercy. 

After the Sabbath, they distributed some of the spoils to those who had been tortured and to the widows and orphans; the remainder they and their children divided among themselves. When they had accomplished this, they made a common petition, imploring the merciful Lord <gloss>KYRION</gloss> to be fully reconciled with His servants.

Later, having engaged the forces of Timothy and Bacchides, they killed over twenty thousand of them and very easily gained control of high strongholds. They divided the spoils, making equal shares for themselves and for those who had been tortured, the orphans, the widows, and also the elderly. 

After carefully collecting the enemy's weapons, they stored them all in strategic places; the rest of the spoils they <margin>Beginning of the account of Timothy</margin> brought to Jerusalem. They also killed Phylarches <note>Literally "the captain of the guard"</note>, a most unholy man who had caused the Jews much suffering.

While they were celebrating the victory in their homeland, they burned Callisthenes, who had set the sacred gates on fire; he had fled into a small house, and thus he received the reward suited to his impiety. 

As for the thrice-cursed Nicanor, who had brought the thousand merchants for the sale of the Jews, he was thoroughly humbled, by the help of the Lord <gloss>KYRIOU</gloss>, by those whom he considered to be the least.

# The Flight of Nicanor and the Downfall of Antiochus

Putting off his cloak <note>original: "χλαμύδα" (chlamys), the distinctive military cloak of a high-ranking Greek officer</note> and fleeing across the mid-country alone like a runaway slave, he arrived at Antioch. He had been extremely successful in one thing: surviving the total destruction of his army. He, who had promised the Romans that he would pay their tribute from the sale of captives in Jerusalem, now went about announcing that the Jews had a Defender <note>The Greek term suggests a champion or supernatural protector</note> and that because of this, the Jews were invulnerable, for they followed the laws ordained by Him.

<margin>89</margin>
**A**round that time, it happened that Antiochus was retreating in disorder from the regions of Persia. For he had entered the city called Persepolis and attempted to rob the temple and seize the city. Because of this, the local people rushed to defend themselves with arms, and it happened that Antiochus was routed by the inhabitants and forced to make a shameful retreat.

**W**hile he was at Ecbatana <note>An ancient city in Media, modern-day Iran</note>, news reached him regarding what had happened to Nicanor and the forces under Timothy. Carried away by his rage, he thought he could vent upon the Jews the injury done to him by those who had put him to flight. Therefore, he ordered his charioteer to drive without stopping until the journey was completed. Yet the judgment of Heaven already accompanied him. For in his arrogance he had said: "When I arrive there, I will make Jerusalem a graveyard <note>original: "πολυάνδριον," literally a place of many men, used to mean a common grave or cemetery</note> for the Jews."

**B**ut the all-seeing Lord <gloss>KYRIOS</gloss>, the God <gloss>THEOS</gloss> of Israel, struck him with an incurable and invisible blow.

But it happened that he fell from his chariot as it rushed along with a roar; and through this painful fall, all the limbs of his body were wrenched.

**H**e who just a moment ago thought he could command the waves of the sea—because of his superhuman pride—and imagined he could weigh the heights of the mountains in scales, was now cast down to the ground and carried in a litter <note>A portable bed or sedan chair</note>, demonstrating the power of God <gloss>THEOU</gloss> to everyone. The result was that worms swarmed out of the body of this ungodly man, and while he was still living in anguish and pain, his flesh fell off. Because of the stench, the whole army was burdened by his decay. The man who shortly before thought he could touch the stars of heaven—no one could now carry him because the weight of the stench was intolerable.

Then, at last, broken in spirit, he began to set aside his great arrogance and come to his senses under the divine scourge, for his pains intensified with every passing moment. When he could no longer endure even his own smell, he said: "It is right to be subject to God <gloss>THEO</gloss>, and for a mortal not to think proud thoughts."

# The Deathbed Vows of Antiochus

The holy city, which he had intended to level to the ground and turn into a mass grave <note>original: "πολυάνδριον" (polyandrion), referring to a common burial pit for many people</note>, he now promised to declare free. As for the Jews, whom he had previously judged unworthy of even a burial—planning to throw them out with their infants to be eaten by birds and wild animals—he now promised to make them all equal to the citizens of Athens. The holy Temple, which he had previously plundered, he would now adorn with the finest offerings. He would restore all the sacred vessels many times over, and he would provide from his own revenues the expenses required for the sacrifices. Beyond this, he promised he would even become a Jew himself and would travel to every inhabited place proclaiming the power of God.

But as his pains did not cease at all—for the just judgment of God had come upon him—and despairing of his own health, he wrote to the Jews the letter set out below, which has the character of a humble petition. It was written in this way:

"To the excellent Jews, our citizens: much joy, health, and prosperity. King Antiochus, their leader <note>original: "στρατηγός" (strategos), literally a general or military commander</note>, wishes you health. If you and your children are well and your affairs are as you wish, I give great thanks, having my hope in heaven. Remembering your honor and goodwill with affection, as I was returning from the regions of Persia and fell into a troublesome illness, I thought it necessary to take care for the common safety of you all. I do not despair of my condition; on the contrary, I have great hope that I will escape this illness. But seeing that my father, at the times when he led expeditions into the upper provinces <note>The eastern territories of the empire, such as Media and Persia</note>...

<column-break/>

...appointed his successor, so that if anything unexpected should happen or any distressing news should arrive, those in the country would know to whom the government had been left and would not be disturbed. Furthermore, observing how the neighboring rulers and those bordering the kingdom are watching for an opportunity and waiting for what might happen, I have designated my son Antiochus as king. I have often entrusted and commended him to most of you when I was traveling through the upper satrapies <note>original: "σατραπείας" (satrapeias), administrative provinces of the Persian and Seleucid empires</note>.

I have also written to him the things set out below. Therefore, I urge and ask you to remember the benefits you have received both publicly and privately, and that each of you maintain your existing goodwill toward me and my son. For I am convinced that he will follow my own policy with fairness and kindness and will get along well with you."

So the murderer and blasphemer, after suffering the worst agonies—just as he had inflicted on others—ended his life in a most pitiable fate in the mountains of a foreign land. His body was taken away by Philip, his foster-brother <note>original: "σύντροφος" (syntrophos), a title for a close companion raised with the king</note>. But Philip, fearing the son of Antiochus, moved across to Egypt to the court of Ptolemy Philometor <note>The Greek ruler of Egypt from the rival Ptolemaic dynasty</note>.

# The Rededication of the Temple and the Rise of Eupator

...sacrifices after three years. They also offered incense and lit the lamps and performed the presentation of the loaves. Having done these things, they besought the <term>Lord</term><note>original: "KN", an abbreviation for "Kyrion" (Lord)</note>, prostrating themselves on the ground, that they might never again fall into such evils. They prayed that if they should ever sin, they might be disciplined by Him with gentleness and not be handed over to blasphemous and barbarian nations. 

Now it happened that on the very same day the Temple had been profaned by foreigners, the cleansing of the Temple took place: on the twenty-fifth day of the same month, which is <note>original: "Χασελεύ" (Chasaleu), the Jewish month of Chislev, occurring in November/December</note> Chislev. They celebrated with gladness for eight days in the manner of the Festival of Tabernacles, remembering how only a short time before they had been wandering in the mountains and caves like wild animals during the season of that festival. Therefore, carrying wreathed wands <note>original: "θύρσους" (thyrsoi), ritual branches usually associated with Greek processions but here adapted for Jewish celebration</note> and beautiful branches, and even palm fronds, they offered hymns of thanks to Him who had successfully brought about the cleansing of His own holy place. 

They also decreed by a public ordinance and vote that the whole nation of the Jews should observe these days every year. Such was the end of Antiochus, the one called Epiphanes.

We shall now relate the events concerning Antiochus Eupator, the son of that impious man, summarizing the chief evils of the wars. When he took over the kingdom, he appointed a certain Lysias to be in charge of affairs and named Ptolemy, called Macron, as the regional governor <note>original: "στρατηγόν" (strategos)</note> of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia. Ptolemy took the lead in maintaining justice toward the Jews because of the wrongs that had been done to them, and he attempted to deal with them peacefully.

<column-break/>

But because of this, he was slandered by the King’s "Friends" <note>A formal title for high-ranking royal advisors in the Hellenistic court</note> before Eupator. He heard himself called a traitor at every turn because he had abandoned Cyprus, which had been entrusted to him by King Philometor, and had defected to Antiochus Epiphanes. Since he could not maintain his authority with dignity, he ended his life by taking poison. 

Meanwhile, Gorgias became the governor of those regions; he maintained a force of mercenaries and took every opportunity to stir up war against the Jews. At the same time, the Idumeans <note>The Edomites, traditional rivals of Israel located to the south</note>, who controlled strategic strongholds, were harassing the Jews; they welcomed refugees from Jerusalem and attempted to keep the war going. 

Maccabaeus and his men, having made a formal petition and besought <term>God</term><note>original: "ΘΝ", an abbreviation for "Theon" (God)</note> to be their ally, rushed upon the strongholds of the Idumeans. Attacking vigorously, they took control of these positions and repelled all who were fighting upon the walls. They slaughtered those who fell into their hands, killing no fewer than twenty thousand men. 

When no fewer than nine thousand others had fled together into two very strong towers, which were well supplied with everything needed to withstand a siege, Maccabaeus left Simon and Joseph, along with Zacchaeus and a sufficient number of men to conduct the siege. He himself departed for places where he was more urgently needed. 

However, Simon’s men were overcome by greed. They were persuaded by some of the men in the towers to take money; having accepted seventy thousand drachmas <note>A silver coin; this was a massive bribe</note>, they allowed some of the enemy to slip away. When word was brought to Maccabaeus about what had happened...

# The Campaigns of Judas Maccabaeus

Column 1:
Gathering the leaders of the people, he <note>Referring to Judas Maccabaeus</note> accused them of having sold their brothers to the enemy by releasing them against them. These men, having become traitors, he then put to death; and immediately he took possession of the two towers. Prospering in everything by the use of arms, he destroyed in the two strongholds more than twenty thousand men.

But Timothy, who had previously been defeated by the Jews, gathered a vast multitude of foreign forces and assembled no small number of horses that came from <term>Asia</term><note>In this context, Asia refers to the Seleucid territories in Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey)</note>. He arrived intending to take Judea as a captive of war. 

As he drew near, those with the <term>Maccabee</term><note>Judas Maccabaeus; "Maccabee" likely means "The Hammer"</note> turned to the supplication of <term>God</term><note>original: "ΘΥ", an abbreviation for "Theou" (God)</note>, sprinkling earth upon their heads and girding their loins with sackcloth. Falling down at the base of the altar, they besought Him to be merciful to them and to be an enemy to their enemies and an adversary to their adversaries, just as the <term>Law</term><note>The Torah or Pentateuch</note> declares.

<margin>bracket</margin>Rising from their prayer, they took up their arms and advanced a considerable distance from the city. When they drew near to the enemy, they kept to themselves. Just as the dawn was breaking, both sides joined in battle. The one side had, as a guarantee of success and victory, their piety along with their refuge in the <term>Lord</term><note>original: "ΚΝ", an abbreviation for "Kyrion" (Lord)</note>; the others made their own rage the leader of their struggle.

Others likewise climbed up during the distraction and set fire to the towers of those inside; lighting fires, they burned the blasphemers alive. Still others broke through the gates.

Having accomplished these things with hymns and thanksgiving, they blessed the Lord, who acts with great benevolence toward <term>Israel</term><note>original: "ΙCΛ", an abbreviation for "Israel"</note> and gives them the victory.

### The Letters of Peace and the Treachery at Joppa

“Concerning these matters, I have ordered these men and my own representatives to discuss them with you in detail. Farewell. Written in the year one hundred and forty-eight <note>roughly 164 BCE</note>, on the twenty-fourth day of the month of <term>Dioscorinthius</term><note>original: "διοσκορινθίου" - a month name that appears only here; historians suspect it is a corruption of a Macedonian or Cretan month</note>.”

<margin>— H</margin> The King’s letter was as follows:

<insert>B</insert>ing Antiochus to his brother Lysias, greetings. Since our father has passed on to the gods <note>a polite way of saying King Antiochus IV Epiphanes had died</note>, and it is our will that the subjects of our kingdom be undisturbed in the care of their own affairs, and having heard that the Jews do not consent to our father’s transition to <term>Greek customs</term><note>original: "ελληνικα" (hellenika) - refers to the forced adoption of Greek religion and culture</note> but prefer their own way of life and request that their own laws be allowed them—choosing therefore that this nation also be free from disturbance, we decree that their Temple be restored to them and that they may live according to the customs of their ancestors. You will therefore do well to send messengers to them and give them <term>the right hand of friendship</term><note>original: "δεξιάς" (dexias) - a formal gesture of a peace treaty or pledge of safety</note>, so that knowing our purpose, they may be of good heart and happily settle into the management of their own lives.

To the Jewish nation, the King’s letter was this:

<insert>B</insert>ing Antiochus to the <term>Senate</term><note>original: "γερουσίᾳ" (gerousia) - the council of elders</note> of the Jews and to the rest of the Jewish people, greetings. If you are well, it is as we desire; we also are in good health. Menelaus <note>the controversial High Priest who had cooperated with the Greeks</note> has informed us that you wish to return to your own homes and attend to your own affairs. To those who return by the thirtieth day of the month of <term>Xanthicus</term><note>roughly April</note>, there shall be a pledge of friendship and safety, so that the Jews may use their own food and laws as they did before. And no one among them shall in any 

<column-break/>

way be harassed for things done in ignorance. I have also sent Menelaus to reassure you. Farewell. Written in the year one hundred and forty-eight, on the fifteenth day of Xanthicus.

<insert>C</insert>he Romans also sent them a letter as follows: “Quintus Memmius and Titus Manius, legates of the Romans, to the people of the Jews, greetings. Concerning those things which Lysias the King’s kinsman has granted you, we also give our consent. But concerning the matters he judged should be referred to the King, send someone at once after you have considered them, so that we may present them in a way that suits you; for we are on our way to Antioch. Therefore, hurry and send messengers so that we also may know what your opinion is. Health to you. In the year one hundred and forty-eight, on the fifteenth of Xanthicus.”

<margin>12</margin> After these agreements were made, Lysias went away to the King, while the Jews returned to their farming. 

<insert>T</insert>ut among the local governors, Timothy and Apollonius son of Gennaeus, as well as Hieronymus and Demophon, and in addition to these, Nicanor the <term>Cypriarch</term><note>original: "κυπριάρχης" - likely the commander of the mercenary troops from Cyprus</note>, would not allow them to live in peace or enjoy tranquility. 

The people of Joppa <note>modern Jaffa</note> committed a particularly horrific crime: they invited the Jews who lived among them to board boats they had provided, along with their wives and children, as if there were no ill-will existing between them. This was done according to a public decree of the city.

### Retaliation for the Treachery at Joppa

...the decree. When they had accepted this, and since they wished to live in peace and had no cause for suspicion, they were led out—being no fewer than two hundred in number.

When Judas heard of the cruelty committed against those of his own race, he gave orders to the men with him. Calling upon the Righteous Judge, <term>God</term><note>original: "ΘΝ" - a scribal abbreviation (nomen sacrum) for the Greek word 'Theon'</note>, he attacked the murderers of his brothers. He set fire to the harbor by night and burned the ships; those who had fled there for refuge, he put to the sword. Because the town was closed against him, he withdrew, but he intended to return and uproot the entire community of the citizens of Joppa.

But learning that the people in Jamnia also intended to act in the same way toward the Jews living among them, he attacked the Jamnites by night. He set fire to the harbor and the fleet, so that the glow of the light was visible in Jerusalem, two hundred and forty stadia <note>approximately 27 miles or 44 kilometers</note> away.

When they had moved nine stadia from there during their march against Timothy, no fewer than five thousand Arabs and five hundred cavalry attacked him. A fierce battle took place, and by the help of <term>God</term><note>original: "ΘΥ" - a scribal abbreviation (nomen sacrum) for 'Theou'</note>, Judas's men were successful. Being defeated, the nomads begged Judas for <term>the right hand of friendship</term><note>original: "δεξιαν" (dexian) - a formal pledge of peace or a treaty of protection</note>, promising to give him livestock and to be helpful in other matters. Judas, realizing they would truly be useful in many ways, agreed to make peace with them. After receiving the pledge, they departed to their tents.

He also attacked a certain city...

<column-break/>

...which was fortified with earthworks and surrounded by walls, inhabited by a mixed multitude of nations; its name was Caspin. Those inside, trusting in the strength of their walls and their stores of food, behaved arrogantly toward Judas and his men. They insulted them, and furthermore, they blasphemed and spoke things that are not permitted.

But Judas and his men called upon the Great Sovereign of the World—who, without battering rams or siege engines, overthrew Jericho in the time of Joshua. They rushed fiercely against the wall and, having taken the city by the will of <term>God</term><note>original: "ΘΥ"</note>, they performed an unspeakable slaughter. The nearby lake, which was two stadia wide <note>about 370 meters</note>, appeared to be filled with the blood that flowed into it.

Departing seven hundred and fifty stadia from there, they reached Charax, to the Jews called Tubians. They did not find Timothy in those parts, for he had left those places without accomplishing anything, though he had left behind a very strong garrison in one location. Dositheus and Sosipater, who were captains under Maccabaeus, went out and destroyed the men Timothy had left in the fortress, more than ten thousand of them.

But Maccabaeus, having arranged his army into cohorts, placed them in command of the divisions and rushed against Timothy, who had with him one hundred and twenty thousand infantry and two thousand five hundred cavalry. When Judas learned of his approach, he sent the women ahead...

### The Rout at Karnion and the Capture of Ephron

...and the rest of the baggage to the place called Karnion; for that town was difficult to besiege and hard to reach because of the narrowness of all the approaching passes.

**W**hen the first cohort of Judas appeared, a great fear and terror fell upon the enemy, caused by the manifestation of the One who oversees all things <note>original: "τοῦ τὰ πάντα ἐφορῶντος" (tou ta panta ephorōntos) — a reference to God as the all-seeing Overseer</note>. They rushed into flight, scattering in every direction, so that they were often harmed by their own men and pierced by the points of their own swords.

**J**udas pursued the chase with great vigor, cutting down those wicked men until he had destroyed about thirty thousand men.

**T**imothy himself, having fallen into the hands of the men under Dositheus and Sosipater, begged with much deceit to be released alive. He claimed that he held many of their parents and brothers, and if he were killed, it would result in their neglect <note>Timothy is using hostages as leverage, implying their safety depends on his survival</note>. When they had finally accepted his word that he would restore these people unharmed, they released him for the sake of saving their brothers. 

Then Judas marched against Karnion and the Atargation <note>the temple of the Syrian goddess Atargatis</note> and slaughtered twenty-five thousand people.

**A**fter the rout and destruction of these enemies, he also marched against Ephron, a fortified city where Lysias lived with people of many different nations. Strong young men stationed in front of the walls fought vigorously, and there was a great supply of war engines and missiles available to them.

**B**ut calling upon the Sovereign <note>original: "Δυνάστην" (Dynastēn) — the Almighty</note> who by his power crushes the strength of enemies, they took the city under their control. They laid low about twenty-five thousand of those inside.

**S**etting out from there, they rushed—

<column-break/>

—toward Scythopolis <note>the "City of the Scythians," modern-day Bet She'an</note>, which is six hundred stadia <note>approximately 68 miles or 110 kilometers</note> from Jerusalem. But the Jews who were settled there testified to the goodwill that the Scythopolitans had shown toward them, and their kind treatment during times of misfortune. 

They thanked them and urged them to continue being well-disposed toward their race in the future. Then they arrived in Jerusalem, as the Festival of Weeks <note>Pentecost</note> was near.

**A**fter the festival called Pentecost, they rushed against Gorgias, the governor of Idumea. He came out with three thousand infantry and four hundred cavalry. When they joined in battle, it happened that a few of the Jews fell.

**D**ositheus, one of Bacenor's men, a powerful horseman, gripped Gorgias and, catching him by his cloak, dragged him along by sheer strength. He intended to take the accursed man alive, but one of the Thracian horsemen charged at him and cut off his shoulder; so Gorgias escaped to Marisa.

**W**hen the men under Esdris had been fighting for a long time and were exhausted, Judas called upon the <term>Lord</term> <gloss>KN = Kyrion</gloss> <note>original: "KN" - a scribal abbreviation for 'Kyrion', the Greek word for Lord</note> to appear as their ally and leader in the battle. Raising the battle cry in his ancestral tongue with hymns, he made an unexpected attack on the men under Gorgias and routed them.

Judas gathered his army and went to the city of Adullam. As the seventh day of the week was approaching, they purified themselves according to the custom and kept the Sabbath there.

**O**n the following day, as it had become necessary, Judas's men went to take up the bodies of those who had fallen and to bring them back to rest with their kinsmen...

### The Sin of the Fallen and the Offering for the Dead

...to restore them to their ancestral graves. But they found under the tunics of each of the dead sacred tokens <term>sacred tokens</term><note>original: "ἱερώματα" (hierōmata) — these were likely small amulets or votive objects taken from a pagan temple in Jamnia</note> of the idols of Jamnia, from which the Law prohibits the Jews. It became clear to everyone that this was the reason these men had fallen. 

**S**o they all blessed the ways of the Righteous Judge, the Lord, who makes hidden things manifest. They turned to petition, asking that the sin committed might be completely blotted out. The noble Judas exhorted the people to keep themselves sinless, having seen with their own eyes what had happened because of the sin of those who had fallen. 

**A**fter taking a collection from each man, he sent about two thousand silver drachmas to Jerusalem to provide a sin offering. He acted very well and honorably, taking the resurrection into account. For if he had not expected the fallen to rise again, it would have been superfluous and foolish to pray for the dead. But looking to the splendid reward laid up for those who fall asleep in godliness, it was a holy and pious thought. Therefore he made the atonement for the dead, so that they might be released from their sin.

<margin>Chapter 13</margin> <gloss>In the year 149</gloss><note>original: "ΤΩ ΡΜΘ" — 149 in the Seleucid era, corresponding to approximately 163 BCE</note> Word reached Judas and his men that Antiochus Eupator was coming with a multitude against Judea, and with him Lysias his guardian and manager of affairs, each having a Greek force of one hundred and ten thousand infantry, five thousand three hundred cavalry,

<column-break/>

and twenty-two elephants, and three hundred scythed chariots. 

**M**enelaus <note>a former High Priest who had usurped the office and promoted Hellenization</note> also joined them and with hypocrisy urged Antiochus on, not for the safety of his country, but thinking he would be established in his own office. 

**B**ut the King of Kings stirred up the anger of Antiochus against the scoundrel. When Lysias pointed out that this man was the cause of all the troubles, the king ordered him to be taken to Beroea <note>modern-day Aleppo, Syria</note> and put to death according to the custom of the place. Now in that place there is a tower fifty cubits high <note>approximately 75 feet</note> filled with ash, and it had a circular machine hanging sheer on all sides into the ash. There, if anyone is guilty of sacrilege or has committed other exceptional crimes, they all push them to their destruction. 

**B**y such a fate it happened that the lawbreaker Menelaus died, not even receiving burial in the earth. And this was very just; for since he had committed many sins against the altar, whose fire was pure and whose ash was holy, in ash he met his death.

**B**ut the king, burdened with a barbarian mindset, came intending to show the Jews the worst of the things that had happened in his father's time. When Judas learned of these things, he commanded the people to call upon the Lord day and night, that if ever at any other time, so now he would help those who were about to be deprived of the Law, their country, and the holy Temple; and not to allow the people, who had just recently enjoyed a brief respite, to fall into the hands of blasphemous nations.

### The Appeal to the Lord and the Night Raid

**H**aving done all these things together, and having implored the **Lord** <note>original: "KY" — Kurios</note> with weeping and fasting and prostrating themselves for three days without ceasing, Judas encouraged them and ordered them to be ready. After meeting privately with the elders, he decided that before the King's army should invade Judea and take control of the city, they would go out and decide the matter with the help of **God** <note>original: "ΘY" — Theos</note>.

**G**iving the command to the **Creator** <note>original: "KTΩ" — Ktistou</note> of the world, and exhorting those with him to fight nobly unto death for the laws, the Temple, the city, their fatherland, and their way of life, he stationed his army. Giving to those around him the watchword **"Victory from God,"** he took the best of the chosen young men and made a night attack upon the royal court. He killed about two thousand men in the camp and also slew the lead elephant along with its mahout <note>original: "συν τω κατά σκηνούντι" — literally "the one dwelling with [it]" in the tent or tower</note>. Finally, they filled the camp with fear and confusion and withdrew successfully. This happened just as the day was dawning, because of the protection of the **Lord** which helped him.

**T**he King, having had a taste of the daring of the Jews, tried to take their positions by strategy. He advanced against Beth-zur <term>Beth-zur</term><note>A strategic fortress on the road to Jerusalem</note>, a strong fortress of the Jews, but he was repulsed, he failed, and he was defeated. Judas sent those inside what was necessary...

<column-break/>

...to the enemies. But Rhodocus <term>Rhodocus</term><note>A Jewish soldier who acted as a spy for the Greeks</note>, from the Jewish ranks, was searched for, caught, and imprisoned.

### The Treaty and the Return to Antioch

**T**he King spoke a second time to the people in Beth-zur; he gave his right hand <note>a gesture of a peace treaty</note>, received theirs, and departed. He attacked Judas's men but was defeated. He then received news that Philip, who had been left in charge of affairs, had revolted in Antioch. He was confounded; he appealed to the Jews, submitted, and swore to all their rights. He reached an agreement and offered a sacrifice; he honored the sanctuary and showed kindness to the place. He also received Maccabeus and left him as governor <note>original: "στρατηγόν" — strategon</note> from Ptolemais to the region of the Gerrenes <note>original: "ΓENNHPΩ" — likely referring to the Gerrenes near Gaza</note>.

Then he <margin>the invasion</margin> departed for Antioch. This is how the matter of the King's invasion and his retreat went.

# The Treachery of Alcimus and the Mission of Nicanor

**D**emetrius <note>King Demetrius I Soter, who took the throne in 161 BC</note>, in the one hundred and fifty-first year <note>approximately 161 BC in the Seleucid calendar</note>, was approached by Alcimus <term>Alcimus</term><note>A leader of the Hellenizing Jews who sought the High Priesthood through Greek favor</note>, who brought him a golden crown and a palm branch, and in addition to these, the olive branches that were customary in the Temple. On that day, he kept his peace. But when he found an opportunity for his own foolishness, he was called into a council by Demetrius and was asked what disposition and purpose the Jews held. To this, he replied: 

"Those among the Jews called **Hasideans** <term>Hasideans</term><note>original: "Ασιδαίοι" — meaning "pious ones," a group strictly devoted to the Jewish Law</note>, who are led by **Judas Maccabeus**, keep the war alive and stir up sedition, not allowing the kingdom to attain stability. Therefore, having been deprived of my ancestral glory—I mean the High Priesthood—I have now come here for a second time. First, I am truly concerned for the King’s interests, and second, I am looking out for my own fellow citizens. For because of the unfaithfulness of those I mentioned, our whole race is suffering no small misfortune. 

**W**hen you have informed yourself on each of these matters, O King, take thought for our country and our surrounded race, according to the gracious benevolence you show toward all. For as long as **Judas** remains alive, it is impossible for affairs to find peace."

**W**hen he had said such things, the other "Friends of the King" <note>A formal title for high-ranking royal advisors</note>, who were hostile toward **Judas**, further incited **Demetrius**. He immediately appointed **Nicanor**, who had been the master of the elephants <note>original: "ελεφαντάρχην" — a high military rank</note>, and having named him governor of Judea, he sent him out. He gave him written orders to kill **Judas** himself, to scatter those with him, and to install

**B**ut when the Jews heard of **Nicanor's** advance and the gathering of the gentiles, they sprinkled themselves with dust and made supplication to the One who established His people forever, who always upholds His own portion with His manifest presence. # The Betrayal of the Treaty and the Threat to the Temple

Nothing was out of place. He dismissed the gathered crowds and kept **Judas** constantly in his presence, having a sincere personal affection <note>original: "ψυχικῶς" (psychikōs) — meaning soulfully or with deep inner regard</note> for the man. He urged him to marry and have children; so Judas married, settled down, and shared in the common life.

But **Alcimus**, seeing their goodwill toward each other and the treaties they had made, took a copy of the agreements and went to **Demetrius**. He told him that **Nicanor** was harboring thoughts hostile to the state, for he had appointed **Judas**, the conspirator against the kingdom, as his successor.

The King, becoming enraged and incited by the slanders of that most wicked man, wrote to **Nicanor**, stating that he was heavily burdened by the treaties and ordering him to send **Maccabeus** to **Antioch** in chains immediately. When this reached **Nicanor**, he was confounded and took it hard that he must break the established terms when the man had committed no wrong. However, since it was not possible to oppose the King, he watched for an opportunity to carry this out by a stratagem.

But **Maccabeus**, seeing that **Nicanor** was conducting himself more harshly toward him and that his accustomed greeting had become ruder, realized that this severity did not come from a good motive. Gathering a significant number of his followers, he went into hiding from **Nicanor**.

When **Nicanor** realized he had been nobly out-generaled by the man, he went to the great and holy Temple while the priests were offering the prescribed sacrifices and commanded them to hand the man over. When they declared under oath that they did not know where the man he sought was, he stretched out his right hand toward the sanctuary <note>original: "νεών" (neōn) — referring to the inner temple building</note>

<column-break/>

and swore this: "If you do not hand over **Judas** to me in chains, I will level this sanctuary of God <note>original: "ΘΥ" — abbreviation for "Θεοῦ" (theou)</note> to the ground, tear down the altar, and erect here a glorious temple to **Dionysus** <note>The Greek god of wine; this was a direct threat of pagan desecration</note>." Having said these things, he departed.

Then the priests, stretching out their hands toward heaven, called upon the One who has always been the defender of our nation, saying:

"You, O Lord of all, who have need of nothing, were pleased that a temple for your dwelling should be among us. And now, O Holy One of all holiness, preserve forever undefiled this house which has so recently been purified."

A man named **Razis**, one of the elders of **Jerusalem**, was denounced to **Nicanor**. He was a man who loved his fellow citizens and was held in high regard, called "Father of the Jews" because of his goodwill. In the former times of the "state of separation" <note>original: "ἀμιξίας" (amixias) — referring to the period when the Jews strictly avoided Greek customs</note>, he had been brought to trial for his **Judaism** and had risked both body and soul for the faith with all steadfastness. **Nicanor**, wishing to make clear the hostility he felt toward the Jews, sent over five hundred soldiers to arrest him, for he thought that by arresting him, he would inflict a great calamity upon them.

But as the crowds were about to capture the tower and were forcing the courtyard gate, calling for fire to be brought to set the doors ablaze, **Razis**, finding himself surrounded, nobly fell upon his sword. He chose to die rather than fall into the hands of these criminals and be treated with insults unworthy of his noble birth. However, because of the haste of the conflict and the crowding of the masses, he did not strike a fatal blow...

# The Noble Death of Razis and the Arrogance of Nicanor

As the troops were breaking through the gateways and forcing the outer door, and were about to set the house on fire, **Razis** <note>A prominent elder in Jerusalem known as "the father of the Jews" for his loyalty to his people</note>, finding himself surrounded, nobly threw himself from the wall into the crowds. The crowds quickly drew back, leaving a space, and he fell into the middle of the empty opening. Still breathing and burning with courage, he stood up, despite the blood flowing like a fountain and his wounds being severe. He ran through the crowds and, standing upon a steep rock, now completely drained of blood, he pulled out his own entrails and, taking them in both hands, flung them at the crowds. Calling upon the **Lord of Life and Spirit** to restore these to him again, he died in this manner.

<margin>15</margin> But **Nicanor**, having heard that those with **Judas** were in the regions of **Samaria**, planned to attack them with total safety on the day of rest <note>The Sabbath, the holy day of rest in Judaism</note>. When the Jews who were forced to follow him said:

> "Do not destroy them so savagely and like a barbarian, but show honor to the day that has been prioritized with holiness by the One who sees all things."

The thrice-wretched man <note>original: "τρισαλιτήριος" (trisalitērios) — a term of extreme contempt meaning "thrice-accursed"</note> asked:

> "Is there a Sovereign in heaven who commanded the keeping of the **Sabbath** day?"

When they declared:

> "It is the living **Lord** Himself, the Sovereign in heaven, who commanded the observance of the seventh day."

The other replied:

> "And I am a sovereign on earth, who commands you to take up arms and carry out the king’s business."

Nevertheless, he did not succeed in carrying out his cruel plan. **Nicanor**, in his total arrogance and boasting, had determined to set up a public monument

<column-break/>

of victory over those with **Judas**. But **Maccabeus** <note>The nickname of Judas, meaning "The Hammer"</note> remained unceasingly confident with total hope that he would obtain help from the **Lord**. He exhorted his men not to be terrified by the attack of the Gentiles, but to keep in mind the help that had come to them from Heaven in the past, and to expect now the victory that would come to them from the **Almighty**. 

Comforting them from the **Law** and the **Prophets**, and reminding them of the struggles they had already completed, he made them more eager. Having stirred their spirits, he gave them his orders, at the same time pointing out the treachery of the Gentiles and their violation of oaths. He armed each of them, not so much with the security of shields and spears as with the encouragement of good words. 

He also told them a reliable dream, a vision that gladdened them all. His vision was this: he saw **Onias** <note>Onias III, the former High Priest known for his piety</note>, who had been High Priest—a noble and good man, modest in his bearing, gentle in his manner, distinguished in his speech, and one who from childhood had practiced all the ways of virtue—stretching out his hands and praying for the whole Jewish community. 

Then there appeared in the same way a man distinguished by his gray hair and dignity, and there was a marvelous and most majestic authority around him. **Onias** responded, saying:

> "This is the lover of the brothers, the one who prays much for the people and the holy city: **Jeremiah**, the prophet of God."

**Jeremiah** stretched out his right hand and gave to **Judas** a golden sword, and as he gave it, he spoke these words:

> "Take this holy sword as a gift from God, with which you shall strike down your adversaries."

# The Battle of Adasa and the Prayer of Judas Maccabeus

Encouraged by the words of **Judas**—which were truly noble and capable of stirring up courage and refining the souls of the young—the Jews resolved not to remain in a defensive camp. Instead, they determined to take the offensive bravely and, with total manliness, engage in hand-to-hand combat to decide the matter. This was because the city, the holy things, and the **Temple** <note>The Second Temple in Jerusalem, which the Seleucids sought to desecrate</note> were in grave danger. Their concern for wives and children, and for brothers and relatives, was of secondary importance to them; their greatest and primary fear was for the consecrated **Sanctuary**. Meanwhile, those left behind in the city were in no small state of agony, troubled as they were by the thought of a battle in the open field.

While everyone was awaiting the coming judgment of the conflict, the enemy had already closed in. The army was drawn up in battle array, the **beasts** <note>original: "θηρίων" (thēriōn) — specifically referring to war elephants, a terrifying component of Seleucid warfare</note> were stationed in a strategic position, and the cavalry was deployed on the flanks. **Maccabeus**, observing the arrival of the vast multitudes, the varied preparation of their weapons, and the ferocity of the beasts, stretched out his hands toward heaven. He called upon the **Lord** <note>original: "ΚΝ," a scribal abbreviation (Nomen Sacrum) for "Kyrios" or Lord</note> who works wonders, knowing that victory is not achieved through arms, but that He grants it to those who are worthy according to His own judgment.

He prayed in this manner:

> "You, **Sovereign Lord**, sent your angel in the time of **Hezekiah** the king of **Judea**, and he struck down one hundred and eighty-five thousand from the camp of **Sennacherib** <note>A reference to the miraculous deliverance of Jerusalem from the Assyrians described in 2 Kings 19</note>. So now also, **Ruler of the Heavens**, send a good angel before us to spread fear and trembling. By the greatness of your...

<column-break/>

...arm, let those who have come with blasphemy against your holy people be struck with terror."

With these words, he ended his prayer. Then **Nicanor** and his men advanced with the sound of trumpets and war songs. But **Judas** and his men engaged the enemy with invocations and prayers. Fighting with their hands but praying to **God** <note>original: "ΘΝ," scribal abbreviation for "Theon" or God</note> in their hearts, they laid low no fewer than thirty-five thousand men, greatly cheered by the manifestation of **God**.

When the action was over and they were retreating with joy, they discovered that **Nicanor** had fallen in his full armor. With shouts and confusion, they blessed the **Sovereign** in their ancestral language <note>Aramaic or Hebrew</note>. Then **Judas**—who was in every way the prime champion for his fellow citizens, both in body and soul, and who had maintained the goodwill of his youth toward his kinsmen—ordered them to cut off **Nicanor’s** head and his arm up to the shoulder and carry them to **Jerusalem**.

When he arrived there, he called together his kinsmen and the priests. Standing before the altar, he sent for those who were in the **Citadel** <note>The Akra, a fortress in Jerusalem held by a pro-Seleucid garrison</note>. He showed them the head of the vile **Nicanor** and the hand of that blasphemer, which he had boastfully stretched out against the holy house of the **Almighty**. He also cut out the tongue of the ungodly **Nicanor** and said he would give it piece by piece to the birds, and he ordered that the "reward of his folly" <note>Nicanor's severed head and hand</note> be hung up opposite the **Temple**.

Then they all looked toward heaven and blessed the **Lord** who had manifested Himself, saying:

> "Blessed be He who has kept His own place undefiled!"

Then he fastened Nicanor's...

### THE THIRD BOOK OF MACCABEES

They all decreed by a public vote never to let this day pass unobserved, but to celebrate the thirteenth day of the twelfth month—called Adar <note>original: "αδα" (Ada); the twelfth month of the Hebrew calendar, roughly February/March</note> in the Aramaic tongue <note>original: "τη κυριακη φωνη" (tē kyriakē phōnē); literally "the local/common speech," referring to the Aramaic used by the Judeans</note>—which is the day before Mordecai’s day <note>The Feast of Purim, commemorating the events of the Book of Esther</note>.

This, then, is how the matters concerning Nicanor turned out. Since that time, the city has been held by the Hebrews, and I will end my story here. If it is well written and skillfully composed, that is what I desired; but if it is poorly done and mediocre, it was the best I could manage. For just as it is harmful to drink wine alone, or water alone, whereas wine mixed with water is pleasant and yields a delightful taste, so too the arrangement of the narrative delights the ears of those who read the work. And here shall be the end.

representatives to him from the council <term>Gerousia</term> <note>The "Gerousia" was the traditional senate or council of elders in Jerusalem that handled civil and religious governance</note> and the elders to greet him and bring him gifts of hospitality, and to rejoice over the events that had occurred, it happened that he became even more eager to visit them as soon as possible. ## THE CRY OF THE PEOPLE
Those who were around him <note>Referring to the King's own retinue who were witnessing the scene</note>, seeing these things, turned to invoke the **Almighty** <note>original: "παντοκράτορα" (pantokratora); a title for God meaning "Ruler of All"</note> along with our people, entreating Him not to overlook this lawless and arrogant deed. Because of the constant and agonizing cry of the gathered crowds, there was an invincible shout. It seemed not only that the people were crying out, but that the walls and the entire ground echoed, as if they would all rather exchange their lives for death right then than see the desecration of the Holy Place.

## THE PRAYER OF THE HIGH PRIEST
Then he <note>Simon the High Priest</note>, King of the Heavens and Master of all creation, Holy among the holy ones, sole Ruler, Almighty, attend to us who are suffering under a profane and lawless man, who is puffed up with insolence and strength. For You are the creator of all things and the Ruler who governs the universe; You are a just Governor, and You judge those who perform deeds of insolence. 

You destroyed those in former times who committed injustice—the **Giants** <note>Referring to the Nephilim or the generation of the Flood</note> who trusted in their own strength and boldness—by bringing upon them an unmeasured flood of water. You burned the **Sodomites** <note>Residents of Sodom and Gomorrah</note> with fire and sulfur when they became notorious for their vices, making them an example to those who would come after. You tested the bold **Pharaoh**, who had enslaved Your holy people Israel, with many and varied punishments, and so You made known Your power; in these acts You revealed Your great might. When he pursued them with chariots and a multitude of crowds, You submerged him in the depths of the sea. But those who trusted in You, the Master of all creation,

<column-break/>

You brought through safely. When they beheld the works of Your hand, they praised You, the Almighty. You, O King, having created the infinite and boundless earth, chose this city and sanctified this place for Your name, though You have need of nothing. You glorified it with Your magnificent presence, and to the honor of Your great and honorable name, You promised to maintain this house through all things. For You said: "If an apostasy <note>original: "ἀποστροφὴ" (apostrophē); a turning away from faith or a rebellion</note> should happen among us, and distress overtakes us, and we come to this place and pray, You will hear our prayer." 

And indeed, You are faithful and true; for many times when our fathers were afflicted, You helped them in their humiliation and rescued them from great evils. Behold now, Holy King, because of our many and great sins, we are suffering and subjected to our enemies, and we are left in a state of weakness. In our downfall, this bold and profane man attempts to insult the Holy Place dedicated to Your name and Your glory upon the earth. For Your dwelling place, the heaven of heavens, is unreachable by men; yet because You were pleased to place Your glory among Your people Israel in this place, do not let us be punished by the impurity of these men. Do not hold us accountable for this desecration, so that the lawless may not boast in their wrath, nor rejoice in the pride of their tongues, saying: "We have trampled the house of sanctuary <note>original: "οἶκον τοῦ ἁγιασμοῦ" (oikon tou hagiasmou); the Temple</note> just as the houses of the idols are trampled!"

## THE FALL OF THE KING
He <note>God</note> then scourged the insolent and impious man, who was puffed up with boldness, striking him from one side to the other. He shook him like a reed is shaken by the wind, so that he lay helpless upon the ground, paralyzed in his limbs, unable even to speak, having been struck by a **righteous judgment** <note>The text suggests a physical stroke or seizure interpreted as divine punishment</note>. 

When his friends and bodyguards saw the sharp punishment that had overtaken him, they were struck with great fear. Terrified that he might die, they quickly carried him out, utterly overwhelmed by dread. 

## THE KING’S BITTERNESS
In time, after he had recovered, he in no way came to a state of repentance. Instead, he departed with bitter threats. <unclear>M</unclear> Having returned to Egypt, he increased his wickedness, encouraged by his associates who were estranged from all justice. He was not only satisfied with his countless acts of licentiousness, but he proceeded to such a level of audacity that he spread evil reports in those places. Many of his friends, looking closely at the King's purpose, followed his will themselves. He proposed publicly a grievance against the nation <note>the Jewish people</note>, and upon the wall <note>or perhaps a tower/pillar</note> of the court, he inscribed a decree: 

<column-break/>

## THE DECREE OF PERSECUTION
That none of those who did not sacrifice to their gods should enter their own holy places; and that all Jews should be subjected to a **registration** <term>census: "λαογραφία" (laographia); a poll-tax registration that reduced the status of the person to that of a commoner or serf</term> and be reduced to a slave-like condition. Those who objected were to be taken by force and put to death. He further ordered that those who were registered were to be branded by fire on their bodies with the symbol of an **ivy leaf**, the sign of **Dionysus** <note>The Greek god of wine; the ivy was his sacred symbol. This branding was a supreme mark of desecration for a Jew.</note>. These people were to be restricted to their previously assigned lower status.

<margin>⸕</margin> <note>A mark in the margin indicating a significant clause in the decree</note>
However, so that he would not appear to be an enemy to all, he added: "If any of them choose to join those who are initiated into the **mystery rites** <note>pagan religious ceremonies</note>, they shall have equal citizenship with the Alexandrians."

## THE RESPONSE OF THE FAITHFUL
Some of those in the city, who loathed the requirements of the city's religion, easily gave themselves up, thinking they would gain great glory from their future association with the King. However, the majority stood firm with a noble soul and did not depart from their religion. By exchanging money for their lives, they fearlessly attempted to save themselves from the registration. They remained hopeful of obtaining divine help, and they detested those who had separated from them, judging them to be enemies of the nation and excluding them from common social interaction and utility. 

Because of this, the King was further enraged, so that he was not only angry with those in Alexandria, but he became more harshly opposed to those in the countryside. He gave orders to speed up the process of gathering them all together, to put them to death by the most cruel fate.

## ACCUSATIONS AGAINST THE NATION
Because of these things, a hateful rumor was spread against the nation by those who sought to punish them. They took this as an opportunity for ill-doing, or rather, it happened because the laws <note>The Mosaic Law, particularly dietary and religious restrictions</note> hindered their usual needs.

But the Jews maintained an unswerving goodwill and faith toward the kings. However, because they worshipped **God** <note>original: "ΘΝ" (Theon), a *nomen sacrum* or sacred abbreviation for "God"</note> and lived according to His law, they maintained a separation in regards to food. For this reason, they appeared hateful to some. But by adorning their social conduct with the practice of righteous deeds, they were well-esteemed and held as holy in appearance by all men.

Therefore, the foreigners took no account of the well-reported good deeds of the nation, which were spoken of by everyone. Instead, they gossiped about the difference in their worship and their food, claiming that these people were not of the same mind as the king or his military forces, but were hostile and opposed to the greatest matters. Thus, they held a bad reputation. 

The Greeks in the city <note>Likely referring to Alexandria, the cultural capital of the Ptolemaic Empire</note>, though in no way wronged by them, were disturbed by the unexpected trouble they saw surrounding these men and the unforeseen gatherings taking place. They were not strong enough to help, for the king's disposition was tyrannical. However, they encouraged them and were distressed, assuming that these things would surely change; for such a large community, having committed no wrong, would not be so overlooked. 

Already, some neighbors, friends, and business partners, secretly drawing some aside, gave pledges to shield them and to offer every effort to save them.

<column-break/>

## THE ROYAL EDICT OF PHILOPATOR
These people <note>the Greeks and allies of the Jews</note> paid close attention to providing assistance for their rescue. On the other hand, those who boasted in their present prosperity—as if they did not perceive the power of the **Greatest God** <note>original: "ΜΕΓΙCΤΟϒ Θϒ" (Megistou Theou), the Greatest God; Θϒ is a sacred abbreviation</note>—established an indictment. The King wrote this letter against them to maintain his decree:

**KING PTOLEMY PHILOPATOR** to the generals and soldiers in Egypt and every place, **GREETINGS AND HEALTH**.

I myself am well, and our affairs are prospering. After our campaign into Asia <note>The Fourth Syrian War, ending in the Battle of Raphia (217 BCE)</note>, which turned out as we intended, we were unexpectedly saved—as we believe—by the gods. We expected to receive the gods as providers with much kindness, having intended to set right the matters disturbing Coele-Syria and Phoenicia through our common benevolence. 

Having assigned revenues to the temples in every place, we went up even to Jerusalem to honor the sanctuary of those people with honors. But they, never ceasing from their folly, accepted our presence in word, but in their whole mind, they were eager for what was not right. When we were moved to enter into their sanctuary and to honor it with outstanding and most beautiful offerings, they, carried away by an old arrogance, barred us from the entrance. They were lacking in our power <note>The king implies they lacked the strength to truly stop him, though he was spiritually repelled</note> because of the benevolence we have toward all humans. 

But making their hostility toward us manifest, they are the only ones among the nations who are insolent to kings and their own benefactors; they wish to offer no genuine goodwill.

### THE DECREE OF PHILOPATOR

->**Column 1**<-

"But we, being influenced by these reports and returning with a change of mind, and having met the Jews in Egypt with every humanity as was fitting, acted accordingly. Beyond this, making known to all our forgiveness of past wrongs <note>original: "αμνησικακίαν" (amnesikakian), a political term for amnesty or "forgetting of evils"</note> toward those of their own race, we especially—on account of their alliance and the matters entrusted to them with simplicity from the beginning—dared to do a great thing. We intended to deem them worthy of **Alexandrian citizenship** <note>Alexandrian citizenship was a prestigious status, granting legal and tax privileges usually reserved for Greeks</note> and to appoint them as associates of the eternal priests.

They, however, taking the opposite view and welcoming their innate malice, have constantly leaned toward evil. Not only did they reject the honored citizenship, but both by their speech and their silence, they have expressed their detestation of those few among them who are peaceably disposed toward us. They are constantly hoping that our affairs will fall into total disorder.

Therefore, having been well-persuaded by these proofs that these people are ill-disposed toward us in every way, and taking precaution lest some sudden disturbance should break out against us later, we have viewed these people as traitors and barbarians. We order that, as soon as this letter reaches you, those living among you, together with their children and wives, be sent to us in bonds, bound on every side with iron chains, to meet a cruel and shameful death, as is fitting for such ill-intentioned rebels.

<column-break/>

->**Column 2**<-

For when these have been punished collectively, we are convinced that for the remaining time, our affairs will be established in the best and most stable condition.

Whoever shall shelter any of the Jews, from the infant to the elderly, shall be tortured to death with lashes along with their whole household. But whoever desires to inform on them shall receive the property of the one falling under the penalty, along with two thousand drachmas <note>The original text here is slightly fragmented in the uncial; two thousand drachmas was a common reward in such edicts</note> from the royal treasury, and shall be honored with freedom.

Every place where a Jew is found being sheltered shall be made inaccessible and burned with fire, and it shall appear utterly useless to every mortal being for all time."

<margin>] 21</margin> This was the form of the letter that was written. Everywhere it arrived, a public festival was held for the gentiles <note>original: "εθνεσιν" (ethnesin), referring to the non-Jewish, mostly Greek and Egyptian population</note> with shouting and joy, as the long-standing bitterness of their souls was now openly displayed without restraint. But among the Jews, there was an unceasing mourning and a lamentable cry with tears; their hearts were entirely on fire as they groaned at the unexpected destruction that had been decreed against them.

What city or place, or what inhabited street, was not filled with wailing and mourning for them? For they were sent away with such harshness and pitiless soul by the generals in each city, that at the sight of the extraordinary cruelty, even some of their enemies, having before their eyes the common misery of life and reflecting on the uncertain turn of fortune, took no joy in their ruin.
