### THE DEPORTATION TO ALEXANDRIA

->**Column 1**<-

For the old man, full of gray hair, was led away, his <term>sluggishness</term> <note>original: "νωθρότητα" (nōthrotēta), referring to the physical frailty of the elderly</note> of age stooped by the violent speed of his forced journey. He was stripped of all shame and dignity as he was hurried along. Even the young women, who had recently entered their bridal chambers for the fellowship of marriage, exchanged their joy for lamentation. With their dust-covered hair, fragrant with perfumes but now unkempt, they were led away unveiled. Moving together with one voice, they raised a mournful dirge instead of a wedding song, as if they were young animals being torn away from their flock.

They were dragged by force through the public square until they reached the embarkation point for the ships. There, those who once enjoyed the yoke of marriage were now bound by their necks with unbreakable iron chains, driven by the vigor of youth. Instead of the festivities and youthful leisure they once knew, they spent their days in mourning, looking out at the waters and the wooden planks. They were brought down like wild beasts, led in iron bonds. Some were fastened by their necks to the rowing benches of the ships, while others had their feet secured in inescapable shackles.

Furthermore, a thick wooden deck was placed above them so that, being shrouded in darkness from every side, their eyes would be blinded during the entire voyage, as a form of punishment.

When these people were brought to the place called the "Schoedia" <note>A suburb or landing place near Alexandria</note> and the voyage was completed as the King had decreed, he commanded them to be imprisoned in the **Hippodrome** <note>A large stadium used for horse and chariot racing; here used as a massive open-air prison</note> in front of the city. This place was chosen because it had an enormous circumference and was perfectly situated to make an example of them to all those entering the city or departing from it into the countryside.

<column-break/>

He gave orders that they should not be allowed to associate with his military forces or be granted the protection of the city walls. When the King heard this was being carried out, and learned that those of the same nation who lived in the city were secretly going out to mourn the misery of their brothers, he was filled with rage. He ordered that these people should be treated in exactly the same way as the others, and that no part of their punishment should be lessened.

He commanded that the entire race be registered by name <note>original: "απογραφή" (apographē), a formal census or registration for the purpose of taxation or, in this case, execution</note>. This was not for the usual labor purposes mentioned previously, but to subject them to torture as commanded, and finally to annihilate them within the space of a single day.

The registration was conducted with bitter haste and ambitious zeal from the rising of the sun until its setting. Though the process was unceasing, it remained unfinished even after **forty days**.

During this time, the King was continually filled with great joy. He held constant banquets before all his idols, his mind straying far from the truth. He praised gods that were deaf and unable to speak or help, while failing to give proper regard to the True Power.

After the aforementioned period of time had passed, the scribes came before the King and reported that they were no longer able to continue the registration of the Jews. This was because of their unmeasurable multitude, as many were still in the countryside, while others remained in their homes. Indeed, the task had become impossible for all the officials in Egypt.

### THE PLOT OF THE FIVE HUNDRED ELEPHANTS

->**Column 1**<-

When the King threatened the officials with a hard heart because the strategy for the Jews' escape had been foiled, it clearly happened that concerning the registration of the names given to each scribe, even the **writing reeds** <term>reeds</term> <note>original: "καλάμους" (kalamous), hollow reeds used as pens in antiquity</note> which they were using had run out. Then, summoning Hermon, the official in charge of the elephants, the King—filled with heavy care and an unyielding, unceasing anger—ordered that on the following day, he should give all the elephants, five hundred in number, large portions of frankincense and a great deal of **unmixed wine** <gloss>unmixed wine</gloss> <note>original: "ἀκράτῳ" (akratō), wine not diluted with water, intended to drive the animals into a violent frenzy</note>. While he was giving these orders, the King turned to his feasting, gathering those of his friends and the military who were most hostile toward the Jews.

Hermon, the master of the elephants, carried out the command exactly. The attendants, toward evening, bound the hands of the miserable people and took other precautions for their security throughout the night, believing that the entire race would be destroyed at once at the conclusion of their ruin.

However, that good creation of time, which from eternity has been bestowed upon all by the Giver of all things, a portion of sleep was sent to the King. By the working of the **Master of Oblivion** <term>Oblivion</term> <note>original: "λήθης" (lēthēs), referring to God's power to make the king forget his cruel purpose through sleep</note>, he was held in a most sweet and deep sleep, and thus his unyielding purpose was greatly frustrated.

Because his unchangeable reasoning was greatly deceived regarding the Jews, they escaped the previously appointed hour of death, avoiding the King's madness. They praised their God and again begged the One who is easily reconciled to show the strength of His powerful hand to the arrogant nations.

# THE DIVINE DELAY AND THE KING’S ANGER

->**Column 1**<-

With a **bitter threat**, the King inquired for what reason and cause the mass of people had survived the day, having escaped the fate prepared for them. But when it was explained that the command had been carried out at night, and his friends testified to his own cruelty, he became even more embittered. He declared that since **sleep** <gloss>sleep</gloss> <note>original: "ὕπνος" (hypnos). In this context, it is presented as a gift from God to the Jews to stall their execution.</note> had favored them today, they should, without any delay, prepare the elephants for the coming day in the same manner to utterly destroy the people of the Jews.

When the King had spoken, everyone joyfully and with gladness agreed, and each went to his own home. They did not spend the night in sleep, but in preparing whatever was necessary for those who were to be killed.

As the day began to break, even before the sun had fully risen, the city was already filled with crowds. People were rushing toward the **hippodrome** <term>hippodrome</term> <note>The large stadium where the public execution by elephants was intended to take place.</note> to witness the security of the proceedings and the expected destruction, waiting for the morning with great haste.

But the Jews, continuing in prayer to the **Almighty Lord** <note>original: "τοῦ παντὸC κρατατον" (tou pantos krataton), referring to God as the Sovereign over all things.</note>, made many supplications with tears, begging the Greatest of all to manifest His power to them now as they faced the end of their lives.

The King's officials were already leading the elephants out toward the gate, following the King’s previous command. The King himself was expected to come out to witness the slaughter, while the people of the city waited in great suspense...

->**THIS WAS ACCOMPLISHED**<-

By the working of the **Master of All** <note>original: "παντὰ δεCπότου" (panta despotou)</note>, who governs all things, He placed a **forgetfulness** <gloss>forgetfulness</gloss> <note>original: "λήθην" (lēthēn). # THE KING’S OATH AND THE PRAYER OF ELEAZAR

->**Column 1**<-

The King’s friends brought forward these arguments: "O King, how long will you test us, ordering us for a third time to destroy them, and then again changing your mind and reversing your orders? Because of this, the city is troubled by the expectation of a riot, and the gathered crowd often risks turning into a full-blown revolt." 

The King, having the reasons for the delay explained to him and seeing the changes of mind he had experienced, became even more fixed in his cruelty. Setting a most firm and binding **oath**, he determined that he would send these people to **Hades** <note>original: "εἰϲ ᾅδην" (eis hadēn). The King intends to send the Jews to the underworld, the realm of the dead.</note> without delay, crushed by the feet of the beasts. He also vowed to march against **Judea** and level it to the ground with fire and ash, and to burn their **Temple**—which we are not permitted to enter—with fire, making an end of those who perform sacrifices there for all time.

Then the King’s friends and relatives departed with great joy, trusting his word, and stationed the military forces at the most convenient places in the city to keep guard.

Meanwhile, the commander of the elephants brought the beasts into a state of **frenzy** <note>original: "μανιώδεϲ" (maniōdes). The elephants were intentionally driven into a mad rage using drugs and wine.</note>, nearly as intended, by giving them drinks of unmixed wine flavored with frankincense, and they were equipped with terrifying harnesses. At dawn, as an innumerable crowd moved toward the **hippodrome** <term>hippodrome</term> <note>A stadium designed for horse and chariot racing, here repurposed as an arena for public execution.</note>, he entered the palace and urged the King to proceed with the matter at hand. 

The King’s mind was filled with a heavy and savage anger, and he set out with all his weight together with the beasts, desiring to witness with his own eyes the painful and wretched end of the

<column-break/>

aforementioned people. But when the Jews saw the elephants coming out of the gate, followed by the armed forces and the dust cloud raised by the approaching crowd, and when they heard the heavy, thundering noise, they thought this was the final moment of their lives. 

Reaching the end of their most piteous expectation, they turned to lamentation and groans. They began to kiss one another, embracing their relatives and falling upon their necks—parents with children, and mothers with their young daughters. Other women held **newborn infants** to their breasts, drawing what they believed would be their last milk. 

However, remembering the help they had received from heaven in the past, they cast themselves down with one accord, pulling their infants away from their breasts, and cried out with an exceedingly loud voice. They implored the Ruler of all power to have mercy on them through a **divine manifestation** <note>original: "ἐπιφανείαϲ" (epiphaneias). They are asking for a visible act of God's presence to save them.</note>, as they were already standing at the very gates of Hades.

<margin>/</margin> Then a certain **Eleazar**, a man of distinction among the priests of the land, who was already advanced in age and adorned with every virtue of a long life, settled the elders around him and called upon the **Holy God** <term>God</term> <note>The Greek text uses the "nomen sacrum" θν, a scribal abbreviation for Θεόν (Theon).</note>. He prayed as follows: 

"O King of great power, Most High, Almighty **God** <term>God</term> <note>The Greek text uses the "nomen sacrum" θε, an abbreviation for Θεέ (Thee).</note>, you who govern all creation with mercy: Look upon the seed of Abraham, upon the children of the sanctified Jacob, your own portion, a people who are strangers in a foreign land and are being unjustly destroyed. 

You destroyed the former ruler of Egypt, **Pharaoh** <note>Though the OCR is fragmented here, the context refers to the Exodus.</note>, who multiplied his chariots and was puffed up with lawless boldness and a tongue speaking great things; along with his proud army, you drowned him in the sea."

As the execution looms at dawn, the elderly priest Eleazar stands before the people to offer a final, desperate prayer for divine intervention, reminding God of His past mercies toward Israel.</meta>

# THE PRAYER OF ELEAZAR AND THE DIVINE RESCUE

->**Column 1**<-

**Y**ou, who are appropriately called "Manifest" <note>original: "ΕΠΙΦΑΝΗΣ" (Epiphanes). This is a wordplay on the King’s title, asserting that God is the truly "Manifest" power.</note>, Lord of mercy, look upon the seed of Abraham. You destroyed the countless army of the Egyptian **Pharaoh** <note>original: "ΦΡΑΥΡΩΣΗΤΑΣ" (Pharaō). Referring to the Exodus and the crossing of the Red Sea.</note> when he enslaved Your people and pursued them with chariots and a multitude of weapons, drowning them in the depths of the sea. You, when **Sennacherib** <note>original: "ΛΕΛΛΟΡΧΤΙ" (Sennacherim). The Assyrian king who besieged Jerusalem in the time of King Hezekiah.</note>, the cruel king of the Assyrians, boasted in his power after taking the whole earth captive, You broke his might through an angel, showing Your strength to many nations.

**Y**ou, Lord, when the **Three Youths** <note>original: "ΤΗΝ ΚΑΚΟΦΡΟΝΑ... ΠΥΡΙ" (the evil-minded... fire). Referring to Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael in the Babylonian furnace.</note> in Babylon were cast into the fire to be burned because they would not serve idols, You delivered them unharmed even to the hair of their heads, sending a flame against their enemies instead. You are the one who, when **Daniel** <note>original: "ΛΛΙ ΣΦΟΔΡΟ" (lions). Referring to Daniel in the lions' den.</note> was cast to the ravenous lions beneath the earth, brought him up to the light untouched. 

**A**nd when **Jonah** <note>original: "ΙΩΝΑΝ" (Iōnan). The OCR is fragmentary here, but the context of the prayer follows the traditional sequence of Jonah in the belly of the sea monster.</note> was wasting away in the belly of the sea-born monster, You restored him to his family, showing him mercy. Now, O hater of insolence, Lord of great mercy, protector of all, reveal Yourself quickly to the holy ones of the race of Israel, who are being treated with outrage by the lawless and arrogant Gentiles. 

**R**escue us from the hand of our enemies, O Lord, and save us from a wretched death. Let the foolish see that You are with us and have not turned Your face away. Save us, O Lord, for the sake of Your glory, and let those who have purposed our destruction be terrified by Your mighty power. You alone have the power and the dominion to save us from this plot.

<column-break/>

**T**he whole multitude of **infants** and their parents beseech You with tears. Let it be shown to all that You are with us, Lord. Do not turn Your face from us, but just as You helped our ancestors on this earth when they were overwhelmed by enemies, so now let Your work be accomplished, O Lord.

**W**hen Eleazar had just finished his prayer, having looked upon the beasts <note>the elephants prepared for the massacre</note> and the whole arrogance of the King's forces at the hippodrome, the great-glorious and **Almighty and True God** <note>original: "ΠΑΝΤΟΚΡΑΤΩΡ ΚΑΙ ΑΛΗΘΙΝΟΣ ΘΣ" (Pantokratōr kai alēthinos Theos).</note> manifested His holy face and opened the heavenly gates. Two glorious and terrifying **angels** <note>original: "ΑΓΓΕΛΟΙ" (angeloi).</note> descended, visible to all except the Jews. 

**T**hey stood against the forces of the enemies and filled them with confusion and cowardice. Even the body of the King began to tremble, and his heavy arrogance was forgotten. The beasts themselves <note>the elephants</note> turned back upon the armed forces that followed them, trampling them and destroying them.

**A**nd so the King’s anger was turned into **pity** <note>original: "ΟΚΤΟΝ" (oikton - mercy/pity).</note> and tears because of the things he had previously devised. For hearing the outcry and seeing the people prostrate in prayer, he wept and angrily threatened his friends, saying: "You have overstepped even tyrants in your cruelty! You have attempted to deprive me of my kingdom and my life by plotting against these people who have always been loyal to us!"

<summary>This page records the climactic Prayer of Eleazar, which recites God's historical deliverances (Exodus, Sennacherib, the Three Youths, Daniel, Jonah) to plead for current salvation. It concludes with a divine intervention where two angels terrify the King's army, causing the elephants to trample the soldiers and the King to repent in tears.</summary>

# THE KING’S REPENTANCE AND THE SEVEN-DAY FEAST

->**Column 1**<-

"**Y**ou are attacking your own benefactor! You are attempting an unjust rule by secretly warring against those whose interests do not benefit the kingdom! Our King <note>Ptolemy IV Philopator refers to himself or the royal 'we' here.</note> held this land in faith, yet you have removed the fortifications of the house, gathering everyone without reason. You have treated as nothing those who from the beginning showed a goodwill that stands out above all other nations, and who have many times faced the worst dangers. You have surrounded them with such lawless perils!"

"**T**herefore, loose them! Release the unjust bonds! Send them back to their own homes in peace, canceling the orders you were given. Release the sons of the Almighty Heavenly Living God, who from the time of our ancestors until now has provided undisturbed stability and glory to our affairs."

**T**hese were the words he spoke. And they <note>the Jewish people</note>, having escaped a deadly fate, were inspired in their souls. They began blessing the Holy Savior God, having just escaped death. Then the King, returning to the city, summoned those in charge of the supplies and ordered that wine and all other things suitable for a feast be provided to the Jews for seven days. He decided that in the very place where they expected to meet their destruction, they should instead spend that time in all joy and salvation.

**T**hen those who were previously disgraced and near the gates of Hades—or rather, who had already stepped upon them—instead of a bitter and madness-dripping fate <note>original: "ΜΟΤΟΥ" (motou), often referring to a fatal wound or medical dressing; here it signifies their 'bitter end'.</note>, they set up a cup of salvation. In the place that had been seized for their ruin, they shared a feast, full of joy. Ceasing their mournful songs, they took up a different melody:

<column-break/>

**A** traditional song of the land, praising the miracle-working God. Those who had already cast away all wailing and mourning established dances, a sign of peaceful joy. Likewise, the King himself, gathering a great banquet to celebrate these events, was continually giving thanks and grandly confessing the paradoxical salvation that had come to them. And those who previously intended them for destruction to be food for the wine-drugged [elephants] <note>The "wine-drugged" refers to the practice of giving the execution elephants wine and frankincense to make them more violent.</note>, and who had registered them for death with joy, now groaned, wrapping themselves in shame; their fire-breathing daring was ingloriously extinguished.

**W**hen the Jews, as we said before, had completed the aforementioned time with feasting, singing to Him with confessions and psalms, they established a common law concerning these things for their entire community. They decided to keep the aforementioned days as joyous ones for all coming generations—not for the sake of drinking and gluttony, but because of the salvation that had come to them through God.

**T**hey then petitioned the King, asking for their release to their own homes. The registration of them had lasted from the twenty-fifth of the month of **Pachon** <note>original: "ΕΠΕΚΡΕΙΦΙ" (Epekreyphi - likely a scribal variant or error for Pachon).</note> until the fourth of **Epiphi** <note>original: "ΕΠΙΦΙ" (Epiphi). Epiphi is the eleventh month of the ancient Egyptian calendar.</note>, for forty-two days. The plot for their destruction lasted from the fifth of Epiphi until the seventh—thirteen days. 

**T**he Ruler of all, having gloriously manifested His mercy, rescued them all with one accord. They feasted on everything provided by the King until the fourteenth day, on which they also made their formal petition for their release.

**T**he King approved their request and wrote for them the letter transcribed below:

<summary>King Ptolemy rebukes his advisors, releases the Jewish prisoners, and funds a seven-day celebration in the very hippodrome where they were to be executed. The Jews establish an annual festival to commemorate this divine rescue.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the narrative of 3 Maccabees, following the King’s change of heart. Having realized the divine protection over the Jewish people, King Ptolemy IV Philopator issues a formal decree to his provincial governors to cease all persecution and restore the Jews to their former status.</meta>

# TO THE GENERALS IN THE CITIES
# WITH MAGNANIMOUS EARNESTNESS
# KING PTOLEMY
# PHILOPATOR TO THE GENERALS IN EGYPT
# AND TO ALL THOSE
# APPOINTED OVER AFFAIRS,
# GREETINGS AND GOOD HEALTH.

<margin>Γ</margin> We ourselves are in good health, and our children as well, as the Great God <note>original: "ΜΕΓΑΛΟΥ ΘΕΟΥ" (Megalou Theou). The King now uses a title of high respect for the God of the Jews.</note> directs our affairs as we desire. Regarding the extreme malice of our friends, we have frequently had our attention drawn to it. We were urged to believe that by the gathering of this people into one place, we would punish them with strange punishments as rebels, claiming that our affairs would never remain stable until this was done. However, they <note>the King's advisors</note> held a hatred for this nation until this was carried out. They bound them in houses, treating them harshly with cruel words, or rather, as conspirators. They filled the inquiry and examination with a savage and Scythian-like cruelty <note>Ancient Greeks and Egyptians often used "Scythian" as a synonym for "barbarian" or "extremely cruel."</note>, thinking they would be more harshly disposed. Nevertheless, we have decided that all shall travel together, being inclined to show them favor. Even as we have safely sailed to Pelusium <note>original: "ΠΕΛΟΥΣΑΝΙΩΣ" (Pelousaniōs). A major eastern gateway city to Egypt.</note>, we have heard the voice of the Father <note>The Jewish God</note> given to those who joined together. We have considered the goodwill and loyalty they have shown toward us and our ancestors, and we justly absolve them of any cause or blame whatsoever. We have commanded everyone to return to their own places in every way, and that no one should harm them at all, nor treat them unreasonably concerning what has happened.

<column-break/>

<margin>Γ</margin> For know that if we devise any evil against them, or cause them any grief, we shall have not a man, but the Most High God, the Ruler of all Power, set against us as an avenger of these deeds, in all things and for all time. Be in good health.

<margin>Γ</margin> Upon receiving this letter, they did not immediately hurry to depart, but rather they prayed to the God of all, having freely transgressed <note>This likely refers to the Jewish people's request to deal with those who had "transgressed" by apostatizing to save their lives.</note> the Law of God. They requested only the opportunity for a time of purification, and they asked the King that those of their own race who had voluntarily transgressed the holy Law and the commands of God should receive the punishment they deserved.

<margin>Γ</margin> Those who were appointed over these matters, having said all these things... <unclear>illegible</unclear> gave them over completely, so that those who had transgressed the Law of God might be punished. In all this, the King’s decree was incomparable. After these things were examined with great celebration, as was fitting, they and the whole multitude cried out with joy and prayer. These people, who had been tainted by the law of the defiled, were now restored to the state of the righteous and the affairs of their heritage on that day. Those who had committed these impieties were handled without mercy by their own people. Having obtained complete salvation and release, they departed from the city with all kinds of sweet-smelling flowers <note>original: "ΕΥΩΔΕΣΙ" (euōdesi). Likely referring to garlands or incense used in the celebration.</note>.

<summary>This page contains a royal decree from King Ptolemy Philopator reversing his persecution of the Jews, followed by the Jews' request to punish those among them who abandoned their faith during the crisis.</summary>

->3 MACCABEES<-

<column-break/>

Since I am about to demonstrate a
most philosophical discourse
as to whether Pious Reason <term>Pious Reason: "eusebēs logismos," the Stoic-influenced concept of using religious law and logic to govern human emotions.</term>
is master over the passions,
I would rightly advise you to
eagerly apply yourselves to philosophy.
For Reason is necessary for the
knowledge of everyone, and
moreover, it contains the praise
of the highest virtue—I mean,
of course, Prudence.
For if Reason appears to
exercise mastery over the passions
of self-control <note>The text explores the hierarchy of virtues, specifically how Reason governs physical appetites.</note>,
it is evident that it prevails
over gluttony and desire.
But it is also shown to
rule over the passions that
hinder justice, such as
vanity, and over those passions
that hinder courage, namely
anger, pain, and fear.
How then, some might say,
does Reason rule over the passions
if it does not master forgetfulness
and ignorance? This is a ridiculous
thing to attempt to say! For
Reason does not rule over its
own internal passions <note>referring to cognitive defects like ignorance</note>,
but over the passions of injustice,
such as harsh laughter and
those things contrary to
temperance and prudence,
not so as to uproot them,
but so as to resolve them by
not yielding to them in many ways...

<margin>K</margin> I could better show you from
another source that Pious Reason
is the absolute ruler
of the passions,
but I will make my discourse
much more focused on the
bravery of those who
died for the sake of virtue:
Eleazar, and the seven brothers,
and their mother. For
by their contempt for
sufferings even unto death, they
demonstrated that Reason
prevails over the passions.

It is now my duty to
praise the excellence of those
men who, at that time, died
with their mother for the sake of
nobility and virtue; but I would
also call them blessed for the
honor they received, being
admired not only by all men...

--- Page 1034 ---
<meta>This page continues from the opening of 4 Maccabees. The previous page concluded the narrative of 3 Maccabees and began the philosophical introduction to this new book. This section moves from the historical result of the Maccabean revolt (the purification of the land) into the core philosophical thesis of the work: that religious reason is the sovereign ruler over the emotions.</meta>

...since their courage and endurance, and even because of those who tortured them, they became the cause of the dismantling of the tyranny against the nation. Having conquered the tyrant through their endurance, the fatherland was purified through them. But also concerning...

**T**he argument I am now about to present will allow me to begin the premise as I usually do, and I will proceed to the demonstration concerning them, having shown that the question is clearly sought after. Therefore, let us consider whether **Reason** <note>original: "λογισμός" (logismos). In this context, it refers to "pious reason" or a mind guided by religious principle.</note> is the sovereign master of the emotions.

**D**iscerning then, let us define what Reason is and what emotion is, and how many types of emotions there are, and whether Reason prevails over all of these.

**R**eason, then, is the mind accompanied by right logic, which chooses the life of wisdom.

**W**isdom, then, is the knowledge of divine and human matters and their causes. This is, in fact, the education of the **Law** <note>original: "νόμου" (nomou). Referring to the Torah or Jewish Law.</note>, through which we learn divine things with reverence and human things for our benefit.

**T**he forms of wisdom consist of **prudence**, **justice**, **courage**, and **temperance** <note>original: "φρόνησις... δικαιοσύνη... ἀνδρεία... σωφροσύνη". These are the four cardinal virtues of classical Greek philosophy, here integrated into Jewish thought.</note>. Prudence is the most authoritative of all, for through it, Reason prevails over the emotions. There are two primary comprehensive types of emotions: pleasure and pain. Each of these occurs naturally both in the soul and in many ways around the body. There are many tendencies that follow: before pleasure there is **desire**, and after pleasure there is **joy**. Before pain there is **fear**, and after pain there is **grief**. **Anger** <note>original: "θυμός" (thymos). Often translated as "wrath" or "spirit."</note> is a shared emotion of both pleasure and pain, if one considers when one has fallen into it.

<column-break/>

**W**ithin pleasure there also exists a malicious disposition, the most varied of all the emotions. In the soul, this appears as boastfulness, love of money, love of glory, rivalry, and envy. In the body, it appears as indiscriminate eating, gluttony, and solitary eating. Just as there are two sources of the body and soul—namely, pleasure and pain—there are many offshoots of these emotions. Each of these, **Reason**, the gardener of all, by weeding and pruning, and by binding up and watering, and in every way redirecting them, tames the wild growth of habits and emotions.

**F**or Reason is the leader of the virtues and the sovereign ruler over the emotions. It is observed first through the actions that restrain **temperance** <note>original: "σωφροσύνης" (sōphrosynēs). Self-control or moderation.</note>, proving that Reason is the sovereign master of the emotions. Temperance, then, is the mastery of the desires.

**O**f the desires, some belong to the soul and others are of the body, and Reason appears to prevail over both of these. For when we are moved toward forbidden foods, from where are we turned away from the pleasures within them? Is it not because Reason is able to prevail over the appetites? I believe so. Therefore, when we desire fish and birds and four-footed animals and all kinds of foods that are forbidden to us according to the Law, we abstain because of the sovereignty of Reason. For the emotions of the appetites are held in check and bridled by the temperate mind, and all the movements of the body are curbed by Reason.

<summary>This page introduces the philosophical core of 4 Maccabees, defining Reason (logismos) as the sovereign ruler over emotions and bodily desires. It uses the Jewish dietary laws as a primary example of how religious logic can master physical appetites and lead to virtue.</summary>
<keywords>Reason, Logismos, Wisdom, Law, Cardinal Virtues, Temperance, Emotions, Pleasure and Pain, Dietary Laws, Philosophy</keywords>

AND WHY IS IT A WONDER IF THE 
DESIRES OF THE SOUL FOR THE 
PARTICIPATION IN BEAUTY ARE

<margin>L</margin>IKESWISE THE LAW SAYS, "YOU SHALL

EMOTIONS THAT HINDER JUSTICE.

<margin>E</margin>LSE, IN WHAT MANNER IS A PERSON 
WHO IS BY HABIT A SOLITARY EATER 
AND A GLUTTON TRANSFORMED 
TO BE DISCIPLINED, IF IT WERE NOT 
CLEAR THAT REASON PREVAILS OVER

ONE WHO LIVES BY THE LAW, 
EVEN IF THEY WERE A LOVER OF MONEY, 
FORCES THEIR OWN CHARACTER BY 
LENDING TO THE NEEDY WITHOUT 
INTEREST AND, WHEN THE SEVENTH 
YEAR <note>original: "ἑβδομάδων" (hebdomadōn). Referring to the Sabbatical year or 'Shemitah' where debts were canceled (Deuteronomy 15:1–2).</note> ARRIVES, SUFFERING THE

AND THERE ARE OTHER THINGS

REBUKING HER FOR

FOR IF REASON WERE NOT ABLE TO

<margin>3</margin>
**S**INCE, THEREFORE, IT IS COMMONLY ASKED in mockery: 
"If reason prevails over the passions, why does it not 
prevail over forgetfulness and ignorance?" <note>The author is addressing a counter-argument: if the mind is so powerful, why do we still forget things or make mistakes?</note> 
For it does not appear that the reasoning 
of one's own passions prevails, 
but rather that it rules over the bodily ones. 
For example, none of you 
is able to cut out <note>original: "ἐκκόψαι" (ekkopsai) - to excise or eradicate.</note> desire, 
but reason is able to provide 
the means to not be enslaved 
by desire. None of you is 
able to cut out <note>The scribe repeats this phrase, emphasizing that reason manages rather than deletes human nature.</note> the soul’s 
distress, but it is possible for reason 
to provide help by not 
yielding to the distress of evils. 
For reason is a

## THE RESOLVE AND MARTYDOM OF ELEAZAR

...to endure, and justice to train us; so that in everything we live by the divine laws and teach **piety**, so as to worship only the existing God <note>original: "ΘΝ" — a 'nomen sacrum' (sacred name) abbreviation for "Theon" (God).</note> with true magnificence. Therefore, we do not eat defiled food; for believing that the Law is established by God, we know that the Creator of the world, in his law-giving, sympathizes with our nature. Those things that would be suited to our souls, he has permitted us to eat; but the things that would be contrary, he has forbidden us to taste. 

It is tyrannical of you to not only force us to break the Law, but also to eat so that you may laugh at this defiled eating of ours. But you shall not have this laugh at my expense! Neither shall I violate the sacred oaths of my ancestors regarding the keeping of the Law—not even if you should pluck out my eyes and consume my entrails. 

I am an old man, but my **Reason** <note>original: "λογισμὸν" (logismon) — the faculty of religious reasoning which the author argues can overcome any physical suffering.</note> is not so aged that it lacks the vigor of youth in its devotion to God. Against this, prepare your wheels of torture and blow the fire more fiercely! I do not so pity my own old age that I would, through my own actions, tear down the ancestral Law. I will not lie to you, O Law, my teacher! Nor will I deny you, O beloved Self-Control! I will not put you to shame, O Philosophical Reason! Nor will I dishonor you, O honored Priesthood and knowledge of the Law. 

You shall not defile the honorable mouth of my old age, nor the long years of a life lived according to the Law. My ancestors shall receive me as a pure person into their tombs, unafraid of your terrors even unto death. For you may play the tyrant over the ungodly, but you shall not rule over my religious Reason.

<column-break/>

Neither by ungodly words nor in...
<margin>6 : ~</margin> In this manner, he spoke in reply to the tyrant’s persuasions. The bodyguards standing by dragged Eleazar bitterly to the instruments of torture. And first, they stripped the old man, who was clothed in the beauty of his **piety**. Then, they bound his arms on both sides and scourged him with whips. 
"Obey the king’s command!" 
the herald cried out from above. 

But the high-minded and truly noble Eleazar, as if being tortured in a dream, was in no way turned back. Instead, the old man kept his eyes fixed high toward heaven as his flesh was torn by the whips; he was drenched in blood and his ribs were wounded. Even when he fell to the ground because his body could no longer bear the pain, he kept his Reason upright and unbending. 

One of the cruel bodyguards, leaping upon his stomach, kicked him to make him rise as he fell. But he endured the pains, and looked down upon the compulsion, and bore the outrages. Like a noble athlete <note>original: "γενναῖος ἀθλητὴς" (gennaios athlētēs) — the author uses the metaphor of a sports competition to describe martyrdom.</note> being struck, the old man conquered those who were torturing him. Indeed, with his face covered in sweat and gasping for breath, he was admired even by his torturers for his great courage. 

Therefore, some of the king’s men, partly out of pity for his old age, partly out of sympathy for their past acquaintance with him, and partly in wonder at his endurance, approached him and said:
"Why do you so mindlessly destroy yourself with these evils, Eleazar?"

# THE SACRIFICE OF THE ELDER

We have now come to the point where, with the dignity of his white hair, he might demonstrate the character of a son of God. From Eleazar, as if with the bitter pains of his counsel, he cried out to his brothers:

<margin>M</margin> “Shall we not then, children of Abraham, be eternally wise? Let us not act out a vile drama <note>original: "ΔΡΑΜΑ ΥΠΟΚΡΙΣΩΜΕΘΑ" — refers to playing a role or being a hypocrite on a stage.</note> that is unworthy of the soul! Let us not live for the tyrant who flows against the divine, but rather let us live as those who have guarded the divine life until old age and have lawfully kept the marriage bed. God will see us! Let us not become a model of impiety to the youth, but let us instead become an example of dietary holiness. Let us trust in the time we have left and mock the tyrant. Let us not despise the children's games <note>The author compares earthly life to a temporary game compared to eternity.</note> and the tyrant's threats, as it is unworthy of our pious laws not to fight for them even unto death.”

---

<margin>Y</margin> “You, O children, die nobly and with high birth for the sake of **piety**!” When the tyrant’s guards saw his bravery, they smiled at him. Yet, even as he was acting so wisely, they came toward the merciful one and changed their manner. They led him away to where, through mechanical instruments, they burned him thoroughly, roasting him. They poured strong, boiling bronze <note>original: "ΧΑΛΚΩΣ" — likely meaning molten metal or heated copper vessels.</note> into his nostrils. Even when he was burned down to the bones and about to expire, he stretched his eyes toward God <note>original: "ΘΝ" — a sacred abbreviation for "Theon" (God).</note> and said:

---

<margin>E</margin> “You, O God, know that though it was possible for me to be saved, I am dying through these burning pains for the sake of the Law. Be satisfied with me! Let my punishment be a sufficient penalty for my nation. Make my death a purification <term>purification: "καθαρίσιον" (katharsion) — the idea that a martyr's death can wash away the sins of the people.</term> for them.”

<column-break/>

“Take my blood as their own, and in exchange for their lives, take my life.” And having said these things, the holy man died nobly in his tortures; even in the midst of the king’s cruelties, his **Reason** <note>original: "λογισμῷ" (logismo) — the faculty of religious reasoning.</note> stood firm for the sake of the Law.

---

<margin>O</margin> We confess, therefore, that **Pious Reason** is indeed the master over the passions. For if the passions had mastered Reason, we would have been persuaded to follow them. But now, since my base passions have been conquered, the leadership belongs to Reason. Again, we must confess that the power belongs to Reason, since it even masters external pains, mocking them. It rules not only over the passions—since it rules over our waves of emotion—but also over pleasures, refusing to yield to them.

---

<margin>7.</margin> For just as a supreme pilot <note>The author uses the "Ship of State/Soul" metaphor common in Greek philosophy.</note> steers the ship of our ancestors, so the Reason of our forefathers is the pilot of the ship of **piety**. Though tossed about in the sea of passions and flooded by the storms of the tyrant and the waves of torture, Reason did not move the ship’s course. It was not separated from the path even by the threat of death...

---

<margin>O</margin> Not so! Even though many things happen in the midst of war, the one who endures when the battle is heavy makes his holy soul a conqueror. Through the oath of the ancestors, that soul stands before God, inseparable from Him even in death.

---

<margin>E</margin> Since the father of our ancestors, Eleazar, stretched out his mind for the sake of the nation...

"Why do you delay, O tyrant? For we are ready to die rather than transgress our ancestral commandments. When they had said these things, the tyrant became enraged, not just because they were disobedient, but because they seemed ungrateful. Therefore, at his command, the torturers led forward the eldest of them. After stripping off his tunic, they bound his hands and arms with straps on both sides.

<column-break/>

As they struck him with whips, they grew weary, achieving nothing. They then threw him upon the wheel <term>the wheel: a horrific device where the victim was bound and turned over a fire or pulled until joints dislocated</term>, upon which the noble youth was stretched out until his joints were dislocated. And when the guards said to him, "Agree to eat, so that you may be released from these tortures," he replied: "Your methods are not so strong, O polluted ministers, as to lead my reason astray. Cut my limbs, burn my flesh, and twist my joints! For through all these tortures, I will convince you that only the children of the Hebrews are invincible in the cause of virtue!"

As he said these things, they heaped on more fuel and, tightening the wheel further, they stretched him more. The wheel was defiled on all sides with blood, and the heap of gore extinguished the flames. The pieces of his flesh were flung around the axles of the machine. Though his bone structure was dissolving, the high-minded and Abrahamic <note>original: "ΑΒΡΑΜΙΑΙΟC" — Refers to the patriarch Abraham, symbolizing the highest form of Jewish faithfulness and endurance.</note> youth did not groan. But as if he were being transformed into incorruption in the fire, he endured the racks nobly.

"Imitate me, brothers!" he cried out. "Do not desert me for all eternity, and do not renounce our brotherhood of courage. Fight the sacred and noble warfare for the sake of piety! Through this, may our ancestral Providence <term>Providence: the protective care of God as a spiritual power</term> become merciful to our nation and punish the accursed tyrant!"

### APPROACHING THE END <gloss>the finality</gloss>

The seventh came forward, the youngest of all. The tyrant, though he had been deeply embittered by the older brothers, felt pity <note>The Greek text uses 'katoikteiras,' suggesting the tyrant felt a moment of compassion or perhaps a strategic desire to succeed with at least one brother.</note> for the boy. Seeing him already standing there bound, he summoned him closer and tried to console him, saying: "You see the end of your brothers' madness. Because of their disobedience, they were tortured and have died. You, however, should not imitate them. Otherwise, you too will hasten toward a miserable death before your time. But if you obey, you shall enjoy the king’s friendship and have a role in the affairs of the kingdom."

**A**nd as he made this appeal, he sent for the boy’s mother so that she might take pity on her son and persuade him to seek safety by obeying. The mother, however, encouraged him in the **Hebrew language** <note>original: "ΕΒΡΑΪΔΙ ΦΩΝΗ" — This likely refers to Aramaic, the common spoken language of Judea at the time, which the Greek captors would not have understood.</note>, as we shall describe shortly. Afterward, the boy said, "Release me, for I wish to speak to the King and the friends who are with him." The guards, rejoicing at the boy’s request, quickly released him. He then ran up close to the frying pans <note>The 'tegana' were large, shallow metal basins used as instruments of torture by heating them from below.</note> and said:

"**O** impious tyrant, most wicked of all villains! Are you not ashamed, having received your good things and your kingdom from **God** <note>original: "ΘΥ" — Nomina Sacra for Theou (of God).</note>, to murder His servants and torture the practitioners of piety? For these deeds, **Divine Justice** <note>original: "ΘΕΙΑ ΔΙΚΗ" — The personification of Justice as a divine force.</note> stores up for you a more intense and eternal fire and tortures which shall never let you go throughout all time. 

**A**re you not ashamed, being a man yourself, O most beastly creature, to cut out the tongues of those who have the same feelings and were made from the same elements as you, and to torture them in this way?"

<column-break/>

"Others have died nobly and fulfilled their piety toward **God** <note>original: "ΘΝ" — Nomina Sacra for Theon (God).</note>. But you shall wail miserably for having killed the champions of virtue without cause!" Then, as he was about to die, he said:

"**I** do not desert the testimony of my brothers. I call upon the **God** <note>original: "ΘΝ"</note> of my fathers to be merciful to my race; but you He shall punish both in this present life and after you have died." 
And having offered this prayer, he threw himself into the frying pans and so departed this life.

<margin>13</margin>
**I**f, therefore, the seven brothers despised sufferings even unto death, it is universally admitted that **pious reason** <term>Logismos: The author's central argument that religious devotion provides the rational strength to master physical and emotional pain.</term> is the absolute master of the passions. For just as those who are enslaved to the passions eat forbidden foods <note>original: "EMIEROPHAGESAN" — specifically referring to eating the sacrificial pork demanded by the tyrant.</note>, we say that in this case their mind has been conquered. But it is not so here; rather, by the **reason** that is visible to us, they overcame the passions. There is no better example of the leadership of the mind, for they prevailed over both suffering and pain. How then can one not admit the power of **pious reason** over the passions? 

For they were not turned back by the agonies of the fire. Just as towers standing at the harbor's entrance break the threats of the waves and provide a calm anchorage for those sailing in, so the "seven-towered" right-reasoning of these youths fortified the harbor of piety and conquered the wildness of the passions. They formed a holy choir, encouraging one another, saying: "Let us die as brothers for the sake of the Law! Let us imitate the **three youths in Syria** <note>A reference to Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego from the Book of Daniel, who survived the fiery furnace.</note> who also defied the tyrant’s fire."

### THE VOICES IN THE FURNACE <gloss>the testimony of the martyrs</gloss>

Those who were in the ashes of the furnace
looked down [upon the tortures]; let us not
overlook their proof of **piety** <term>eusebeia: a Greek term for deep religious devotion and dutiful conduct toward God</term>.

steadfast!" Another said: "Remember

Each one of them, looking at one another
brightly rather than at themselves,
were saying: "Let us dedicate

the guardianship of the Law.

who seems to kill;

For the affections of humanity

**O reasonings more kingly than kings!**
And more free than the free!
O sacred and harmonious

Not one of the seven youths

<summary>This page depicts the intense psychological and physical drama of the Mother of the Seven Brothers as she watches her sons' horrific executions. It presents a philosophical argument that her "pious reasoning" (logismos) successfully overthrew her natural "maternal instinct" (philoteknia), elevating her as a martyr more courageous than any man.</summary>
<keywords>4 Maccabees, martyrdom, Mother of the Seven Brothers, logismos (reasoning), eusebeia (piety), philoteknia (maternal love), endurance, religious law, Greek philosophy, virtue</keywords>

--- Page 1050 ---
<meta>This page continues the rhetorical defense of the Mother of the Seven Brothers, specifically contrasting what a "natural" mother might have said in her grief with what this "holy" mother actually said through her devotion to Pious Reason. It concludes her speech to her sons and describes her own death.</meta>

I have demonstrated, then, that not only have men mastered their emotions, but even a woman has looked with disdain upon the greatest of tortures. And it was not so much that the holy old man <note>referring to Eleazar, whose martyrdom preceded the brothers</note> felt pity, nor did the flaming furnace itself feel pity, as did she, the mother who acted as the seal of her seven sons. Like a mother hawk circling her young, her nature followed her seven sons as they were being tortured; but by the **reasoning of piety**, she—the mother—overcame both these things and her own emotions.

For consider this: even if the mother's soul—being a mother's—had lamented over them, she might have said to them: <gloss>“O wretched am I!”</gloss> and perhaps many times, "Thrice-miserable am I, who, having borne seven children, have become the mother of none! O vain pregnancy, and useless ten months of waiting, and fruitless breasts, and painful nursing! For you, O children, I enjoyed a quiet life, but now I endure harsher anxieties. My sons, some of you were nearly of age to marry, yet remain childless; I shall not see your children, nor shall I be called 'Grandmother' and be blessed. I, a woman once rich in children and beautiful children, am now a widow and alone, full of mourning. For when I die, I shall have none of my sons to bury me."

But the holy and God-fearing mother did not lament any of these things for any of them. Neither did she try to turn any of them away from dying. On the contrary, she was not grieved for them as they were dying, but rather—as if they were being translated to immortality—she urged them on toward death for the sake of **piety**, entreating them: <gloss>“O holy piety!”</gloss> You have soldiered with the endurance of an old man and a woman, and against the tyrant—

<column-break/>

—you have conquered, and in your deeds you were found stronger, and in your words more courageous than a man. For when you were arrested with your children, you stood watching Eleazar being tortured, and you said to your children in the **Hebrew language**: <gloss>“O noble children!”</gloss>

"The contest to which you have been called is for the testimony of our nation; compete eagerly for our ancestral Law. For it is shameful that this old man <note>Eleazar</note> should endure the pains for the sake of **piety** <term>eusebeia: the Greek term for religious duty and devotion to God's law</term>, while you, who are younger, shrink from the tortures. Remember that it is because of God that you received a share of the world and enjoyed life, and therefore you owe it to God to endure every labor. For His sake, our father Abraham hurried to sacrifice his son Isaac, the father of our nation; and Isaac, seeing his father’s hand carrying the sword descending upon him, did not shrink. Daniel the righteous was thrown to the lions, and Ananias, Azarias, and Misael <note>also known as Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego</note> were hurled into the furnace of fire and endured it for God's sake.

And you, therefore, having the same faith toward God, do not be distressed, but rationally choose **piety**." By these words, the mother of the seven encouraged each of her sons, and she saw them choosing the harmony of God rather than life. Furthermore, she knew that those who die for God live to God, just as Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the patriarchs do.

<margin>87.</margin> Some of the guards also said that when she herself was about to be seized for death, so that no one would touch her body, she threw herself onto the pyre.

<summary>This page concludes the Mother's exhortation to her seven sons, where she uses the examples of Abraham, Isaac, and Daniel to inspire them to choose martyrdom over apostasy. It ends with the account of her own voluntary death to preserve her bodily purity.</summary>

### OF ATHANASIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA
### AN EPISTLE TO MARCELLINUS
### ON THE INTERPRETATION OF THE PSALMS

-> 738 <note>Greek numerals ζ λ η representing the page number 738</note> <-

I admire your purpose in <term>Christ</term> <note>original: ΧΩ (Christo), a contracted sacred name or "nomen sacrum"</note>, O studious man; for not only do you read all the Scripture, but you especially carry the Psalms with you. And as I have encountered in the book in my possession which contains them all, you are eager to learn from us the meaning of every one of their thoughts, and you have been diligent to learn from us—I mean from those who love learning—the benefit contained within them. For although all the divinely inspired Scripture is a teacher of virtue and of the right faith, as the Apostle said, the Book of Psalms possesses a certain miraculous benefit for the states of souls in <term>men</term> <note>original: ΑΝΟΙΣ (anthropois), "men" or "humanity"</note>. For just as a paradise contains within itself the plantings of all the other books, it sings these in a song, and it contributes its own gifts in addition to these. For those things found in Genesis—the creation of all things and the account of the Patriarchs—it sings, as in the hundred and third <note>Psalm 104 in modern Bibles. ### 107th <note>Psalm 108 in modern Bibles</note> ODE OF A PSALM TO DAVID

<margin>></margin>My heart is ready, O <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘC (Theos)</note>; my heart is ready. I will sing and play a psalm in my glory. Awake, psaltery and harp! I will awake at dawn. I will give thanks to You among the peoples, O Lord, and I will play a psalm to You among the nations. For Your mercy is great above the heavens, and Your truth reaches to the clouds. Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and Your glory over all the earth. That Your beloved ones may be delivered, save with Your right hand and hear me. God has spoken in His holy place: I will rejoice and divide Shechem, and I will measure out the valley of the tents. Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine, and Ephraim is the protection of my head. Judah is my king. Moab is the washpot of my hope. Over Edom <note>original: ΙΔΟΥΜΑΙΑΝ (Idoumaian)</note> I will extend my shoe. The foreigners were subjected to me. Who will lead me into a fortified city? Or who will guide me as far as Edom? Is it not You, O God, who rejected us? And will You not, O God, go out with our forces? Give us help from affliction, for the salvation of man is vain. In God we shall perform power, and He shall bring our enemies to nothing.

### 108th <note>Psalm 109 in modern Bibles</note> TO THE END, A PSALM TO DAVID

O God, do not pass over my praise in silence, for the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful have been opened against me. They spoke against me with a deceitful tongue, and with words of hatred they surrounded me, and they fought against me without cause. Instead of loving me, they slandered me, but I was praying. And they set against me evil for good, and hatred instead of my love.

<column-break/>

<margin>></margin>Set a sinner over him, 
<margin>></margin>and let the <term>accuser</term> <note>original: ΔΙΑΒΟΛΟC (diabolos), often translated as "devil" or "adversary"</note> stand at his right hand. 
<margin>></margin>When he is judged, let him come forth condemned, and let his prayer become sin. Let his days be few, and let another take his <term>office</term> <note>original: ΕΠΙCΚΟΠΗΝ (episkopen), meaning overseership or charge</note>. Let his sons be orphans and his wife a widow. 
<margin>></margin>Let his sons be moved and let them wander and beg; let them be cast out from their ruins. 
<margin>></margin>Let the creditor search out everything he possesses, and let strangers plunder his labors. Let there be no helper for him, nor let there be anyone to pity his orphans. Let his children be for destruction; in a single generation let his name be wiped out. Let the lawlessness of his fathers be remembered before the Lord, and let the sin of his mother not be wiped out. Let them be before the Lord always, and let the memory of them be destroyed from the earth. Because he did not remember to show mercy, but persecuted the needy and poor man, and the one pierced in heart, to put them to death. He loved a curse, and it shall come to him; he did not want a blessing, and it shall be far from him. And he put on a curse like a garment, and it entered like water into his bowels and like oil into his bones. Let it be to him like a garment in which he wraps himself, and like a belt that he always girds around himself. This is the work of those who slander me before the Lord, and those who speak evil against my soul. But You, Lord, Lord, deal with me for the sake of Your name; for Your mercy is kind. Deliver me, for I am poor and needy, and my heart is troubled within me. Like a shadow when it declines, I was taken away; I was shaken off like locusts. My knees have become weak from fasting, and my flesh has changed for lack of oil. And I became a reproach to them; they saw me and shook their heads. Help me, O Lord my God; save me according to Your mercy. And let them know that this is Your hand, and that You, Lord, have done it. They shall curse, and You shall bless. Let those rising up against me be put to shame, but Your servant shall be glad. Let those who slander me be clothed with shame, and let them be wrapped in their disgrace as with a double-cloak. I will give thanks to the Lord greatly with my mouth, and in the midst of many I will praise Him. For He stood at the right hand of the poor, to save my soul from those who persecute it.

->**CONCERNING THE OTHER BOOKS ABOVE ALL**<-

Not being ignorant, he spoke again, saying that in every book of the Scripture, these same things concerning the <term>Savior</term> <note>original: ΠΤΟΥ (Soteros - reconstruction of faded uncial), Savior</note> are especially signified. And there is in all of them a harmony of announcements from the <term>Spirit</term> <note>original: ΠΝC (Pneumatos), Spirit</note>. For just as it is possible to find [these things] more fully in this [book of Psalms], so also they are frequently found in the others. For as Moses speaks through the Scripture, so also Isaiah speaks, and Habakkuk prays. 

In another place again, [Scripture speaks] concerning the undertaking of the passions, and of prophecy, and of legislation, and of history. For all things belong to the same <term>Spirit</term> <note>original: ΠΝC (Pneumatos), Spirit</note>. And each [book] indeed ministers the particular <term>grace</term> <note>original: XΑΡΙΝ (charin), gift or grace</note> given by Him, and readily serves that grace. Every word is prophecy, whether it be legislation or history, which was revealed to us through the <term>grace of the Psalms</term> <note>Athanasius argues that the Psalms contain all other biblical genres within them</note>. Since they say, for this is what the <term>Spirit</term> <note>original: ΠΝ (Pneuma), Spirit</note> says, in whom all the distributions are made according to His nature. 

Let this whole matter be understood: according to the ministry, the distributions of the <term>Spirit of God</term> <note>original: ΠΝC ΘΥ (Pneumatos Theou), Spirit of God</note> occur among them. And for the rest, the grace serving the underlying need—often as the <term>Spirit</term> <note>original: ΠΝC (Pneumatos), Spirit</note> prompts—ministers the word. Thus, one might see <term>Moses</term> <note>original: ΜΟCΗΝ (Mosen), Moses</note>, the lawgiver, sometimes prophesying, and <term>David</term> <note>original: ΔΑΔ (Dauid), David</note>, 

<margin>Prophetic</margin>

[the singer], sometimes commanding. [The soul] is restored through the heart... you sometimes search. Indeed, you sing the Psalms of David, and you read the words of Isaiah according to the place... For thus, and through the Psalms, you have held... which is spoken of in the [Book of] Exodus. These things are spoken with an unfeigned voice, as one who sings the Psalms... Therefore, Isaiah the prophet says... "Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it" <note>This is actually a quote from Psalm 33:15 / 34:14, illustrating the author's point that different books share the same Spirit</note>.

<column-break/>

The order was established with such a particular prophet... 

<margin>Headings</margin>

...for those who act according to the pattern, <term>grace</term> <note>original: XΑΡΙC (charis), grace</note> will be present. Behold, it is pleasing to each of us, not as something foreign, but as our own... and each person in this finds the need... the <term>Spirit</term> <note>original: ΠΝC (Pneumatos), Spirit</note> dwelling within... before all others. 

And the fulfillment of the other laws provides a guarantee for those who have departed, and for those who have observed them. For there is a difference in the books in which one prophesies... but this one [the Psalter] contains the movements of the soul and the changes [wrought] by the <term>Spirit</term> <note>original: ΠΝC (Pneumatos), Spirit</note>, and it contains corrections. It is sketched out within it as a pattern, so that the one who wishes to—as if looking into a mirror—takes up the ministry [of the word]. Thus, this person has been described.

[reveals] the deeds of the kings and the actions of the saints. But in the book of Psalms, the one who hears perceives the fruits of his own soul. In it, he is both refined and taught. He is held together, or again, he can [express] what he suffers. For though there are prohibitions even in the other books, they are outlined here in a Gospel-like manner...

### THE MARVEL OF THE PSALMS

But regarding the Psalms, there is a marvelous <term>paradox</term> <note>original: ΠΑΡΑΔΟΞΟΝ (paradoxon) — something unexpected or contrary to common opinion</note>. In the other books, there are prophecies and records of the <term>hours</term> <note>original: ΩΡC (hōras) — referring to historical times or periods</note>; but these have words that are distinct from all others. Each person sings them as though they were written about himself. He does not receive them as if another were speaking, or as if they were signifying someone else. Instead, he goes through them as if he himself were the one speaking about himself. The things said are such that he refers to <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘΩ (Theō) — a holy abbreviation (nomen sacrum) for "to God"</note> as if he had done these things and were speaking from his own experience. For he will not be in awe of these as if they were the words of the Patriarchs, or Moses, or the other prophets. Rather, he takes them up as his own, written about himself, and sings them with deep <term>struggle</term> <note>original: ΑΓΩΝΩ (agōnō) — spiritual effort or contest</note>. For the Psalms contain both the one who kept the commandment and the one who <term>transgressed</term> <note>original: ΠΑΡΑΒΑΤΑ (parabata)</note> it. It is necessary that all of us are held by these states: either as one who kept the commandment or as one who transgressed it. Each person's work becomes a word in the singing. It is as if one were looking into a <term>mirror</term> <note>original: ΕΙCΟΠΤΡΟΝ (eisoptron)</note> within the Psalm, seeing himself and the movements of his own soul. Thus, he reports them as his own feelings. For the one who reads them accepts the song as if it were said about himself. Being convicted by his <term>conscience</term> <note>original: CΥΝΕΙΔΟΤΟC (syneidotos)</note>, he is pricked at heart and will repent. When he hears of the help that comes to those who believe, and the <term>grace</term> <note>original: ΧΑΡΙΤΟC (charitos)</note> that brings redemption, he rejoices and begins to give thanks to <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘΩ (Theō)</note>. # THE THEMATIC CLASSIFICATION OF THE PSALMS

### THE WAYS OF LIFE AND DEFEAT OF DEMONS

Regarding both of these ways, on each side, the <term>demons</term> <note>original: ΔΑΙΜΟΝΑΣ (daimonas)</note> remain a source of destruction, utterly breaking a person’s hope. And rightly so; yet they are not like the structures found in the <term>porticos of Demosthenes</term> <note>original: ΔΗΜΟΣΘΕΝΗΝ CΤΟΑΙC — a reference to public oratory halls in Athens, used here as a contrast to spiritual architecture</note>. This is why we have said that to act with piety now is to create power. This is the very thing spoken of before: that we should not be merely human, but through God the Father, we should become entirely light. Our whole <term>exhortation</term> <note>original: ΠΡΟΤΡΟΠΗ (protrope) — a persuasive speech or call to action</note> and salvation is to find ourselves in freedom. Because we have learned the divine gate and wisdom through the Word, without mere writing but through persuasion, every holy scripture is a work of virtue. Through faith, these things work for our good, bringing mercy and glory to us, and the divine image of righteousness.

From these readily available testimonies, we proceed by adding where it speaks of the forms and the <term>decrees</term> <note>original: ΚΡΗΜΑΤΙCΜΑΤΩΝ (chrēmatismatōn) — oracular responses or divine decrees</note>. Despite these things, let the divine book be spoken of in <term>columns</term> <note>original: CΕΛΙΔΩΝ (selidōn)</note> for those running toward virtue and wishing to live for God alone. Even for those who are now "sleeping" <note>metaphor for spiritual lethargy or death</note>, it shows the movements and states of the soul. We use these elements to guide those who do not yet direct themselves.

Within this book, some Psalms are written out of love for the righteous. Some are written in the spirit of the <term>prophets</term> <note>original: ΠΡΟΦΗΤΕC (prophētes)</note>, others as prayer, and others as <term>confession</term> <note>original: ΜΟΛΟΓΕΙ (homologei) — shortened from exomologēsis, meaning both confession of sin and confession of praise</note>. 

Those which speak of these various states are: 
**49, 72, 73, 74, 75, 76, 77, 102, 103, 104.**

Those centered on <term>piety</term> <note>original: ΕΥCΕΒΕΙΑ (eusebeia)</note> are especially: 
**111, 112.**

### THE MORNING PRAYER
->It should be said as follows:<-

**O God, my God, I rise early for You.**
**My soul has thirsted for You; how many ways has my flesh longed for You?**
**In a desert, trackless, and waterless land.**
**So I appeared before You in the sanctuary, to see Your power and Your glory.**
**Because Your mercy is better than life, my lips shall praise You.**
**Thus I will bless You in my life, and in Your name I will lift up my hands.**
**May my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness, and my mouth shall praise You with lips of rejoicing.**
**If I remembered You upon my bed, in the early mornings I meditated on You.**
**Because You became my helper, and in the shelter of Your wings I will rejoice.**
**My soul followed close behind You; Your right hand has supported me.**
**But they sought my soul in vain; they shall go into the lower parts of the earth.**
**They shall be delivered into the hands of the sword; they shall be portions for foxes.**
**But the King shall rejoice in God; everyone who swears by Him shall be praised, for the mouth of those speaking unjust things has been stopped.**

O God, the holy God, who rests among the holy ones, Lord, do not ignore the prayers of the poor who rejoice in their hope in You, but rather in the Lord. 

And the choir around you [lifts] the soul; let them receive the prayer with joy. And thus the <term>beatitudes</term>... the choir remains... having nothing else but [uplifted] hands. <meta>The previous page discussed the liturgical use of the Psalms for specific days of the week and spiritual protection. <unclear>May God grant me to speak according to my judgment and to think</unclear> worthily of the things given <note>Wisdom 7:15</note>, because He himself is both the guide of **Wisdom** and the corrector of the wise. For in His hand are both we and our words, all understanding and experience of works. For He Himself gave me unerring knowledge of the things that are—to know the structure of the world and the activity of the elements; the beginning, the end, and the middle of times; the changes of the sun's turns <note>original: "τροπων αλλαγας" referring to the solstices</note> and the variations of seasons; the cycles of years and the positions of stars; the natures of animals and the rages of wild beasts; the powers of spirits <note>original: "ΠΝΑΤΩΝ" (pneumaton); here referring to the winds or spiritual forces</note> and the reasonings of men; the varieties of plants and the powers of roots.

Whatever is hidden and whatever is manifest I learned. For the artisan <note>original: "τεχνιτις" (technitis), meaning a female master-craftsman or architect</note> of all things taught me—**Wisdom**. For in her there is a spirit <note>original: "ΠΝΑ" (pneuma)</note> that is intelligent, holy, unique, manifold, subtle, mobile, clear, unpolluted, distinct, invulnerable, loving the good, keen, irresistible, beneficent, humane, steadfast, sure, free from care, all-powerful, all-seeing, and penetrating through all spirits <note>original: "ΠΝΑΤΩΝ"</note> that are intelligent, pure, and most subtle.

For **Wisdom** is more mobile than any motion; she pervades and penetrates through all things by reason of her purity. For she is a breath of the power of **God** <note>original: "ΘΥ" (Theou)</note> and a pure emanation of the glory of the **Almighty** <note>original: "ΠΑΝΤΟΚΡΑΤΟΡΟΣ"</note>; therefore nothing defiled gains entrance into her. For she is a reflection of eternal light, a spotless mirror of the working of **God**, and an image of His goodness. Though she is but one, she can do all things, and while remaining in herself, she renews all things; and passing into holy souls from generation to generation, she prepares them to be friends of **God** and prophets. For **God** <note>original: "ΘΣ" (Theos)</note> loves nothing so much as the one who lives with **Wisdom**. For she is more beautiful than the sun, and excels every constellation of stars. Compared with the light, she is found to be superior; for night succeeds the light, but evil does not prevail over **Wisdom**.

<column-break/>

She reaches mightily from one end to the other, and she orders all things well. I loved her and sought her from my youth; I desired to take her for my bride, and I became a lover of her beauty. She glorifies her noble birth by having **God** as her companion, and the Lord of all loved her. For she is an initiate in the knowledge of **God** and an appraiser <note>original: "αιρετις" (hairetis), one who chooses or decides</note> of His works. 

If riches are a desirable possession in life, what is richer than **Wisdom**, who works all things? If understanding is at work, who more than she is the artisan of what exists? And if anyone loves righteousness, her labors are virtues; for she teaches self-control and prudence, justice and courage <note>The four "Cardinal Virtues" of classical philosophy, here integrated into biblical tradition</note>; nothing in life is more profitable for mortals than these. 

And if anyone longs for wide experience, she knows the things of old and can infer the things to come; she understands the subtleties of words and the solutions of riddles; she has foreknowledge of signs and wonders and of the outcomes of seasons and times. Therefore I determined to take her to live with me, knowing that she would be a counselor of good things and a comfort in cares and grief. 

Because of her I shall have glory among the crowds and honor in the presence of the elders, though I am young. I shall be found keen in judgment, and in the sight of rulers I shall be admired. When I am silent they will wait for me, and when I speak they will pay attention; and if I talk at greater length, they will put their hands on their mouths <note>A gesture of respectful silence and awe</note>. 

Because of her I shall have immortality, and leave an everlasting remembrance to those who come after me. I shall govern peoples, and nations will be subject to me; dread tyrants will be afraid when they hear of me; among the people I shall show myself good, and in war courageous. When I enter my house, I shall find rest with her; for companionship with her has no bitterness, and life with her has no pain, but gladness and joy. When I considered these things within myself and thought in my heart that in kinship with **Wisdom** there is immortality...

<summary>This page contains a poetic and philosophical praise of Wisdom from the Wisdom of Solomon, describing her divine attributes as a reflection of God and the source of all human knowledge and virtue. The narrator (traditionally Solomon) describes his quest to take Wisdom as his "bride" to gain immortality and perfect judgment.</summary>
<keywords>Wisdom, Sophia, immortality, cardinal virtues, nature of God, divine attributes, Solomon, Septuagint</keywords>

<meta>The previous page introduced the personification of Wisdom from the Wisdom of Solomon, describing it as an artisan and a breath of the power of God. This page continues the philosophical and theological exploration of harmony, shifting focus to the use of Psalms as a means to bring the "governing part" of the human soul into accord with divine Reason, using the biblical example of David and Saul.</meta>

<warning>The bottom half of the first column is significantly faded and damaged, making many words difficult to read with certainty.</warning>

To use this as a guide and to be easily grasped within this melody, having impressed the activity of the passions <note>original: "παθητικής ενεργείας" (pathētikēs energeias); referring to the emotional or reactive part of the human nature</note> of the body with **Reason**, let it lead so as to obey **Reason**. This is so that one does not become a slave to the passions, bound by an invisible chain, but instead might govern with attention and a light that is subordinate to all things good. Thus, the soul obeys and serves the judgment of the **governing part** <term>original: "ἡγεμονικόν" (hegemonikon); the Stoic and Patristic term for the seat of reason and the "ruling" part of the mind</term> through the tranquility of one’s thoughts. For this reason, it seems that the melody of odes and psalms is offered to **God** alone—the melody within the psalms being, as it were, a certain unspoken melody of the soul joined in harmony with rhythm.

These spiritual contemplations are carried everywhere, bearing the movements of desire, and not according to every word, but the melody of a rhythmic life achieved through the formation of a faithful character. **Sing**, he says, **to the Lord; I will sing with understanding** <note>Psalm 47:7</note>. For the understanding of the faith belongs to all the faithful, and the understanding of the subject at hand <unclear>Reason</unclear> <unclear>stretches</unclear> the theme for those among you who use a "psalm of understanding."

But let it be so: while the form of a psalm is performed through a musical instrument, <unclear>let not these things</unclear> be merely singing along... <margin>...</margin> what then does one understand regarding these things <unclear>...</unclear> the recognition of what is being said <unclear>...</unclear> and the prayer to **God**. Could we say that these things are the recognition of the teaching of the <unclear>Prophets</unclear>? So that if anyone <unclear>advances</unclear> the mind toward <unclear>...</unclear> pious joy as a bodily <unclear>sign</unclear>... <margin>...</margin> of those <unclear>understanding</unclear> <unclear>the one singing</unclear> and with <unclear>...</unclear> of energy toward this <unclear>...</unclear> just as the soul is in harmony <unclear>with God</unclear>. Such a <unclear>disposition</unclear> <unclear>of the</unclear> soul [silences] every <unclear>...</unclear> of desire <unclear>...</unclear> and it is clearly evident how **Reason** <unclear>...</unclear> of all <unclear>...</unclear> the members. With the <unclear>...</unclear> stripped bare, it [leads] to the higher <unclear>...</unclear> places... <unclear>He protects us in harmony.</unclear>

<column-break/>

...in its distribution; so that words and rhythms might benefit not only themselves but also those who behold and hear them in a mystical way. Thus, the blessed **David**, by singing in silence, was well-pleasing to **God** and drove away **Saul’s** grief and his manic passion <note>referring to 1 Samuel 16:23, where David's harp-playing soothes King Saul's troubled spirit</note>, and he prepared his soul for tranquility. 

In this same way, the priests, by singing, [soothe] the troubled souls of the people and unite them in concord—a heavenly choir of sons directed toward **God**. For this is why the Psalms are said to be "sung": not because of a preoccupation with vocal beauty, but as a proof of the harmony of the thoughts within the soul. The reading of the melody is such that, from the word, there arises a most calm state—rhythmic and steady. For one indeed finds "in the **Lord**" both the lyre and the ten-stringed psaltery <note>original: "δεκαχόρδῳ ψαλτηρίῳ"</note>. 

Again, it was a symbol and a shadow of the diligence according to the virtues; **God** uses the senses of the body as strings, and the <unclear>thoughts</unclear> of the soul as cymbals. And finally, the sound and the highest trembling... all these movements and life, so that even the things <unclear>inscribed for us</unclear> [surpass] human rhythm and the actions of the body. For in this way, those who sing well to their own soul—as those who have [received] the light of the **Divine**—are preserved through the Savior <unclear>...</unclear> and singing together <unclear>...</unclear> for those who long for the melody of good things. The melody of the words is harmonized [with the soul] and is a [remedy] for the passions. And according to others, it transforms sensible things toward the mind. One must prefer what is sweet <unclear>to the</unclear> **Spirit**, as it happens to each soul in all things faithful, as if they were <unclear>God-breathed</unclear> things within it...

<summary>This page explores how the Psalms and musical harmony serve as a metaphor for the moral alignment of the soul's passions with Reason. It highlights the biblical example of David's music healing Saul as a model for how spiritual melody brings tranquility and concord to the believer.</summary>
