# INTRODUCTION

THE <term>Codex Alexandrinus</term> (one of the oldest and most complete Greek Bibles in existence) first came into notice in Europe when it was offered to King James I by Cyril Lucar, patriarch of Constantinople, about the beginning of 1625.¹ The intermediary was Sir Thomas Roe, British Ambassador at Constantinople, who was on friendly terms with the patriarch and gave him diplomatic support in his controversies with his clergy, and incidentally interested himself in securing books and antiquities for influential persons in England. King James died before the manuscript had been placed in the ambassador’s hands, but at the beginning of 1627 Cyril renewed his offer as a new year’s gift to his successor.² In this way the manuscript entered the library of Charles I, whose binding, with the royal arms and the initials <term>C. R.</term> <note>Latin: *Carolus Rex*, meaning King Charles</note>, it still bears. It was probably at this date that it was divided into four volumes,³ the first three containing the Old Testament, and the fourth the New Testament and the Epistles of Clement of Rome.

The librarian of the Royal Library at this period was Patrick Young, who cannot be accused of underrating the importance of making the contents of the new manuscript known to the world. It is in his hand that the old <term>folio-numeration</term> <note>The system of numbering the individual leaves of the book rather than pages</note> (making allowance for the 25 leaves lost at the beginning of the New Testament) is written, the modern chapter numeration indicated in the margins, and notes of <term>lacunae</term> <note>original: "lacunae"</note> <note>Gaps or missing sections in the original text</note> (as at leaf 126 b of the New Testament) inserted, and the like. In 1633 he published the <note>original: "*editio princeps*"</note> first printed edition of the Clementine Epistles from this manuscript, and he also issued proposals for an edition of the entire Old and New Testaments. Nothing came of these, but evidence of Young’s preparations remains in transcripts of the books Joshua–2 Chronicles, with corrections in his hand (now preserved in the British Library as Harleian Manuscript 7522 A, leaves 1–334), and a handwritten transcript of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and Song of Solomon (in the same collection, leaves 335–379), with voluminous notes and <term>collations</term> <note>Detailed comparisons between different versions of a text to find variations</note> (leaves 380–401, and Harleian Manuscript 7522 B).⁴ In 1657, five years after Young’s death, the notes which he had prepared for his edition (as far as Numbers 14) were printed in volume 6 of Walton’s Polyglot Bible. Volume 5 of the same work contained a collection of the principal readings of the Codex Alexandrinus in the New Testament, prepared by Alexander Huish, <term>prebendary</term> <note>A senior member of the clergy associated with a cathedral</note> of Wells.

A second attempt to procure a complete edition of the manuscript was made after the Restoration (when the monarchy was returned to England), when (at some date between 1675 and 1685) bishops Fell and Pearson obtained permission from the King that the manuscript itself should be sent to Dr. Thomas Smith, Fellow of Magdalen

² <note>original: "*Op. cit.*"</note> In the work already cited, p. 618.

What purported, however, to be an edition of the Psalter from this <term>MS.</term> <note>abbreviation for manuscript</note> was printed at Oxford in 1678 by Thomas Gale (afterwards dean of York); but this, in which no indication is given of the editor's corrections of errors, alterations of spelling, and the like, nor even of the great <term>lacuna</term> <note>a gap or missing section</note> involving Psalms 49–79 (which is supplied from some source unspecified), in no way serves the purpose of a critical edition. At last, in 1707–20, a complete edition of the Old Testament was produced by J. E. Grabe,^2 in which all deviations from the manuscript were distinguished by being printed in smaller type, the original reading being at the same time given in the margin. The New Testament was <term>collated</term> <note>critically compared against other versions</note> for Mill's great edition in 1707, and Grabe had made preparations for an edition of it ^3; but this project was not realized until 1786, when an edition in <term>uncial</term> <note>a style of writing using large, rounded capital letters common in ancient Greek manuscripts</note> type specially cast for the purpose was produced by C. G. Woide.^4 Woide was an assistant librarian of the British Museum, and his work was promoted and assisted by the authorities of the Museum, into whose keeping the manuscript had passed in 1757, when the Royal Library was presented to the nation by King George II. Another officer of the British Museum, the Rev. H. H. Baber, Keeper of Printed Books from 1812 to 1837, produced a <term>facsimile</term> <note>an exact copy or reproduction</note> edition of the Psalter with Woide's type in 1812,^5 and then proceeded to the still more laborious task of producing a similar facsimile edition of the entire Old Testament, in specially cast uncial type, which was published in 1816–21, the third volume containing elaborate notes on the readings of the manuscript.^6 The most praiseworthy work of Grabe, Woide, and Baber will always retain a considerable value, not only for the information contained in their prefaces and notes, but as evidence of the condition of the manuscript at the dates when they so carefully and elaborately examined it; but as reproductions of the manuscript itself they have inevitably been superseded through the invention of photography. As early as 1856 a photographic facsimile of the Epistles of Clement (which were not included in Woide's publication) was issued by the Trustees of the British Museum, at the request of the Divinity Professors and other members of Oxford and Cambridge Universities, under the editorship of Sir F. # INTRODUCTION 7

(of the Trustees of the Museum) the first volume of a complete <term>facsimile</term> <note>an exact reproduction or copy of a manuscript</note> of the whole <term>MS.</term> <note>abbreviation for manuscript</note> in permanent <term>autotype</term> <note>an early photographic printing process using carbon pigments to prevent fading</note>. The New Testament (with the <term>Clementine Epistles</term> <note>early Christian letters attributed to Clement of Rome, which were once bound with the Bible</note>) was published first, and was followed by the Old Testament in three volumes, corresponding to the volumes into which the <term>MS.</term> itself is divided.¹ The whole was edited by Mr. (now Sir) E. Maunde Thompson, then Keeper of the Department of Manuscripts. The **Codex Alexandrinus** <note>a 5th-century manuscript containing most of the Greek Bible</note> was thus the first <term>MS.</term> (with the exception of the Utrecht Psalter) to be placed beyond the reach of destruction, so far as this can be assured by photography, and this publication remains as the best (and for most purposes the completely adequate) substitute for the original, which is thereby saved from much of the wear and tear of handling. The present issue of a <term>facsimile</term> on a reduced scale is intended to serve the same purpose at a much lower cost. The reduction of scale (about 3 : 5 in linear measurements, or 2 : 5 in superficial area), especially when counterbalanced by the improvements in photography during the last generation, does not interfere with legibility; and it is believed that for most purposes students will find this edition perfectly adequate. As in the case of the larger <term>facsimile</term>, the volume containing the New Testament and <term>Clementine Epistles</term> is issued first; but it is hoped to follow it with the Old Testament in due course.

The history of the **Codex Alexandrinus**, before it passed from the hands of Cyril Lucar to Sir Thomas Roe, is more obscure. There can be little doubt that Cyril brought it with him from Alexandria (where he had previously been <term>patriarch</term> <note>a high-ranking bishop in the Eastern Orthodox Church</note>) to Constantinople.² An Arabic note at the foot of the first page of Genesis records that it was 'made an inalienable gift to the Patriarchal cell in the city of Alexandria', and this is signed by 'Athanasius the humble', <term>i. e.</term> <note>original: "id est", meaning 'that is'</note> probably Athanasius III, <term>patriarch</term> from the latter part of the 13th century till 1308 or later. A Latin note of the 17th <term>cent.</term> <note>century</note> to the effect that this gift was made in the year 814 of the <term>era of the Martyrs</term> <note>a dating system starting from 284 A.D.; year 814 corresponds to 1098 A.D.</note> (equal to A.D. 1098) has no apparent authority. Another Arabic note (translated by Dr. Richard Bentley, who was Royal Librarian from 1693 to 1724), of about the same date as that mentioned above, records the tradition that the <term>MS.</term> was written by Thecla the martyr; and this tradition is repeated in Cyril's autograph note on the second fly-leaf, with the addition that Thecla's name was originally written at the end of the <term>MS.</term>, which was lost in consequence of the ill-treatment which the Christians and their books suffered after the <term>Mahomedan</term> <note>an archaic term for Muslim</note> conquest of Egypt. All tradition, consequently, points to the belief that the <term>MS.</term> was written in Egypt, and had always remained there; and there is no reason to question it.³ Although criticism has not yet satisfactorily determined the exact relation of the text of the **Codex Alexandrinus** either to the Egyptian <term>recension</term> <note>a specific revision or version of a text</note> by Hesychius of the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, or to the Egyptian text of the New Testament, all the available evidence points to Alexandria as its most probable birth-place.

Clearly that must have been the information conveyed by Roe when the <term>MS.</term> came to England. Its Alexandrine origin and connexion is taken for granted in all early references to it.

Wetstein, written in 1664, in which he states, on the authority of Matthaeus Muttis, a deacon of Cyril's, that the <term>MS.</term> was found at Mount Athos, but very little weight can be attached to evidence so vague. Clearly the <term>MS.</term> was at Alexandria about 1300 and again about 1600, and there is no great likelihood that it was at Athos in the interval. If Cyril had himself discovered it there, and restored it to Alexandria, he would not be likely to conceal the fact.

# INTRODUCTION

A general consensus of opinion now assigns the writing of the **manuscript** to the first half of the fifth century¹; and recent developments of <term>palaeographical</term> <note>the study of ancient writing systems and the deciphering of historical manuscripts</note> knowledge, though they do not yet justify dogmatism in dating early <term>vellum uncials</term> <note>manuscripts written in large, rounded capital letters on high-quality animal skin</note>, tend to confirm rather than shake this view. It cannot well be earlier than the second half of the fourth century because it contains the works of **Athanasius** <note>a 4th-century Bishop of Alexandria</note> and **Eusebius** <note>a 4th-century historian and bishop</note> placed before the Psalms; and to date it later than the fifth century would be to ignore the evident signs of age and primitive simplicity which it bears in comparison with other <term>uncial</term> <note>a style of writing using only large, capital letters</note> manuscripts. The **Vatican** and **Sinaitic** codices are likely of an earlier date, and the **Codex Ephraemi** and the **Sarravianus** (which contains the <term>Pentateuch</term> <note>the first five books of the Bible</note>), along with a few very fragmentary manuscripts, are thought to be about the same age; but no other Greek Biblical manuscript currently known is comparable to it.

In its present condition, the **Codex Alexandrinus** consists of 773 leaves, measuring approximately 12 5/8 inches by 10 3/8 inches. Of these, 630 belong to the Old Testament,² and 143 to the New Testament. Ten leaves have been lost from the Old Testament: one containing **1 Kings** (also known as **1 Samuel**) chapter 12, verse 20 to chapter 14, verse 9; and nine containing **Psalms** 49 [50], verse 20 to 79 [80], verse 10. In the New Testament, 25 leaves have been lost from the beginning of **Matthew** (1:1–25:6, along with the prefixed table of chapters), two leaves containing **John** 6:50–8:52, and three leaves containing **2 Corinthians** 4:13–12:6. One leaf is missing after folio 142 containing **1 Clement** 57, § 6–63, § 4, and one (connected to the last-mentioned) containing the end of the so-called **Second Epistle of Clement** (from chapter 12, § 5). Additionally, an unknown number of leaves has been lost from the end of the manuscript, which contained the **Psalms of Solomon**; these are mentioned in the table of contents at the beginning of the Old Testament as following the **Clementine Epistles**. If five leaves are allowed for these, the manuscript in its original state would have consisted of 820 leaves. An Arabic numbering, added before these parts were lost and assigned to the 14th century, is written in the outer lower corner of the <term>verso</term> <note>the back side of a leaf</note> of the leaves. The <term>quires</term> <note>groups of folded sheets gathered together</note>, as originally arranged (before a modern re-binding into groups of 6 leaves), usually consisted of eight leaves, numbered in Greek characters at the top of the first page. This numbering, like the Arabic leaf-numbering, runs continuously through the whole manuscript, with the New Testament (including the lost three quires and one leaf at the start) occupying quires 85 to 106.

The writing is arranged in double columns of between 46 and 52 lines, with 50 or 51 being the most common. The ruling is irregular. In the New Testament, a line is ruled for every line of writing up to folio 95, where there is a change of handwriting; after this, the ruling is usually for every other line only. In the Old Testament, alternate ruling is most common but not universal. The columns are enclosed between single vertical bounding lines, except in volume 3, where (after folio 18) the bounding lines are double. The first line or lines of each book are written in red³; red ink is also used for the titles of the <term>chapters</term> <note>original Greek: κεφάλαια</note> at the head of the columns in the Gospels, and for the numbering of the <term>chapters</term> <note>original Greek: κεφάλαια</note> and the notes for the <term>Eusebian canons</term> <note>a system for finding parallel passages between different Gospels</note> in the margins. The section numbering for the Eusebian system is in black. Red ink is also used for the titles of Psalms and for introductory verses and headings in the Prophets. Simple ornamental patterns in red and black ink appear at the ends of the books. The titles of books may sometimes be written by the same hand as—

---

¹ Earlier estimates ranged from the time of the **Council of Nicaea** (according to **Cyril Lucar**) to the tenth century (according to **Casimir Oudin**).
² **Young's** <note>Patrick Young, the first scholarly librarian of the codex in the 17th century</note> numbering gives 639, due to a mistake where numbers 461 to 469 are skipped. He also skips number 168 to represent a lost leaf, but this is balanced by the fact that he does not include the very first leaf containing the table of contents. Modern numbering, which includes fly-leaves containing 17th-century writing, gives a total of 779 leaves.
³ The number and arrangement of these red lines varies according to the scribe's preference. For instance, in **1 Peter**, lines 1, 2, 5, and 6 are red; in **1 John**, lines 1 and 3; and in **2 John**, lines 1 and 4.

# INTRODUCTION 9

the original scribe (<note>original: "e. g." — for example</note> those at the end of **Mark**, **John**, **James**, **1 Peter**, **Hebrews**, **1 Timothy**), but sometimes they are certainly not so (<note>original: "e. g."</note> **Matthew**, **Luke**, **Acts**). The ink has faded very differently in different parts of the **manuscript**, sometimes taking a reddish hue; the fading is greatest on the <term>flesh-side</term> <note>the smoother, lighter side of the parchment that originally faced the animal's body</note> of the **vellum**. In many parts of the **manuscript**, the ink has corroded the **vellum** into holes (<note>original: "e. g."</note> especially in folios 102–108 of the **New Testament**, and in volume iii). The initial letters of paragraphs are enlarged and (except in the poetical books) stand in the margin; but in many parts of the **manuscript** (in accordance with a common practice), if a paragraph ends near the beginning of a line, the next paragraph is begun in the same line, after a short blank interval, without enlargement, and the first letter of the next line is enlarged and stands in the margin. As in other early <term>uncial</term> <note>written in large, capital letters</note> **manuscripts**, the letters at the ends of lines are often reduced in size. Punctuation is partly by blank spaces at the end of sentences, and partly by a "high point" <note>a dot placed near the top of the letter line, similar to a modern period</note>, and is the work of the original scribes. Quotations are indicated by arrow-head marks in the margin, opposite all the lines of the passage in question.

Five scribes seem to have been employed in writing the **manuscript**. Two of these shared the **Old Testament** and the **Clementine Epistles** <note>early Christian writings once considered part of the biblical canon by some</note>, while three took part in the **New Testament**. The <term>Octateuch</term> <note>the first eight books of the Old Testament: Genesis through Ruth</note> appears to have been written by a single scribe, in a large, rather widely spaced hand (I), with initial letters usually large. It is a strong, solid hand, of square formation, the only letters which project much from the line being <note>Greek letter Rho</note> **P**, <note>Greek letter Phi</note> **Φ**, <note>Greek letter Psi</note> **Ψ**, and, to a less extent, <note>Greek letter Upsilon</note> **Υ**. This last letter has rounded or irregular-shaped thickenings at the upper extremities. In **Kings** and **Chronicles** a second hand appears (II). It is rather smaller and more compact than I, and differs from it in certain small details. A fresh paragraph is apparently never begun in the middle of a line, whereas in I this is frequently the case. Capital letters (which in these narrative books are almost invariably **K** <note>Greek letter Kappa</note>) are generally smaller. **Υ** <note>Upsilon</note> is a heavier letter than in I, opening rather widely at the fork, with square clubbings at the extremities. The width of the ruled columns in this part of the **manuscript** is 3⅜ inches, as against 3⅝ or 3½ inches in the **Octateuch**. At first sight there is an appearance of a further change of hand at the beginning of **3 Kings** <note>equivalent to 1 Kings in modern Bibles</note> (volume i, folio 202); but this is probably due to some difference of pen or **vellum**, since in a few pages the old appearance is resumed.

In the prophetical books (volume ii), scribe number I reappears. **Daniel** ends with a single column on the <term>recto</term> <note>the front side of a leaf</note> side of the leaf. The <term>verso</term> <note>the back side of a leaf</note> of that leaf is left blank (contrary to usage at the end of a book), and then II resumes with **Esther**, and writes that book, **Tobit**, **Judith**, **1 and 2 Esdras** [<note>original: "i. e."</note> that is, **1 Esdras** and **Ezra** + **Nehemiah**]. Then I writes **1–4 Maccabees**, completing volume ii. Of the poetical books (volume iii), II writes the **Psalms**, while I writes **Job**, **Proverbs**, **Ecclesiastes**, **Song of Solomon**, **Wisdom**, and **Ecclesiasticus**.

In the **New Testament**, the first two **Gospels** are written in a hand (III) which bears some resemblance to I, but is assuredly not the same. The letters are a trifle taller, the writing is more compact, and the space between both lines and letters is less. With **Luke** a new hand (IV) appears, with the beginning of a new <term>quire</term> <note>a gathered set of parchment sheets</note>. This is a smoother, softer, lighter hand, and the ink is a reddish-brown, which has not flaked as the ink of the **Old Testament** often has. Capital letters are rather small. Paragraphs often begin in the middle of a line (as is also the case in III). A noticeable letter is <note>Greek letter Pi</note> **Π**, the cross-stroke of which is regularly prolonged on both sides of the perpendiculars (**Π**),¹ while in III this is not the case. The extremities of **Υ** <note>Upsilon</note> are—

***

¹ It may be observed that the principal corrector of this part of the **manuscript** does not use this form; <note>original: "cf."</note> compare the long corrections on folios 45 and 55.

# INTRODUCTION 10

slightly knobbed, and it usually projects very little below the line. At 1 Corinthians 10:8<sup>b</sup> (with the words "and they fell") scribe no. III resumes. The change is made at the beginning of a <term>quire</term> <note>a bundle of parchment sheets folded together; here, the 100th bundle</note> (folio 96, the first leaf of quire 100), and a different system of ruling appears in the new quire (see above). This scribe writes all the remaining Epistles. The last, that to Philemon, ends on the <term>recto</term> <note>the front side</note> of a leaf; the *verso* <note>the back side</note> of this (as in the case of Daniel) is left blank, and a new scribe (V) begins the Apocalypse on the next leaf. The ruled column of writing here becomes broader (3⅝ inches as against 3¼ inches in the preceding portion), and the hand is rather smaller and thicker, of the same general character as scribe II, but without the peculiarities of the latter regarding the shape of the letter Υ <note>the Greek letter Upsilon</note> and the practice of beginning paragraphs with a fresh line. These peculiarities reappear, however, with the Clementine Epistles, which seem certainly to have been written by scribe II. The vellum here is in bad condition, and the ink much faded; and considerable portions have been ruined by the use of <term>galls</term> <note>an acidic substance made from oak apples, used by historical scholars as a reagent to make faded ink visible, which often permanently damaged the parchment</note> as a reagent.

The distribution of work among the five scribes is consequently as follows:

| Scribe | Books of the Bible |
| :--- | :--- |
| **I** | **Octateuch** <note>the first eight books of the Old Testament</note>, **Prophets**, **Maccabees**, **Job**–**Ecclesiasticus**. |
| **II** | **Kings**, **Chronicles**, **Esther**–**Esdras**, **Psalms**, **Clementine Epistles**. |
| **III** | **Matthew**, **Mark** (including the table of <term>chapters</term> <note>original: "κεφάλαια" — chapter headings</note> for **Luke**), **1 Corinthians 10:8**–**Philemon** (**Hebrews** precedes the **Pastoral Epistles**). |
| **IV** | **Luke**–**1 Corinthians 10:8** (including the **Catholic Epistles**, which follow **Acts**). |
| **V** | **Apocalypse** <note>the Book of Revelation</note>. |

The manuscript has been extensively corrected, though much more in some books than in others. The amount of correction is greatest in the **Pentateuch** <note>the first five books of the Bible</note>, where whole sentences have frequently been erased and a new text substituted, and least in the books of **Kings**. The usage in critical editions, to indicate the various correctors, is as follows:

**A** indicates the reading of the manuscript when there has been no alteration.
**A*** indicates the original reading of the manuscript before an alteration was made.
**A¹** indicates the reading of a correction when it was made by the original scribe.
**Aᵃ, Aᵇ, Aᶜ**, etc., indicate readings added by subsequent correctors.

With a very few exceptions, all the corrections are of early date, and it is often very hard to discriminate between the hands; especially as allowance has to be made for the fact that an erasure alters the surface of the vellum, and that consequently the ink of a rewritten passage necessarily has a different appearance, even when the scribe is the same. The attribution of corrections to the various correctors must consequently be taken with some reserve. There are, however, a considerable number of passages where the corrector has been obliged to continue his writing in the margins, where the surface of the vellum has not suffered, and where consequently he can write his natural hand; and with the help of these it is possible to arrive at some conclusions with regard to the various correctors. It would appear that, while the original scribes (especially Scribe I) made many corrections in their own work (including, in the case of Scribe I, the insertion of many omitted letters in a very small hand), by far the greater number of corrections, and especially of the more important and extensive corrections, are due to corrector **Aᵃ**. The natural hand of **Aᵃ** is rounder and smoother than those of the original scribes, with the possible exception of Scribe IV, but it does not seem to be materially later in date.¹ Another corrector—

---

¹ Whether this principal corrector is the same throughout the whole manuscript cannot be affirmed without a more exhaustive comparison than has yet been made, but it does not seem impossible. The remarks here made with regard to the various correctors rest mainly on a full examination of the **Octateuch** in connection with the larger Cambridge **Septuagint** <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>.

# INTRODUCTION 11

(A<sup>b</sup>) <note>the scholarly designation for a specific corrector who worked on the manuscript</note> makes a number of small alterations in a thin and delicate hand, but he is not responsible for any long passages. In addition, it may be mentioned that on some pages, where the original writing has almost faded away, some relatively recent hand has retouched or rewritten it. This is especially seen in the first page of **Genesis** <note>the first book of the Old Testament, which describes the creation of the world</note>, but sporadically also elsewhere.

The character of the text of the **Codex Alexandrinus** <note>original: "Codex Alexandrinus"; a 5th-century manuscript of the Greek Bible, one of the oldest and most complete in existence</note> does not come within the scope of this introduction. On this subject, reference must be made to the standard works on the **textual criticism** <term>the academic study of manuscript variations to determine the original wording of a text</term> of the **Septuagint** <note>original: "Septuagint"; the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> and **New Testament**.

->### CONCERNING THE LEPER<-

...suffering from a fever; and immediately they told him about her. And coming forward, he raised her up, taking her by her hand; and the fever left her immediately; and she began to serve them.
<margin>7 / 70 <note>These marginal numbers refer to the Eusebian Canons, an ancient cross-referencing system used to find parallel passages in the four Gospels.</note></margin> When evening came, when the sun had set, they brought to him all those who were ill and those possessed by demons. And the whole city was gathered together at the door. And he healed many who were ill with various diseases, and he cast out many demons; and he did not permit the demons to speak, because they knew him.
<margin>8 / 200 <note>The scribe uses "C" to represent the number 200 in the Greek numeral system.</note></margin> And early in the morning, while it was still very dark, he rose and went out; and he went away to a deserted place, and there he prayed. And Simon and those with him pursued him. And when they found him, they said to him, "Everyone is looking for you." And he said to them, "Let us go to the neighboring towns, so that I may preach there also; for this is why I have come." And he was preaching in their synagogues throughout all Galilee and casting out demons.
<margin>9 / 200</margin> And there came to him a leper, begging him and kneeling before him, and saying to him, "If you are willing, you can make me clean."
<margin>10 / 200</margin> And **Jesus** <note>original: "**ΙC**," a <term>nomen sacrum</term> (sacred name) for "Iēsous."</note>, moved with compassion, stretched out his hand and touched him; and he said to him, "I am willing; be cleansed." And when he had spoken, immediately the leprosy left him, and he was cleansed. And warning him sternly, he immediately sent him away; and he said to him, "See that you say nothing to anyone; but go, show yourself to the priest, and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, as a testimony to them." But he went out and began to preach much, and to spread the word, so that he was no longer able to enter openly

<column-break/>

into a city; but he was outside in deserted places; and they came to him from everywhere.
<margin>11 / 3</margin> And he entered again into Capernaum after some days; and it was heard that he was at home. And immediately many were gathered together, so that there was no longer room, not even at the door; and he spoke the word to them. And they came to
<margin>12 / 20</margin> him, bringing a paralytic carried by four men. And being unable to get near him because of the crowd, they removed the roof where he was; and having dug through, they let down the mat on which the paralytic lay. And seeing their faith, **Jesus** <note>original: "**ΙC**," <term>nomen sacrum</term> for "Iēsous."</note> said to the paralytic, "Child, your sins are forgiven you." But some of the scribes were sitting there, and reasoning in their hearts, "Why does this man speak like this? He blasphemes! Who can forgive sins except one, **God**?" <note>original: "**ΘC**," <term>nomen sacrum</term> for "Theos."</note> And immediately **Jesus** <note>original: "**ΙC**," <term>nomen sacrum</term> for "Iēsous."</note>, perceiving in his **spirit** <note>original: "**ΠΝΙ**," <term>nomen sacrum</term> for "Pneumati."</note> that they were reasoning this way within themselves, said to them, "Why do you reason these things in your hearts? Which is easier: to say to the paralytic, 'Your sins are forgiven,' or to say, 'Rise, take up your mat and walk'? But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins"—he said to the paralytic—"I say to you, rise, take up your mat, and go to your house." And he rose immediately, and taking up the mat, he went out before everyone, so that they were all amazed and glorified **God** <note>original: "**ΘN**," <term>nomen sacrum</term> for "Theon."</note>, saying, "We never saw anything like this!" And he went out again by the sea; and the whole crowd came to him, and he taught them.

<summary>This page records several of Jesus's early miracles, including the healing of a leper and the paralytic lowered through a roof in Capernaum. It highlights the growing conflict with the scribes over Jesus's authority to forgive sins.</summary>

And looking around at them with anger, being grieved at the hardness of their heart, he says to the **man** <note>original: "**ANΩ**," a <term>nomen sacrum</term> for "Anthrōpō."</note>, "Stretch out your hand." They said to him, "Grant us that we may sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory." But Jesus said to them, "You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, or to be baptized with the baptism <note>In this context, baptism and the cup are metaphors for Jesus's upcoming suffering and death</note> with which I am baptized?" They said to him, "We are able." And Jesus said to them, "The cup that I drink, you shall drink; and with the baptism with which I am baptized, you shall be baptized. But to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to grant, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared."

<margin>135</margin>
And when the ten heard this, they began to be indignant with James and John. But Jesus called them to him and says to them, "You know that those who are recognized as rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it is not so among you. Instead, whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant <term>servant</term> <note>original: διάκονος (diakonos) — the root of the word 'deacon,' meaning one who waits on others</note>, and whoever wants to be first among you shall be slave of all."

<margin>136</margin>
"For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many."

<column-break/>

<margin>137</margin>
And they come to Jericho. And as he was going out from Jericho with his disciples and a large crowd, the son of Timaeus, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, was sitting by the road. And hearing that it was Jesus the Nazarene, he began to cry out and say, "Son of David, Jesus, have mercy on me!" And many were rebuking him so that he would be silent; but he cried out all the more, "Son of David, have mercy on me!" And Jesus stopped and said, "Call him." And they call the blind man, saying to him, "Take courage! Get up, he is calling you."

<margin>138</margin>
And throwing off his cloak, he jumped up and came to Jesus. And answering him, Jesus said, "What do you want me to do for you?" And the blind man said to him, "<term>Rabboni</term> <note>original: ΡΑΒΒΟΥΝΙ (Rhabbouni) — an Aramaic title meaning 'my Master' or 'my Teacher,' expressing deep respect</note>, let me see again." And Jesus said to him, "Go; your faith has healed you." And immediately he saw again and followed him on the road.

<margin>139</margin>
And when they draw near to Jerusalem, to Bethphage and Bethany at the Mount of Olives, he sends two of his disciples and says to them, "Go into the village opposite you, and immediately as you enter it, you will find a colt tied, on which no human has ever yet sat. Untie it and bring it. And if anyone says to you, 'Why are you doing this?' say, 'The Lord has need of it,' and immediately he will send it back here."

<margin>140</margin>
And they went away and found a colt tied at a door outside on the open street, and they untie it. And some of those standing there were saying to them, "What are you doing, untying the colt?" And they spoke to them just as Jesus had commanded, and they allowed them to go. And they lead the colt to Jesus.

AND HE BEGAN TO SPEAK TO THEM IN PARABLES:
"A man planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a pit for the winepress and built a tower, and leased it to tenant farmers and went abroad. And at the harvest time, he sent a servant to the tenants so that he might receive some of the fruit of the vineyard from them. But they took him, beat him, and sent him away empty-handed.
And again, he sent another servant to them; and that one they struck on the head with stones <note>original: ΛΙΘΟΒΟΛΗCΑΝΤΕC ΕΚΕΦΑΛΑΙΩCΑΝ — literally "stoning, they wounded his head"</note> and sent him away treated shamefully.
And again, he sent another; and that one they killed. And many others—some they beat, and others they killed.
Having yet one beloved son, he sent him to them last of all, saying, 'They will respect my son.'
But those tenants said among themselves, 'This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.' And taking him, they killed him and threw him out of the vineyard.
What then will the lord of the vineyard do? He will come and destroy the tenants and will give the vineyard to others.
Have you not even read this scripture: 'The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner; this was from the **Lord** <note>original: ΚΥ (Kyriou) — shorthand for Lord</note>, and it is marvelous in our eyes'?"
And they were seeking to seize him, but they feared the crowd; for they knew that he had spoken the parable against them. And leaving him, they went away.
And they sent to him some of the Pharisees and of the Herodians <note>The Herodians were a political faction supporting the dynasty of Herod and Roman rule</note> in order to trap him—

# THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE

<margin>1</margin> Inasmuch as many have undertaken to compile a narrative of the things that have been fulfilled among us, just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word delivered them to us, it seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely from the beginning, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus, so that you may know the certainty concerning the words in which you were instructed.

<margin>3</margin> There was in the days of Herod, the king of Judea, a certain priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah; and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. And they were both righteous <margin>5</margin> before **God** <note>original: ΘΥ — Nomen Sacrum for "Theou" (of God)</note>, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the **Lord** <note>original: ΚΥ — Nomen Sacrum for "Kyriou" (of the Lord)</note> blameless. And they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were advanced in their days.

<margin>3</margin> Now it happened that while he was serving as priest in the order of his division before **God**, according to the custom of the priesthood, it fell to him by lot to burn incense, having entered into the temple of the **Lord**. And the whole multitude of the people was praying outside at the hour of incense. <margin>3</margin> And there appeared to him an angel of the **Lord** standing on the right side of the altar of incense. And Zechariah was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him.

<margin>5</margin> But the angel said to him, "Do not be afraid, Zechariah, because your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John. And there will be joy for you and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth. For he will be great before the **Lord**; and he shall drink no wine nor strong drink <note>original: ϲικερα (sikera) — a loanword from Hebrew meaning fermented liquor or "strong drink"</note>, and he will be filled with the **Holy Spirit** <note>original: ΠΝΣ ΑΓΙΟΥ — Nomen Sacrum for "Pneumatos Agiou"</note> even from his mother's womb."

<column-break/>

<margin>20</margin> "And many of the sons of Israel will he turn to the **Lord** their **God** <note>original: ΚΝ ΤΟΝ ΘΝ — Nomina Sacra for "Kyrion ton Theon"</note>. And he will go before him in the **spirit** <note>original: ΠΝΙ — Nomen Sacrum for "Pneumati" (Spirit)</note> and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the righteous, to make ready for the **Lord** <note>original: ΚΩ — Nomen Sacrum for "Kyriō"</note> a people prepared."

<margin>22</margin> And Zechariah said to the angel, "By what shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in her days."

<margin>22</margin> And the angel answering said to him, "I am Gabriel, who stands before **God**; and I was sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news. And behold, you will be silent and not able to speak until the day these things take place, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their season."

And the people were <margin>80</margin> waiting for Zechariah, and they marveled at his delaying in the temple. But when he came out, he could not speak to them, and they realized that he had seen a vision in the temple; and he was making signs to them and remained mute.

<margin>20</margin> And it happened when the days of his service were completed, he departed to his house. After these days, Elizabeth his wife conceived, and she hid herself for five months, saying, "Thus has the **Lord** <note>original: ΚΣ — Nomen Sacrum for "Kyrios"</note> done for me in the days when he looked upon me to take away my reproach among men."

<margin>13</margin> Now in the sixth month, the angel Gabriel was sent by **God** into a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of **David** <note>original: ΔΑΔ — Nomen Sacrum for "Dauid"</note>; and the name...

And his mercy is from generation to generation to those who fear him. He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts. He has pulled down rulers from thrones and exalted the humble. The hungry he has filled with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty. He has helped **Israel** <note>original: ΙC — Nomen Sacrum for "Israēl"</note> his servant, remembering mercy, as he spoke to our **fathers** <note>original: ΠΡΑC — Nomen Sacrum for "Patras"</note>, to Abraham and to his offspring forever."

# IV. CONCERNING THE CENSUS / V. CONCERNING THE SHEPHERDS LIVING IN THE FIELDS

<margin>3</margin> ...[to call him] by the name of his **father** <note>original: ΠΡΣ — Nomen Sacrum for "Patros" (Father)</note> Zechariah. <margin>1</margin> And his mouth was opened immediately and his tongue [loosed], and he spoke, blessing **God** <note>original: ΘΝ — Nomen Sacrum for "Theon" (God)</note>. And all who heard them laid them up in their hearts, saying, "What then will this child be?" For indeed the hand of the **Lord** <note>original: ΚΥ — Nomen Sacrum for "Kyriou" (Lord)</note> was with him. 

And Zechariah his **father** <note>original: ΠΗΡ — Nomen Sacrum for "Patēr" (Father)</note> was filled with the **Holy Spirit** <note>original: ΠΝΣ ΑΓΙΟΥ — Nomen Sacrum for "Pneumatos Agiou" (Holy Spirit)</note> and prophesied, saying:

And he has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of **David** <note>original: ΔΑΔ — Nomen Sacrum for "Dauid"</note> his servant, just as he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets from of old: salvation from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us;

<margin>3</margin> to perform mercy with our **fathers** <note>original: ΠΡΩΝ — Nomen Sacrum for "Paterōn" (Fathers)</note> and to remember his holy covenant, the oath which he swore to Abraham our **father** <note>original: ΠΡΑ — Nomen Sacrum for "Patera" (Father)</note>, to grant us that we, being delivered without fear from the hand of our enemies, might serve him in holiness and righteousness before him all our days.

<margin>3</margin> And you, child, will be called a prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the face of the **Lord** <note>original: ΚΥ — Nomen Sacrum for "Kyriou" (Lord)</note> to prepare

<margin>2</margin> by which the Dayspring <note>original: anatole — literally "the rising" or "the east," referring to the rising sun as a metaphor for the Messiah</note> from on high has visited us, to shine upon those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace." 

And the child grew and became strong in **spirit** <note>original: ΠΝΙ — Nomen Sacrum for "Pneumati" (Spirit)</note>, and he was in the deserts until the day of his public appearance to **Israel** <note>original: ΙΣΗΛ — Nomen Sacrum for "Israēl"</note>.

### THE SIGN SPOKEN AGAINST OR THE PROPHETESS ANNA

-> ...who is **Christ the Lord** <note>original: XC̄ KC̄ — Nomina Sacra for "Christos Kyrios" (Christ Lord)</note> in the city of **David**. And this shall be the sign for you: you will find a babe wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger. <meta>This page continues the Gospel of John. ...If anyone keeps my word, he shall never taste death <note>original: **ΓΕΥCΗΤΑΙ ΘΑΝΑΤΟΥ** (geusētai thanatou) - literally "taste of death," a Semitic idiom for dying.</note> forever."

"Now we know that you have a demon! Abraham died, and the prophets, and yet you say, 'If anyone keeps my word, he shall never taste death forever.' Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? And the prophets died! Who do you make yourself out to be?"

Jesus <term>ΙC</term> <note>original: **ΙC** (Iēsous). A "sacred name" abbreviation for Jesus.</note> answered, "If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, of whom you say that he is our God <term>ΘC</term> <note>original: **ΘC** (Theos). A sacred name abbreviation for God.</note>. And you have not known him, but I know him. And if I say that I do not know him, I will be a liar like you. But I know him and I keep his word. Abraham your father rejoiced that he would see my day, and he saw it and was glad."

Then the Jews <term>ΙΟΥΔΑΙΟΙ</term> <note>original: **ΙΟΥΔΑΙΟΙ** (Ioudaioi). In John's Gospel, this often refers specifically to the religious leaders in Jerusalem.</note> said to him, "You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?"

Jesus <term>ΙC</term> answered them, "Truly, truly I say to you, before Abraham was, I am." <note>This is a pivotal moment where Jesus uses the divine name "I am," echoing God's self-revelation to Moses.</note>

Then they took up stones to throw at him, but Jesus <term>ΙC</term> hid himself 

<margin>✛</margin> and went out of the temple. And passing by, he saw a man blind from birth. And his disciples asked him, saying, "Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?"

Jesus <term>ΙC</term> answered, "Neither did this man sin, nor his parents, but it was so that the works of God <term>ΘΥ</term> <note>original: **ΘΥ** (Theou), the possessive form of "God."</note> might be revealed in him. We must work the works of him who sent me while it is day; night is coming when no one can work. While I am in the world, I am the light of the world."

Having said these things, he spat on the ground and made clay from the saliva and smeared the clay on his eyes and said to him, "Go, wash in the pool of Siloam <term>CΙΛΩΑΜ</term>," which is translated

"Sent." <note>The author provides a translation of the Hebrew name Siloam (Shiloah) into Greek (Apestalmenos) to emphasize the theme of Jesus being "sent" by God.</note> He went therefore and washed and came back seeing.

The neighbors then and those who saw him before—for he was a beggar—said, "Is this not the one who used to sit and beg?"

<summary>In this passage from John 15 and 16, Jesus promises the coming of the Advocate (the Holy Spirit) and prepares his disciples for their future sorrow and subsequent joy, likened to the pains of childbirth. He emphasizes his direct relationship with the Father and his imminent departure from the world.</summary>

# The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter xvi

**Column 1**

“If you have judged me to be faithful to the 
<margin>entering into my house</margin> Lord <gloss>original: κυρίῳ (Kyriō)</gloss>, come into my house and stay.” And she urged us. 
Now it happened, as we were going to the place of prayer, that a certain slave girl having a spirit <gloss>original: πνεῦμα (pneuma)</gloss> of divination <note>original: πύθωνα (pythōna) — literally a "Python spirit," referring to the serpent that guarded the Oracle of Delphi; it implies she was seen as a medium for Apollo</note> met us, who brought much profit to her masters by fortune-telling. 
This girl followed Paul and us, crying out, saying, “These men are servants of the Most High God <gloss>original: θεοῦ (theou)</gloss>, who proclaim to us the way of salvation!” 
And she did this for many days. 
But Paul, having become greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit <gloss>original: πνεύματι (pneumati)</gloss>, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ <gloss>original: ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ (Iēsou Christou)</gloss> to come out of her!” 
And it came out that very hour. 
But when her masters saw that the hope of their profit was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace <term>agora — the central public square and center of commerce</term> before the rulers. 
And bringing them to the magistrates <term>strategois — the chief administrators of a Roman colony</term>, they said, “These men are throwing our city into confusion; they are Jews and are proclaiming customs which it is not lawful for us to accept or to practice, being Romans.” 
And the crowd rose up together against them. 
And the magistrates, having torn the clothes off them, gave orders to beat them with rods. 
And after laying many blows upon them, they threw them into prison, charging the jailer to keep them securely. 
Having received such a command, he threw them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks <note>original: ξύλον (xylon) — literally "the wood," a heavy timber frame used to restrain and often torture prisoners by forcing their legs apart</note>. 
But toward midnight, Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God <gloss>original: θεόν (theon)</gloss>, and the other prisoners were listening to them. 
Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken;

<column-break/>

and immediately all the doors were opened and everyone's bonds were unfastened. 
When the jailer woke up and saw the doors of the prison opened, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped. 
But Paul cried out with a loud voice, saying, “Do no harm to yourself, for we are all here!” 
And having asked for lights, he rushed in and, trembling with fear, fell down before Paul and Silas. 
And leading them outside, he said, “Sirs <note>original: κύριοι (kyrioi) — the same word used for "lords" or "masters"</note>, what must I do to be saved?” 
And they said, “Believe in the Lord <gloss>original: κύριον (kyrion)</gloss> Jesus <gloss>original: ἰησοῦν (Iēsoun)</gloss> and you will be saved, you and your household.” 
And they spoke the word of the Lord <gloss>original: κυρίου (kyriou)</gloss> to him along with everyone in his house. 
And taking them in that hour of the night, he washed their wounds, and he was baptized at once, he and all his family. 
And bringing them up into his house, he set a table before them and rejoiced with his entire household, having believed in God <gloss>original: θεῷ (theō)</gloss>. 
When it was day, the magistrates sent the officers <term>rabdouchous — literally "rod-bearers" or lictors who carried out the magistrates' orders</term> saying, “Release those men.” 
And the jailer reported these words to Paul, saying, “The magistrates have sent word to release you; now therefore come out and go in peace.” 
But Paul said to them, “They beat us publicly without a trial <note>original: ἀκατακρίτους (akatakritous) — "uncondemned," referring to the violation of their rights to a fair hearing</note>, men who are Roman citizens, and threw us into prison; and now are they casting us out secretly? No indeed! Let them come themselves and lead us out.” 
And the officers reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Romans.

<margin>A</margin> Since these things are undeniable, it is necessary for you to remain calm and do nothing reckless.

<margin>I</margin> For you have brought these men here who are neither temple robbers nor blasphemers of our goddess. But if you seek anything further, it shall be settled in the legal assembly <term>Ennomos Ekklesia — a constitutionally recognized gathering of citizens, as opposed to this riotous mob</term>. For we are in danger of being charged with rioting concerning today’s events, since there is no cause for which we will be able to give an account for this commotion.” And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly.

### The Acts of the Apostles, Chapters xx – xxi

**Column 1**

<margin>></margin>From Miletus, he sent a message to Ephesus and summoned the elders <term>Presbyterous — the "elders" or senior leaders of the local Christian community</term> of the church. <margin>></margin>And now, look, being bound by the Spirit <term>Pneuma — the Holy Spirit</term>, I am going to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there, except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city, saying that bonds and afflictions await me. But I count my life of no value to myself, so that I may finish my race and the ministry <term>Diakonia — service or commission</term> that I received from the Lord Jesus: to testify to the good news of the grace of God.

<margin>></margin>And now, look, I know that none of you, among whom I went about preaching the kingdom, will see my face again.

<margin>></margin>Therefore, I testify to you this very day that I am clean from the blood of all; for I did not shrink from proclaiming to you the whole counsel of God. <column-break/>

## Paul Before the Council and the Plot Against His Life

**Column 1**

But when Paul perceived that one part were **Sadducees** <note>A Jewish sect that was often wealthy and priestly; they rejected the idea of the afterlife</note> and the other **Pharisees** <note>A sect known for strict observance of the Law and belief in the resurrection</note>, he cried out in the council: “Men and brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees! When it was day, the Jews formed a conspiracy and bound themselves under a curse, saying that they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul. **Β**ut wishing to know the reason why they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council. **Α**fter many years, I arrived to bring alms to my nation and offerings. In these, they found me purified in the temple, not with a crowd nor with an uproar.

# The Acts of the Apostles
## Paul Before Felix and Festus

**B**ut Felix, having a more accurate knowledge of **the Way** <note>original: "τῆς ὁδοῦ" (tēs hodou) — a common early term for the Christian movement</note>, adjourned their case, saying, "When Lysias the commander comes down, I will decide your affairs." He gave orders to the centurion that Paul should be kept in custody but should have some **liberty** <term>anesin — a relaxation of strict confinement, allowing for personal comforts</term>, and that none of his own people should be prevented from serving him or coming to him.

**A**fter some days, Felix arrived with Drusilla, his own wife, who was Jewish. He sent for Paul and heard him speak concerning faith in Christ Jesus. But as Paul was discussing righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come, Felix became afraid and answered, "For the present, go your way; when I find an opportunity, I will summon you." At the same time, he was hoping that money would be given to him by Paul; for this reason, he sent for him more frequently and conversed with him.

**W**hen two years had passed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. Wishing to grant a favor to the Jews, Felix left Paul in prison.

<margin>Chapter 25</margin> **F**estus, therefore, having arrived in the province, went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea after three days. The chief priests and the leading men of the Jews presented their case against Paul to him. They urged him, asking for a favor against Paul, that he might have him brought to Jerusalem—for they were preparing an ambush to kill him along the road. 

**H**owever, Festus answered that Paul was being kept in custody at Caesarea, and that he himself intended to go there shortly. "Therefore," he said, "let those among you who are powerful come down with me, and if there is anything wrong with the man, let them accuse him."

<column-break/>

**A**fter staying among them not more than eight or ten days, he went down to Caesarea. On the next day, he sat on the **judgment seat** <term>bēma — the official judicial bench of a Roman magistrate</term> and commanded Paul to be brought. When he arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many serious charges which they were not able to prove. 

**P**aul said in his defense, "I have committed no offense either against the law of the Jews, or against the temple, or against Caesar." 

**B**ut Festus, wishing to grant a favor to the Jews, answered Paul and said, "Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem to be tried there before me concerning these things?" 

**B**ut Paul said, "I am standing before Caesar’s judgment seat, where I ought to be tried. I have done no wrong to the Jews, as you yourself know very well. If, then, I am a wrongdoer and have committed anything worthy of death, I do not seek to escape death; but if there is nothing to the things of which these men accuse me, no one can hand me over to them. I **appeal to Caesar**!" <note>As a Roman citizen, Paul exercised his legal right to have his case heard by the Emperor in Rome.</note>

**T**hen Festus, after conferring with his council, answered, "You have appealed to Caesar; to Caesar you shall go."

**W**hen some days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice arrived at Caesarea to welcome Festus. Since they were staying there many days, Festus laid Paul's case before the king, saying, "There is a man left as a prisoner by Felix. When I was in Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews informed me about him, asking for a sentence of condemnation against him."

To them I answered that it is not a Roman custom to give up any man for favor before the accused meets the accusers face to face and receives a place of defense concerning the charge.

<margin>Ζ</margin>instead, they had certain questions against him about their own **religion** <note>original: "δεισιδαιμονίας" (deisidaimonias) — a word that can mean either "religion" or "superstition" depending on the speaker's tone</note> and about a certain **Jesus**, who had died, whom Paul claimed to be alive. 
<margin>Α</margin>t a loss as to the investigation of these things, I asked if he would be willing to go to Jerusalem and there be judged concerning these matters. But when Paul appealed to be kept for the decision of the **Emperor** <note>original: "Σεβαστοῦ" (Sebastou), the Greek equivalent of the Latin title 'Augustus'</note>, I ordered him to be kept until I could send him to Caesar. 
<margin>Α</margin>grippa said to Festus, "I myself was wishing to hear the man." "Tomorrow," he said, "you shall hear him." So on the next day, when Agrippa and Bernice came with great **pomp** <note>original: "φαντασίας" (phantasias) — referring to a grand, public procession with royal splendor</note> and entered the audience hall with the commanders and the prominent men of the city, and at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in. 
<margin>Κ</margin>and Festus said, "King Agrippa and all the men present with us, you see this man about whom the whole multitude of the Jews petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer. But I found that he had done nothing worthy of death; and since he himself appealed to the **Emperor** <note>original: "Σεβαστὸν" (Sebaston)</note>, I decided to send him."

<column-break/>

"Concerning him, I have nothing definite to write to my **Lord** <term>Lord — original: "ΚΩ" (Kyriō), an abbreviated form of 'Kyrios.' In this context, it refers to the Roman Emperor, likely Nero.</term>. Therefore, I have brought him before you, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that after the examination has taken place, I may have something to write. For it seems unreasonable to me, when sending a prisoner, not to signal the charges against him." <margin>26.</margin>
<margin>Α</margin>grippa said to Paul, "It is permitted for you to speak for yourself." Then Paul, stretching out his hand, began his defense: "Concerning all the things of which I am accused by the Jews, King Agrippa, I consider myself fortunate to be about to make my defense before you today; especially since you are an expert in all the customs and questions among the Jews. Therefore, I beg you to listen to me patiently. 
<margin>Τ</margin>he manner of my life from my youth, which was spent from the beginning among my own nation and in Jerusalem, is known by all the Jews. They have known me from of old, if they are willing to testify, that according to the strictest **sect** <note>original: "αἵρεσιν" (hairesin) — the origin of the word 'heresy', but here used to mean a specific school of thought</note> of our religion, I lived as a **Pharisee**. 
<margin>Κ</margin>and now I stand on trial because of the hope of the promise made by **God** <term>God — original: "ΘΥ" (Theou), abbreviated sacred name.</term> to our fathers, which our twelve tribes, worshiping earnestly night and day, hope to attain. Concerning this hope, I am accused by the Jews, O King! 
<margin>Τ</margin>hy is it judged unbelievable among you if **God** <term>God — original: "ΘϹ" (Theos), abbreviated sacred name.</term> raises the dead? 
<margin>Ε</margin>xactly so, I indeed thought to myself that I ought to do many things contrary to the name of **Jesus** <term>Jesus — original: "ΙΥ" (Iēsou), abbreviated sacred name.</term> of Nazareth; which I also did in Jerusalem; and many of the saints I shut up in prisons, having received authority from the chief priests. And when they were being put to death, I cast my vote against them. And in all the synagogues, I punished them often and tried to force them to blaspheme..."

<margin>—</margin>...to receive care. Crossing the open sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra in Lycia. There the centurion found an **Alexandrian ship** <note>These were large grain ships that traveled between Egypt and Rome</note> sailing for Italy and put us on board. For many days we sailed slowly, and with difficulty we arrived off Cnidus. Since the wind did not allow us to go further, we sailed under the lee of Crete off Salmone. Passing it with difficulty, we came to a certain place called **Fair Havens**, near which was the city of Lasaea. 

<margin>—</margin>Much time having passed and the voyage now being dangerous because **the Fast** <note>original: "νηστειαν" (nēsteian) — referring to Yom Kippur, the Jewish Day of Atonement, which occurred in late September or early October, marking the end of the safe sailing season</note> was already over, Paul advised them, saying, "Men, I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives." 

<margin>—</margin><insert>But</insert> the centurion was persuaded more by the pilot and the ship-owner than by what was said by Paul. Since the harbor was unsuitable for wintering, the majority decided to set sail from there, if somehow they could reach Phoenix to winter, a harbor of Crete facing both southwest and northwest. 

<margin>—</margin><insert>When</insert> a moderate south wind blew, thinking they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close inshore. <column-break/>

The ship was caught and could not face the wind, so we gave way and were driven along. <margin>—</margin>Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda, we were barely able to get control of the ship's boat <note>The "boat" was a smaller skiff usually towed behind the ship</note>. Fearing they would run aground on the **Syrtis** <note>original: "συρτιν" (syrtin) — dangerous sandbars and shallows off the coast of North Africa</note>, they lowered the gear and so were driven along. <margin>—</margin>Because we were violently storm-tossed, the next day they began to throw the cargo overboard. And on the third day, with their own hands, they threw the ship's tackle overboard. 

<margin>—</margin>When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and no small storm pressed on us, all hope of our being saved was finally abandoned. Since they had been without food for a long time, Paul <insert>then</insert> stood up in their midst and said, "Men, you should have followed my advice not to sail from Crete and so have spared yourselves this injury and loss. Now I urge you to take heart, for there will be no loss of life among you, only of the ship. For this very night there stood by me an angel of the **God** <note>original: "θυ" (thy), abbreviation for "Theou" (God)</note> to whom I belong and whom I worship, saying, 'Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar; and behold, **God** <note>original: "θϲ" (ths), abbreviation for "Theos" (God)</note> has granted you all those who sail with you.' Therefore, take heart, men, for I believe **God** <note>original: "θω" (thō), abbreviation for "Theō" (God)</note> that it will be exactly as I have been told. But we must run aground on some island." 

When the fourteenth night had come, as we were being driven across the **Adriatic Sea** <note>In ancient geography, this term referred to a larger area of the central Mediterranean than it does today</note>, about midnight the sailors suspected that they were approaching some land. So they took soundings and found twenty **fathoms** <note>original: "οργυιας" (orgyias) — a measurement based on the span of outstretched arms, roughly 6 feet</note>; and after a short distance, they took soundings again and found fifteen fathoms.

Having willed it, he gave birth to us by the word of truth, so that we might be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures. Know this, my beloved brothers: let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God <note>original: "ΘΥ" (Theou), a Nomina Sacra for God.</note>.

<margin>Δ</margin> Therefore, putting away all filthiness and excess of wickedness, in <margin>Ϋ</margin> humility receive the implanted word which is able to save your souls.

<margin>Γ</margin> But be doers of the word and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves. For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man observing his natural face in a mirror; for he observed himself and has gone away, and immediately forgot what kind of person he was. But the one who looks into the perfect law, the law of liberty, and remains in it—not becoming a forgetful hearer but a doer of work—this man will be blessed in his doing. If anyone thinks he is religious, not bridling his tongue but deceiving his heart, this person’s religion is worthless. Religion that is pure and undefiled before God <note>original: "ΘΩ" (Theō), Nomina Sacra for God.</note> and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from the world.

<margin>β</margin> My brothers, do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ <note>original: "ΚΥ ΗΜΩΝ ΙΗ ΧΥ" (Kyriou hēmōn Iēsou Christou), Nomina Sacra for 'Our Lord Jesus Christ'.</note>, the Lord of glory, with partiality.

For if a man with gold rings and in fine clothing enters your assembly <note>original: "συναγωγην" (synagōgēn). While often meaning 'synagogue,' in this early Christian context it refers to the gathering or meeting of the believers.</note>, and a poor man in filthy clothing also enters, and you look with favor on the one wearing the fine clothing and say, "You sit here in a good place," and to the poor man you say, "You stand there," or "Sit under my footstool," have you not made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?

Listen, my beloved brothers: did not God <note>original: "ΘC" (Theos), Nomina Sacra for God.</note> choose the poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom which he promised to those who love him? But you have dishonored the poor man. Do not the rich oppress you, and do they not drag you into courts? Do they not blaspheme the honorable name by which you are called? If you indeed fulfill the royal law according to the Scripture, "You shall love your neighbor as yourself," you are doing well.

<margin>Ε</margin> But if you show partiality, you commit sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors. For whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become accountable for all of it. For he who said, "Do not commit adultery," also said, "Do not murder." If you do not commit adultery but do murder, you have become a transgressor of the law. So speak and so act as those who are to be judged by the law of liberty. For judgment is without mercy to the one who has shown no mercy. Mercy triumphs over judgment.

What use is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Is that faith able to save him?

GRACE TO YOU AND PEACE FROM **GOD** <note>original: "ΘY"</note> OUR FATHER AND THE **LORD JESUS CHRIST** <note>original: "KY IH YX"</note>. FIRST, I THANK MY **GOD** <note>original: "ΘΩ"—Theo</note> THROUGH **JESUS CHRIST** <note>original: "IH YX"</note> FOR ALL OF YOU, BECAUSE YOUR FAITH IS BEING PROCLAIMED IN THE WHOLE WORLD. FOR **GOD** <note>original: "ΘC"—Theos</note> IS MY WITNESS, WHOM I SERVE IN MY **SPIRIT** <note>original: "ΠNI"—Pneuma</note> IN THE GOSPEL OF HIS SON, HOW UNCEASINGLY I MAKE MENTION OF YOU ALWAYS IN MY PRAYERS, ASKING IF SOMEHOW NOW AT LAST I MAY SUCCEED BY THE WILL OF **GOD** <note>original: "ΘY"</note> IN COMING TO YOU. FOR I LONG TO SEE YOU, SO THAT I MAY IMPART SOME SPIRITUAL <note>original: "ΠNIKON"—pneumatikon</note> GIFT TO YOU TO STRENGTHEN YOU; THAT IS, THAT WE MAY BE MUTUALLY ENCOURAGED AMONG YOU BY EACH OTHER'S FAITH, BOTH YOURS AND MINE. 

AND I DO NOT WANT YOU TO BE UNAWARE, BROTHERS, THAT MANY TIMES I INTENDED TO COME TO YOU—BUT WAS PREVENTED UNTIL NOW—SO THAT I MIGHT HAVE SOME FRUIT AMONG YOU JUST AS ALSO AMONG THE REST OF THE NATIONS. TO BOTH GREEKS AND BARBARIANS <term>barbarians: "barbarois"—a term used to describe those who did not speak Greek or participate in Hellenistic culture</term>, BOTH TO THE WISE AND THE FOOLISH, I AM A DEBTOR. FOR HIS INVISIBLE ATTRIBUTES FROM THE CREATION OF THE WORLD ARE CLEARLY SEEN, BEING UNDERSTOOD THROUGH THE THINGS THAT ARE MADE—BOTH HIS ETERNAL POWER AND DIVINITY—SO THAT THEY ARE WITHOUT EXCUSE. 

BECAUSE, ALTHOUGH THEY KNEW **GOD** <note>original: "ΘN"—Theon</note>, THEY DID NOT GLORIFY HIM AS **GOD** <note>original: "ΘN"</note> OR GIVE THANKS, BUT THEY BECAME FUTILE IN THEIR THINKING AND THEIR SENSELESS HEART WAS DARKENED. THEREFORE **GOD** <note>original: "ΘC"</note> GAVE THEM UP IN THE LUSTS OF THEIR HEARTS TO IMPURITY, <margin>in them</margin> <note>original: "EN AY"—en autois; a marginal correction or emphasis for the following phrase</note> TO THE DISHONORING OF THEIR BODIES AMONG THEMSELVES, WHO EXCHANGED THE TRUTH OF **GOD** <note>original: "ΘY"</note> FOR A LIE AND WORSHIPED AND SERVED THE CREATURE RATHER THAN THE CREATOR, WHO IS BLESSED FOREVER, AMEN. FOR THIS REASON **GOD** <note>original: "ΘC"</note> GAVE THEM UP TO PASSIONS OF DISHONOR; FOR EVEN THEIR FEMALES EXCHANGED THE NATURAL USE FOR THAT WHICH IS AGAINST NATURE. LIKEWISE ALSO THE MALES, LEAVING THE NATURAL USE OF THE FEMALE, WERE CONSUMED IN THEIR DESIRE FOR ONE ANOTHER, MALES WITH MALES COMMITTING SHAMELESSNESS, AND RECEIVING IN THEMSELVES THE PENALTY WHICH WAS NECESSARY FOR THEIR ERROR.

->Rom. i. 28—ii. 26<-

And since they did not see fit to acknowledge **GOD** <note>original: "ΘN"—Theon; a "Nomina Sacra" abbreviation for God</note>, **GOD** <note>original: "ΘC"—Theos</note> gave them up to a debased mind to do what is not proper. They were filled with all unrighteousness, wickedness, evil, and greed; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, and malice. They are gossips, slanderers, **GOD**-haters, insolent, haughty, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, foolish, faithless, heartless, and ruthless. Although they know the righteous decree of **GOD** <note>original: "ΘY"—Theou</note>—that those who practice such things are deserving of death—they not only do them but also give approval to those who practice them.

<margin>— 2</margin> Therefore you are without excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things. We know that the judgment of **GOD** <note>original: "ΘY"</note> is according to truth against those who practice such things. Do you suppose, O man—you who judge those who practice such things and yet do them yourself—that you will escape the judgment of **GOD** <note>original: "ΘY"</note>? Or do you despise the wealth of His kindness and forbearance and patience, unaware that **GOD'S** <note>original: "ΘY"</note> kindness leads you to repentance? But because of your hard and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath when **GOD'S** <note>original: "ΘY"</note> righteous judgment will be revealed. He will repay each one according to his works: to those who by patience in good work seek for glory and honor and immortality, He will give eternal life;

<margin>—</margin> but for those who are self-seeking and do not obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, there will be wrath and fury. There will be affliction and distress for every human soul who does evil, the Jew first and also the Greek, but glory and honor and peace for every

<column-break/>

one who does good, the Jew first and also the Greek. For there is no partiality with **GOD** <note>original: "ΘΩ"—Theo</note>. For all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law. For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before **GOD** <note>original: "ΘΩ"</note>, but the doers of the law who will be justified. For when Gentiles, who do not have the law, by nature do what the law requires, they are a law to themselves, even though they do not have the law. They show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness, and their conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse them on 그 day when **GOD** <note>original: "ΘC"</note> judges the secrets of men according to my gospel through **JESUS CHRIST** <note>original: "IΥ ΧΥ"—Iesou Christou</note>.

<margin>— ></margin> But if you call yourself a Jew and rely on the law and boast in **GOD** <note>original: "ΘΩ"</note> and know His will and approve what is excellent, because you are instructed from the law; and if you are sure that you yourself are a guide to the blind, a light to those who are in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of children, having in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth—you then who teach others, do you not teach yourself? While you preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples? You who boast in the law dishonor **GOD** <note>original: "ΘN"</note> by breaking the law. For, as it is written, “The name of **GOD** <note>original: "ΘY"</note> is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.”

<margin>— ></margin> For circumcision indeed is of value if you obey the law, but if you break the law, your circumcision becomes uncircumcision. So, if a man who is uncircumcised keeps the righteous requirements of the law...

<meta>This page continues the text of Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, moving from the end of chapter 2 into the central theological arguments of chapter 3. The previous page discussed the inward nature of true faith and began the critique of those who rely solely on the outward sign of circumcision.
