--- Page 1572 ---
<meta>This page marks the beginning of the First Epistle of Clement, an influential letter from the late 1st century AD. In the Codex Alexandrinus, this letter follows the Book of Revelation, as it was highly revered and often read in early Christian assemblies, though it was eventually not included in the official New Testament canon. It serves as a bridge between the apostolic era and the early Church Fathers.</meta>

### THE FIRST EPISTLE OF CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS

THE CHURCH OF GOD <term>which sojourns</term> <note>original: ΠΑΡΟΙΚΟΥCΑ (paroikousa); this term describes Christians as "resident aliens" or pilgrims whose true home is in heaven.</note> at **Rome** to THE CHURCH OF GOD which sojourns at **Corinth**, to those who are called and sanctified by the will of **God** through our Lord **Jesus Christ**. **Grace** to you and **peace** from **Almighty** <note>original: ΠΑΝΤΟΚΡΑΤΟΡΟC (pantokratōros); the All-Ruling one.</note> God through Jesus Christ be multiplied. Because of the sudden and repeated **calamities** and reverses <note>Likely referring to the persecutions of Christians in Rome under Emperor Domitian around 95-96 AD.</note> which have befallen us, we consider that we have been somewhat slow in turning our attention to the matters in dispute among you, beloved; and especially that detestable and unholy **sedition** <note>original: CΤΑCΕΩC (staseōs); a technical term for a factional uprising or political rebellion.</note>, so alien and strange to the elect of God, which a few headstrong and self-willed persons have kindled to such a pitch of madness that your name, once so revered and renowned and lovely in the sight of all men, has been greatly reviled. For who that had stayed among you did not approve your all-virtuous and steadfast **faith**? Who did not admire your sober and gentle **piety** in Christ? Who did not proclaim the magnificent character of your **hospitality**? And who did not congratulate you on your perfect and sound **knowledge**? For you did all things without respect of persons, and you walked according to the ordinances of God, submitting yourselves to your **leaders** <note>original: ΗΓΟΥΜΕΝΟΙC (hēgoumenois); those in positions of authority.</note> and rendering the proper honor to the **elders** <note>original: ΠΡΕCΒΥΤΕΡΟΙC (presbyterois); the senior leaders of the church, from which the word "priest" eventually derived.</note> among you. You enjoined the young to think moderate and honorable thoughts; and the women you charged to perform all their duties with a blameless, honorable, and pure conscience, truly loving their own husbands; and you taught them to remain within the rule of

<column-break/>

<unclear>subjection, and to manage their households with dignity, being entirely discreet. Moreover, you were all humble-minded and free from arrogance, yielding rather than demanding submission, more glad to give than to receive, and content with the provisions of God. And giving heed to His words, you laid them up diligently in your hearts, and His sufferings were before your eyes. Thus a profound and rich peace was given to all, and an insatiable desire for doing good,</unclear> and an abundant outpouring of the **Holy Spirit** fell upon everyone. Being full of holy counsel, with excellent zeal and a pious confidence, you stretched out your hands to **Almighty God**, entreating Him to be merciful if you had committed any sin unwillingly. You struggled day and night for the entire **brotherhood**, so that the number of His elect might be saved through mercy and a good conscience. You were sincere and simple, and free from malice toward one another. Every **sedition** and every **schism** <note>original: CΧΙCΜΑ (schisma); a tear or division within the community.</note> was abominable to you. You mourned over the transgressions of your neighbors; you judged their shortcomings to be your own. You were without regret in every good work, ready for every good deed. Adorned with a most virtuous and honorable **way of life** <note>original: ΠΟΛΙΤΕΙΑ (politeia); refers to one's conduct as a citizen of a community.</note>, you performed all things in the fear of Him; the commandments and the ordinances of the Lord were written on the tablets of your **heart**. All glory and prominence was given to you.

<summary>Clement begins his letter by apologizing for a delay caused by persecutions in Rome and then praises the Corinthian church for their former reputation for peace, hospitality, and order before their current internal conflict began.</summary>
<keywords>Clement of Rome, Corinthians, sedition, hospitality, elders, Holy Spirit, persecution, church order</keywords>

<margin>35</margin> Let us consider the strange sign that happens in the eastern lands, that is, in the regions near Arabia. There is a bird which is called the Phoenix <note>The Phoenix was a popular symbol in early Christian writing, used to illustrate the concept of resurrection through a "natural" miracle.</note>. This bird is the only one of its kind and lives for five hundred years. When it approaches the time of its dissolution and death, it makes a nest for itself out of frankincense, myrrh, and other spices, into which, when its time is fulfilled, it enters and dies. But as its flesh decays, a certain worm is born, which is nourished by the moisture of the dead creature and grows feathers. Then, when it has become strong, it takes up that nest containing the bones of its ancestor and carries them from the land of Arabia all the way to Egypt, to the city called Heliopolis <note>original: ΗΛΙΟΥΠΟΛΙΝ (Hēlioupolin), meaning "City of the Sun." An ancient Egyptian center of worship.</note>. There, in the sight of everyone, it flies to the altar of the Sun and places them there, and then starts on its return journey. The priests then examine the records of the dates and find that it has come precisely when the five-hundredth year is completed.

<margin>36</margin> Do we then think it a great and wonderful thing if the Creator of all things shall bring about the resurrection of those who have served him holily in the assurance of a good faith, when even through a bird he shows us the greatness of his promise? For he says somewhere...

Referring to the underworld or the realm of the dead.</note>, there you are.” Where then shall one go, or where shall one flee from him who encompasses all things?

...Let us therefore flee from those things and approach our merciful and compassionate Father, who has made us a portion of His choice for Himself.

And in another place He says: "Behold, the Lord takes for Himself a nation from the midst of nations, just as a man takes the first-fruits of his threshing floor; and from that nation shall come forth the Holy of Holies." <note>This appears to be a free adaptation or a combination of various scriptural passages, common in early Christian writing.</note> 

<margin>320</margin>Since we are then a portion of the Holy One, let us do all things that belong to holiness. Let us flee from slanders, foul and impure embraces, drunkenness and rioting <note>original: NΕΩΤΕΡΙΣΜΟΥΣ (neōterismous), literally "innovations," but here referring to revolutionary or rebellious behavior.</note>, detestable lusts, abominable adultery, and hateful pride. 

<margin>330</margin>"For God," He says, "opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble." <note>A common early Christian citation of Proverbs 3:34.</note> Let us therefore join ourselves to those to whom grace has been given by God. Let us clothe ourselves in harmony, being humble-minded and self-controlled, keeping ourselves far from all whispering and slander, being justified by works and not by words. 

For He says: "Shall he who speaks much also hear in return? Or does the one who is ready with his tongue think he is righteous? Blessed is the one born of woman who is short-lived. Do not be a man of many words." <note>Clement is quoting the book of Job 11:2-3 from the Septuagint version.</note> 

Let our praise be in God, and not from ourselves; for God hates those who praise themselves. Let the testimony of our good deeds 

<margin>340</margin>be given by others, just as it was given to our righteous fathers. Boldness, arrogance, and daring belong to those cursed by God; but gentleness, humility, and meekness belong to those blessed by God.

Let us therefore cling to His blessing, and let us see what the paths of blessing are. Let us unroll the records of the things that happened from the beginning. For what reason was our father Abraham blessed? Was it not because he wrought righteousness and truth through faith? 

<column-break/>

Isaac, with confidence, knowing the future, was led gladly to the sacrifice. 

Jacob, with humility, departed from his own land because of his brother <note>Referring to his flight from Esau to Laban.</note>, and went to Laban and served him; 

<margin>320</margin>and there was given to him the twelve scepters <note>term: "scepters" (ΣΚΗΠΤΡΟΙ) here refers to the twelve tribes of Israel, symbolizing authority and lineage.</note> of Israel. If anyone examines these things individually and in order, he will recognize the greatness of the gifts given by Him. For from Jacob come all the priests and Levites who minister at the altar of God. 

<margin>330</margin>From him comes the Lord Jesus according to the flesh. From him come kings and rulers through the line of Judah. And his other "scepters" are in no small glory, since God promised: "Your seed shall be as the stars of heaven." 

All of them, therefore, were glorified and magnified, not through themselves or their own works, or the righteous acting which they performed, 

<margin>340</margin>but through His will. And so we, having been called through His will in Christ Jesus, are not justified through ourselves or through our own wisdom or understanding or piety, or the works which we have wrought in holiness of heart, but through faith, by which the Almighty God has justified all who have been from the beginning of time. 

<margin>350</margin>To Him be the glory forever and ever. Amen. 

What then shall we do, brothers? Shall we be idle in doing good and desert the practice of love? May the Master never allow this to happen to us! 

Rather, let us hasten with energy and readiness of mind to perform every good work. 

For the Creator and Master of all things Himself rejoices in His works. 

For by His supremely great power He established the heavens, and by His incomprehensible understanding He arranged them...

<meta>This page continues from the First Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians. While the previous page focused on the need for humility and gratitude for God's gifts, this section (Chapters 42–45) shifts to the formal organization of the church. Clement is defending the authority of the leaders (bishops and deacons) whom the Corinthians have apparently attempted to remove from office. He argues that this order was established by the Apostles, who anticipated such disputes.</meta>

...they came to pass with both of them <note>referring to Christ being sent by God and the Apostles by Christ</note> by the will of God. Having therefore received their instructions and being fully assured through the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, and confirmed in the word of God with the fullness of the Holy Spirit, they went forth preaching the good news that the kingdom of God was about to come.

<margin>p. 255</margin> Preaching then through countries and cities, they appointed their first-fruits—having tested them by the Spirit—to be bishops <term>episkopous: literally 'overseers' or guardians of the community</term> and deacons <term>diakonous: assistants or ministers</term> of those who were to believe. And this was no new thing; for indeed, for many ages it had been written concerning bishops and deacons. For thus says the Scripture in a certain place: "I will appoint their bishops in righteousness and their deacons in faith." <note>A loose adaptation of Isaiah 60:17</note>

And what wonder is it if those to whom such a work was entrusted by God in Christ appointed the aforesaid persons? For even the blessed Moses, a "faithful servant in all his house," recorded in the sacred books all the things commanded him; and the rest of the prophets followed him, bearing witness together to the laws ordained by him. For when jealousy arose concerning the priesthood, and the tribes were quarreling as to which of them should be adorned with that glorious name, he commanded the twelve tribal leaders to bring him rods, with the name of each tribe inscribed on each. And taking them, he bound and sealed them with the rings of the tribal leaders and laid them away in the tabernacle of testimony upon the table of God. And having closed the tabernacle, he sealed the doors just as he had the rods, and said to them: "Brothers, whichever rod shall bud, this one has God chosen to serve as priest and minister to Him." When morning came, he called together all Israel, the six hundred

<column-break/>

thousand men, and showed the seals to the tribal leaders; and he opened the tabernacle of testimony and brought out the rods; and the rod of Aaron was found not only to have budded but also to be bearing the fruit of almonds. What do you think, beloved? Did Moses not know beforehand that this would happen? He certainly knew it; but so that no disorder <term>akatastasia: instability, confusion, or rebellion</term> should arise in Israel, he acted in this way so that the name of the true and only God might be glorified; to whom be glory forever and ever, amen.

And our apostles knew through our Lord Jesus Christ that there would be strife over the title of oversight <term>episkopēs: the office of the bishop</term>. For this reason, therefore, having received perfect foreknowledge, they appointed the aforesaid persons and afterwards gave a permanent rule <term>epinome: a legal provision or instruction for succession</term> so that, if these should fall asleep, other approved men should succeed to their ministry. 

Those, therefore, who were appointed by them or afterwards by other eminent men with the consent of the whole church, and who have ministered blamelessly to the flock of Christ with humility, quietly and without self-interest, and who have been well-spoken of for a long time by all—these men we do not consider to be justly removed from their ministry. For it will be no small sin for us if we eject from the oversight those who have offered the gifts blamelessly and holily.

Blessed are those elders <term>presbyteroi: senior leaders</term> who have gone before, who had a fruitful and perfect departure <note>original: analusin, referring to death as a release or dissolution</note>; for they do not fear that anyone should remove them from the place established for them. For we see that you have removed some who were living honorably from the ministry which had been blamelessly respected by them. You are contentious, brothers, and zealous for things that pertain to salvation.

But now, consider who they are that have **perverted** you, and have diminished the dignity of your renowned **brotherly love**. It is **shameful**, brothers, extremely shameful, and unworthy of your conduct in Christ, to hear that the very steadfast and **ancient Church of the Corinthians** is rebelling against its **elders** <term>presbyterous: the senior leaders or priests of the community</term> because of one or two persons. And this report has not only reached us, but also those who are **differently inclined** <note>meaning non-Christians or outsiders</note> from us, so that **blasphemies** are brought upon the name of the Lord because of your **folly**, and you are creating danger for yourselves. Let us therefore remove this with all speed, and let us fall down before the **Master**...

<meta>This page transitions from the final benediction and closing remarks of the First Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians into the opening of the so-called Second Epistle of Clement. The previous page concluded with an exhortation to discipline and obedience; here, the letter ends with a prayer for the church and the dispatch of messengers. The second column begins a new work, which modern scholars identify not as a letter, but as an early Christian sermon—the oldest surviving one outside the New Testament.</meta>

<warning>The left side of the page is significantly darkened and slightly faded, particularly impacting the first few characters of each line in the left column.</warning>

<unclear>...</unclear> May **God** <note>original: "ΘΝ" (Theon) — a contracted sacred name.</note>, the all-seeing Master of spirits and **Lord** <note>original: "ΚΥΡΙΟΝ" (Kyrion)</note> of all flesh, who chose the **Lord Jesus Christ** <note>original: "ΚΝ ΙΗΝ ΧΡΝ" (Kyriou Iesoun Christon)</note> and us through Him to be a **chosen people** <term>laon periousion: a "treasured possession," a phrase used in the Greek Old Testament to describe Israel, here applied to the Church.</term>, grant to every soul that calls upon His magnificent and holy Name: faith, fear, peace, patience, long-suffering, self-control, purity, and sobriety, so that they may be well-pleasing to His Name through our High Priest and Guardian, **Jesus Christ** <note>original: "ΙΗΣΟΥ ΧΡΙΣΤΟΥ"</note>, through whom be to Him glory and majesty, might and honor, both now and for ever and ever. Amen.

Now, as for those sent from us, Claudius Ephebus and Valerius Bito, together with Fortunatus, send them back to us in peace with joy and with speed, so that they may more quickly report the peace and harmony we have prayed for and desired, and that we too may more quickly rejoice in your good order.

The grace of our **Lord Jesus Christ** <note>original: "ΚΥ ΙΗ ΧΡ"</note> be with you and with all everywhere who have been called by **God** <note>original: "ΘΕΟΥ"</note> and through Him, to whom be glory, honor, might and majesty, and an eternal throne, from everlasting to everlasting. Amen.

<margin>3</margin> Brothers, we ought to think of **Jesus Christ** <note>original: "ΙΗΣΟΥ ΧΡΙΣΤΟΥ"</note> as of **God** <note>original: "ΘΕΟΥ"</note>, as of the Judge of the living and the dead. And we ought not to think meanly of our salvation. For when we think meanly of Him, we also expect to receive but little. And those who listen as if to small things are doing wrong. And we ourselves, [consider] from where we were called, by whom, and to what place, and how many things **Jesus Christ** <note>original: "ΙΗΣΟΥΣ ΧΡΙΣΤΟΣ"</note> endured to suffer for our sake.

What recompense, then, shall we give to Him? Or what fruit worthy of what He has given us? How many holy things do we owe Him! For He has given us the light. He has addressed us as a Father addresses sons. He saved us when we were perishing. What praise, then, shall we give Him, or what payment in return for what we have received? We were blinded in our understanding, worshiping stones and wood, and gold and silver and bronze—the works of men. Indeed, our whole life was nothing but death.

While we were thus wrapped in darkness and our vision was filled with such a mist, we recovered our sight. By His will, we have laid aside the cloud that enveloped us. For He had mercy on us, and in His compassion He saved us, having seen in us much wandering and destruction, and that we had no hope of salvation except that which comes from Him. For He called us when we were nothing, and He willed that from "not being," we should "be." 

"Rejoice, O barren woman who does not bear; break forth and shout, you who are not in labor; for the children of the desolate are more than those of her who has a husband." <note>A quotation from Isaiah 54:1, also cited in Galatians 4:27.</note> When He said, "Rejoice, O barren woman who does not bear," He spoke of us; for our Church was barren before children were given to her. And when He said, "Shout, you who are not in labor," He means this: that we should offer up our prayers simply to **God** <note>original: "ΘΕΟΝ"</note>, not becoming weary like women in labor...

<meta>This page continues the transition from the end of the First Epistle of Clement into the document known as the "Second Epistle of Clement." Despite its name, scholars identify this text as a very early Christian sermon or homily—perhaps the oldest surviving example outside of the New Testament—rather than a letter. The speaker is currently interpreting scripture to show how the "desolate" people (the Gentiles) have become more numerous than the "married" people (the Jewish nation).</meta>

<warning>The text on the far left edge of column one is faded and worn, with some characters partially obscured by the gutter or aging of the vellum.</warning>

For he said: "**The children of the desolate are many more than she who has a husband**" <note>This is a quotation from the prophet Isaiah (54:1), also cited by the Apostle Paul in Galatians 4:27.</note>. This was said because our people seemed to be **desolate** <term>eremos: literally a wilderness or desert; here meaning abandoned or without a relationship with the Divine.</term> and away from **God** <note>original: "ΘΥ" (Theou) — a contracted sacred name.</note>. But now, having believed, we have become more numerous than those who seemed to possess **God** <note>original: "ΘΝ" (Theon)</note>.

And another Scripture says: "**I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners.**" <note>A reference to the words of Jesus found in the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, and Luke.</note> This means that it is necessary to save those who are perishing. For it is a great and wonderful thing not to give support to things that are standing firm, but to things that are falling. So also **Christ** <note>original: "ΧΣ" (Christos)</note> willed to save the things that were perishing, and He saved many, having come and called us who were already perishing.

Seeing then that He has shown us such great mercy—firstly, that we who are living do not sacrifice to dead gods, nor do we worship them, but through Him we have come to know the **Father** <note>original: "ΠΡΣ" (Patros)</note> of truth. What then is the true knowledge toward Him, except not to deny the one through whom we have known Him? For He Himself says: "**Whoever confesses me before men, I will confess him before my Father.**" <note>Refers to Matthew 10:32.</note>

This, then, is our reward, if we confess the one through whom we were saved. But in what way do we confess Him? By doing what He says, and not disregarding His commandments; and by honoring Him not only with our lips, but with all our heart and all our mind. For He also says in **Isaiah**: "**This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.**" <note>original: quoting Isaiah 29:13.</note>

Let us not, therefore, merely call Him **Lord** <note>original: "ΚΝ" (Kyrion)</note>, for this will not save us. For He says: "**Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will be saved, but the one who does righteousness.**" <note>Refers to Matthew 7:21.</note> So then, brothers, let us confess Him in our works: by loving one another, by not committing adultery, nor speaking against one another, nor being envious, but by being self-controlled, merciful, and good. We ought to

<column-break/>

suffer with one another, and not be greedy. In these works let us confess Him, and not in the opposites. And we should not fear **men** <note>original: "ΑΝΩΝ" (Anthropon)</note> but rather **God** <note>original: "ΘΝ" (Theon)</note>.

For this reason, if you do these things, the **Lord** <note>original: "ΚΣ" (Kyrios)</note> has said: "**Even if you were gathered with me in my very bosom, yet did not keep my commandments, I would cast you out and say to you: 'Depart from me, I know not where you are from, you workers of lawlessness.'**" <note>An "Agraphon" or "unwritten saying"—a quote attributed to Jesus that is not found in the four standard Gospels.</note>

Therefore, brothers, let us leave behind our temporary stay in this world and do the will of Him who called us; and let us not be afraid to depart out of this world. For the **Lord** <note>original: "ΚΣ" (Kyrios)</note> says: "**You shall be as lambs in the midst of wolves.**" But **Peter** answered and said to Him: "**What if the wolves should tear the lambs?**" **Jesus** <note>original: "ΙΣ" (Iesous)</note> said to **Peter**: "**Let the lambs not fear the wolves after they are dead; and as for you, do not fear those who kill you and can do nothing more to you; but fear Him who, after you are dead, has authority over soul and body to cast them into the Gehenna of fire.**" <note>This unique dialogue between Peter and Jesus is not found in the New Testament and likely comes from an early apocryphal source like the Gospel of the Egyptians.</note>

And know, brothers, that our stay in this world of the flesh is small and lasts but a short time, but the promise of **Christ** <note>original: "ΧΥ" (Christou)</note> is great and wonderful: the rest of the coming Kingdom and of eternal life.

What then must we do to obtain these things, except to conduct ourselves holily and justly, and to regard these worldly things as foreign to us, and not to desire them? For in desiring to possess these things, we fall away from the righteous path. For the **Lord** <note>original: "ΚΣ" (Kyrios)</note> says: "**No servant can serve two masters.**" <note>Refers to Luke 16:13.</note> If we desire to serve both **God** and wealth...

--- Page 1592 ---
<meta>This page continues the text of the "Second Epistle of Clement," which began on the previous page with an exhortation to recognize the mercy of God. The author is now moving from the call of the Gentiles to the practical necessity of choosing between the temporary pleasures of this world and the eternal rewards of the next.</meta>

...they say; and another thing: "it is not profitable for us <note>original: "αϲυμφερον" (asympheron) — disadvantageous or useless.</note> if a man should gain the whole world but lose his soul." This age and the age to come are two enemies. This one [this age] speaks of adultery, corruption, love of money, and deceit; but that one [the future age] bids farewell to these things. We must therefore think that it is better to hate the things here, because they are small, short-lived, and perishable; but to love those things—the good and imperishable things.

**F**or if we do the will of **Christ** <note>original: "χυ" (Christou)</note>, we shall find rest; but if not, nothing shall rescue us from eternal punishment if we disobey His commandments.

**A**nd the Scripture also says in Ezekiel, that "even if Noah and Daniel and Job should rise up, they shall not rescue their children in the captivity." <note>A reference to Ezekiel 14:14–20, emphasizing individual responsibility for sin.</note>

**I**f even such righteous men as these cannot, by their own righteousness, rescue their children, with what confidence shall we enter the kingdom of **God** <note>original: "θυ" (Theou)</note> if we do not keep our baptism pure and undefiled? Or who shall be our advocate <term>parakletos: an intercessor or legal defender; the same word used for the Holy Spirit in the Gospel of John.</term> if we are not found having holy and righteous works?

**S**o then, my brothers, let us strive, knowing that the contest is at hand. We see that many sail to compete in perishable contests, but not all are crowned—only those who have labored much and competed well.

**L**et us therefore strive so that we all may be crowned.

**L**et us run the straight road, the incorruptible contest, and let many of us sail to it and strive so that we may be crowned. And even if we cannot all be crowned, let us at least get near 

<column-break/>

to the crown.

We ought to know that he who competes in a perishable contest, if he is found corrupting the rules <note>original: "ευταξιαν" (eutaxian) — literally "good order" or the disciplined regulations of the games.</note>, is flogged, removed, and thrown out of the stadium.

**W**hat do you think? What shall he suffer who corrupts the contest of incorruptibility? For of those who have not kept the **seal** <term>sphragis: a common early Christian term for baptism, viewed as a "seal" of ownership by God that must be kept intact.</term>, he says: "Their worm shall not die and their fire shall not be quenched, and they shall be a spectacle to all flesh." <note>Quoting Isaiah 66:24; also famously quoted in the Gospel of Mark regarding the afterlife.</note>

**W**hile we are on earth, then, let us repent. For we are clay in the hand of the craftsman.

**I**n the same way that a potter, if he makes a vessel and it is twisted or broken in his hands, reshapes it again; but if he has already cast it into the furnace of fire, he can no longer help it. So also we, while we are in this world, let us repent with our whole heart for the evil things we have done in the flesh, so that we may be saved by the **Lord** <note>original: "κυ" (Kyriou)</note> while we still have time for repentance. For after we have departed from the world, we are no longer able to confess or repent there. Therefore, brothers, by doing the will of the **Father** <note>original: "πρϲ" (Patros)</note>, keeping the flesh pure, and guarding the commandments of the **Lord**, we shall receive eternal life.

**F**or the **Lord** <note>original: "κϲ" (Kyrios)</note> says in the Gospel: "If you have not kept that which is small, who will give you that which is great? For I say to you, he who is faithful in very little is also faithful in much." <note>This is a variation of the saying found in Luke 16:10-12.</note> This, then, is what He means: keep the flesh pure and the **seal** unspotted, so that we may receive eternal life. And let none of you say that this flesh is not judged or does not rise again. Consider this: in what state were you saved? In what state did you recover your sight, if not while you were in this flesh? We must therefore guard the flesh as a temple of **God**. In the same way...

<summary>The author urges the audience to reject the worldly "enemies" of adultery and greed in favor of the "straight road" of Christ. Using the metaphor of an athletic contest and a potter's clay, he emphasizes that repentance is only possible during this life and that the body must be kept pure as a temple of God.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Second Epistle of Clement" (an early Christian sermon likely written in the mid-2nd century). The previous page concluded with a warning that our righteous ancestors cannot save us if we are found lacking in holy works. This section focuses on the "resurrection of the flesh" and the necessity of living a virtuous life to inherit the Kingdom of God.</meta>

...being in the flesh, you were called; so also in the flesh you shall come <note>The author is emphasizing the physical resurrection, a major point of debate in early Christianity.</note>. Since **God** <note>original: "ΘC" (Theos)</note>, who saved us, being first Spirit <note>original: "ΠΝΑ" (Pneuma)</note> became flesh and thus called us, so also we shall receive our reward in this flesh.

**L**et none of you say that this flesh is not judged nor does it rise again. Understand this: in what state were you saved? In what state did you recover your sight, if not while you were in this flesh? We must, therefore, guard the flesh as the temple of **God**. For just as you were called in the flesh, so shall you come in the flesh. If **Christ** <note>original: "XC" (Christos)</note>, the Lord who saved us, being first Spirit, became flesh and thus called us, so also we shall receive our reward in this flesh.

**L**et us therefore love one another, that we may all come into the kingdom of **God**. While we have time to be healed, let us give ourselves to **God** the Healer, giving Him a reward. And what reward? Repentance from a sincere heart. For He is the Foreknower of all things and knows what is in our hearts. Let us therefore give Him praise, not with our mouths only, but from the heart, so that He may receive us as sons.

**F**or the **Lord** <note>original: "KC" (Kyrios)</note> also said: "My brothers are these who do the will of my **Father** <note>original: "ΠΡC" (Patros)</note>."

**T**herefore, my brothers, let us do the will of the **Father** who called us, that we may live; and let us rather pursue virtue, but let us abandon vice as the forerunner of our sins, and let us flee ungodliness, lest evils overtake us. For if we are zealous to do good, peace will pursue us. For this reason, it is not possible for a man to find [peace] who introduces human fears, preferring the enjoyment of the present rather than the promise of the future. For they are ignorant of how much torment the enjoyment of the present brings, and what delight the promise of the future holds. And if they alone did these things, it might be bearable; but now they continue teaching evil to innocent souls, not knowing that they will have a double judgment—both themselves and those who hear them.

**W**e, therefore, let us serve **God** with a pure heart, and we shall be righteous; but if we do not serve Him

<column-break/>

because we do not believe the promise of **God**, we shall be wretched. For the prophetic word also says: "Wretched are the double-minded <term>diphychoi: literally 'double-souled'; those who waver in faith or are indecisive between the world and God.</term> who doubt in their heart, who say, 'All these things we heard even in the days of our fathers, but we, though waiting day after day, have seen none of them.'"

**O** foolish ones! Compare yourselves to a tree. Take a vine: first it sheds its leaves, then a bud appears, after these a sour grape, and then the ripe cluster.

**S**o also my people has had instabilities and afflictions; but afterward it shall receive good things. Therefore, my brothers, let us not be double-minded, but let us endure in hope, so that we may also receive the reward. For He is faithful who promised to pay to each the recompense of his works. If, therefore, we have done righteousness before **God**, we shall enter into His kingdom and receive the promises "which ear has not heard nor eye seen, nor has it entered into the heart of man." <note>A paraphrase of 1 Corinthians 2:9, referencing Isaiah 64:4.</note>

**L**et us then wait for the kingdom of **God** from hour to hour in love and righteousness, since we do not know the day of **God’s** appearing. For the **Lord** Himself, when asked by someone when His kingdom would come, said: "When the two shall be one, and the outside as the inside, and the male with the female, neither male nor female." <note>This is an "agraphon," a saying attributed to Jesus not found in the canonical Gospels, but appearing in the apocryphal Gospel of Thomas and Gospel of the Egyptians.</note> Now "the two are one" when we speak the truth to each other, and in two bodies there is one soul without hypocrisy. And "the outside as the inside" means this: the "inside" signifies the soul, and the "outside" signifies the body. Therefore, just as your body is visible, let your soul also be evident in your good works. And "the male with the female, neither male nor female" means this... <unclear>that</unclear>

<summary>This page contains an early Christian exhortation emphasizing the physical resurrection of the body and the necessity of sincere repentance. It famously includes an "agraphon" (unrecorded saying) of Jesus regarding the arrival of the Kingdom of God when the internal and external selves are unified.</summary>
